beitrag.zahnfuellung-rausgefallen.bloeck.text: What should you do if a filling suddenly falls out? Why does this happen in the first place – and how urgently do you need to see a dentist? Many people first reach for temporary filling material or home remedies, but what actually helps and what doesn't? We explain how to respond correctly in an emergency, avoid risks, and what treatment makes sense afterwards.
In brief
A lost filling isn't always noticed straight away. In some cases, it goes unnoticed at first – especially when there's no pain. Typical signs include:
Your bite suddenly feels different from what you're used to.
You can feel a small dip or edge in the tooth with your tongue.
Food debris gets stuck more often in one particular spot.

Watch out for such changes. They're often the first sign that a filling is no longer fully intact. Many people mistake a lost filling for a broken tooth. However, while a missing filling usually leaves a fairly smooth surface, a broken tooth often has sharp edges, greater sensitivity, and a larger, more noticeable defect.
First aid: what to do now

If a filling has fallen out, one thing matters most: protecting the affected tooth in the short term and avoiding discomfort until dental treatment can take place. The dentists at KU64 have already treated many patients after losing a filling and know the typical situations from daily practice – from a temporary filling suddenly coming loose to a filling falling out while biting into an olive pit. They explain what matters now and how you can protect your tooth step by step in the short term.
1. Rinse your mouth gently
It's best to rinse your mouth with lukewarm water to remove any food debris. Important: please don't use hot water, as this can irritate the tooth further.
2. Keep the tooth clean
Be sure to keep gently cleaning the affected area. This helps prevent bacteria from settling in the open spot.
3. Try to take the pressure off the chewing surface

A lost filling is not an unusual problem and should be treated promptly, even if there is no pain at first. Short-term solutions such as temporary filling material or dental cement can protect the tooth for a while, but they are no substitute for proper treatment. What matters now is keeping the tooth clean, avoiding strain on it, and arranging a dental appointment as quickly as possible to prevent further damage such as decay or inflammation.
Try chewing on the other side. This helps avoid putting pressure on the sensitive tooth.
4. Use a temporary filling
For a short time, a temporary filling material can help protect the tooth – but please use it only as a stopgap.
5. Book an appointment
Even if it doesn't hurt straight away: book an appointment and have the tooth treated by your dentist as soon as possible. The earlier we can act, the better the chances of saving the tooth.
When the filling falls out: reach for dental putty first?

If a filling has come loose, dental putty or dental cement can help bridge the time until your dentist appointment in an emergency – especially on holiday, when dental care isn't immediately available. Both products are sold as temporary solutions in pharmacies, drugstores or online, and are ready to use straight away. They mould to the tooth and seal the hole for a short time, protecting the area from external irritation, pain and food debris. To use them, gently clean the tooth, rinse your mouth with lukewarm water and press a small amount carefully into the affected spot. Dental cement hardens a little firmer than dental putty, but it, too, only offers temporary help and does not replace a visit to the dentist.

Dental putty or dental cement from the drugstore can protect the tooth in the short term, but it does not replace an appointment with the dentist. We advise against using it for a long period, as bacteria can build up and inflammation can develop if the tooth isn't treated professionally.
Lost a filling? Get in touch with our dental team and book an appointment at KU64 quickly.
Emergency fix or risk? When you should steer clear of home remedies
One bite – and suddenly the filling won't hold

Countless tips circulate online on how to temporarily repair a lost filling yourself – from chewing gum to homemade pastes. But can simple home remedies really replace a lost filling in the tooth? Our short answer: not really. Much of it carries more risk than benefit for the tooth.

While dental putty and cement are specifically designed to temporarily cover the hole, improvised solutions often lack exactly this fit and stability. They don't hold reliably, come loose quickly or don't sit tightly enough.

Classic home remedies such as oils or pastes are particularly risky. They can even make the condition of the tooth worse. In our day-to-day practice, we've repeatedly seen such solutions put extra strain on the affected area or make later treatment more difficult.

It can happen now and then in everyday life: you bite into a hard piece of bread or brush your teeth, and suddenly you feel something foreign in your mouth. The filling has fallen out. What seems harmless at first quickly raises questions: Is this a dental emergency? Can I just wait and see? And how do I protect the tooth until I can get to the dentist?

How gentle rinses can help
You should always take a lost filling seriously – even without pain. The sooner we treat the tooth, the simpler and gentler the treatment can be.

Home remedies do not replace a filling that has come out, but gentle rinses can be helpful for care and relief. They help keep the affected area clean and a little more comfortable until your appointment at the dental practice. It's important to rinse gently only and avoid vigorous mouth movements. The following rinses can be used to help:
lukewarm salt water
bicarbonate of soda or baking powder dissolved in lukewarm water
chamomile tea
sage tea
marigold solution
antiseptic mouth rinses such as chlorhexidine
Home remedy tip for toothache

If a lost filling is causing pain, it can help to chew gently on a clove or apply a little clove oil to the affected area. Both have anti-inflammatory and antibacterial properties, and provide mild numbing and disinfection. This can ease discomfort for a short while.
Waiting is not a solution: what matters now

Some patients wait as long as there's no pain – that's understandable, but not ideal. Even without discomfort, the tooth is unprotected at this point. Our tip: have the area checked as soon as possible. This helps prevent unnoticed further damage.

If you're unsure how urgent the situation is, a quick self-check can help: pay attention to how the tooth currently feels. The checklist below can help you assess the situation and work out the next steps.
Checklist: Useful steps until your dental appointment

Some patients wait as long as there's no pain – that's understandable, but not ideal. Even without discomfort, the tooth is unprotected at this point. Our tip: have the area checked as soon as possible. This helps prevent unnoticed further damage.

If you're unsure how urgent the situation is, a quick self-check can help: pay attention to how the tooth currently feels. The checklist below can help you assess the situation and work out the next steps.

In fact, it's not unusual for a filling to come out. Materials can wear down over time, decay can develop underneath the filling, or heavy strain can cause it to come loose. People with older fillings are especially affected. What matters now is reacting the right way: an unprotected tooth is sensitive, vulnerable to bacteria, and can deteriorate quickly. The situation becomes particularly critical if pain occurs, an open area is noticeable, or the tooth reacts sensitively.
☐ You feel pain or a pulling sensation in the affected tooth. This can be a sign of irritation or inflammation. Act immediately and have the tooth examined at an appointment as soon as possible.
☐ Your tooth is sensitive to cold, sweet foods or pressure. The tooth is especially vulnerable at this point. Try to avoid these triggers as consistently as possible.
☐ You notice an open area or can feel a hole in the tooth with your tongue. The tooth is unprotected and vulnerable to bacteria. Try not to chew on this side.
☐ The tooth feels sharp-edged or is bothering you in daily life. There's a risk of injury inside the mouth. Protect the area and avoid additional pressure.
☐ You currently have no discomfort and are considering waiting. Even without pain, the tooth is unprotected. Please arrange an appointment soon regardless.

Does at least one of these statements apply to you? Then here's what matters now: have the tooth treated within the next one to two days. If you experience pain or signs of inflammation, please arrange an appointment immediately. Our dental practice team is happy to help with any questions.
Biting down firmly again: how your tooth regains its best form

If a filling has come out, your dentist will first take a closer look at the affected tooth. They will check how large the damage is and whether the tooth's nerve might be affected. Sharp edges are then smoothed and the area thoroughly cleaned, allowing for a stable and gentle restoration.

Smaller defects are closed in the same appointment with a tooth-coloured filling. For larger damage, long-lasting inlays or onlays are used. If your tooth nerve is also inflamed, a root canal treatment secures your tooth before your dentist places a new filling.
By the way: no filling lasts forever
Grinding your teeth at night? An underestimated risk for your fillings

If you hear a “crack” on your next bite and the filling is suddenly gone, it could simply be because it’s seen better days. Some fillings are many years old and have simply reached the end of their lifespan. Fillings are not a permanent solution forever. Even though materials keep improving, fillings are subject to natural wear, despite regular preventive care. Composite fillings usually last around six to eight years, amalgam fillings often seven to twelve years. High-quality restorations such as ceramic or gold inlays can last considerably longer – in some cases even 10 to 30 years – before they need to be replaced at the dental practice.
Less risk, more stability: 4 tips to protect your filling
Even though materials wear down over time, there is a lot you can do yourself to help your filling last as long as possible.
With good care, a little mindfulness in everyday life and regular check-ups, you can significantly extend the lifespan of your filling.

Chew hard foods with care
Foods such as nuts, seeds or hard bread crusts can put considerable strain on existing fillings. Also avoid using your teeth as a “tool”, for example to open packaging.

Avoid strong temperature changes
Switching sharply between very cold and very hot foods can put stress on the filling material. This increases the risk of fine cracks forming.

Brush your teeth thoroughly and regularly
Clean teeth and interdental spaces cleaned with floss help prevent decay under the filling – one of the most common reasons it loosens or falls out.

Attend regular check-ups
During check-ups and regular preventive care, small cracks or leaking spots can be spotted early, before they turn into bigger damage.

Protect your teeth if you grind at night
If you clench or grind your teeth, a custom-fitted splint can help significantly reduce the strain and take pressure off your fillings.
Not sure whether your filling is still stable?

Have our specialists at KU64 check your tooth now and receive an individual recommendation for the right treatment if your filling no longer sits securely or could fall out. This way, we can act in time before the hole gets bigger, the tooth suffers further damage and more extensive dental work such as implants or crowns becomes necessary later on. If you have any questions, please get in touch with our practice team and arrange an appointment.

Pressures of up to 480 kilograms per square centimetre can occur. Over time, this puts enormous strain even on stable fillings. Anyone who regularly grinds their teeth has a significantly higher risk of fillings loosening or falling out. A night guard protects your teeth. beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.anriss.text: If you wear dentures, you want to be sure they're clean, hygienic and well cared for. We explain what really matters: from the right daily routine to stubborn nicotine stains and the home remedy myths we keep coming across in the practice.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.0..text: If you wear dentures, you want to be sure they're clean, hygienic and well cared for. We explain what really matters: from the right daily routine to stubborn nicotine stains and the home remedy myths we keep coming across in the practice.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.10.text: If you suffer from persistent bad breath despite daily cleaning, a simple trick can help you check whether your dentures are the cause. Place the dentures in a sealed plastic bag for five minutes. If the bag smells when you open it, the odour isn't coming from your mouth or teeth, but from the dentures.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.11.text: Clean three times a day: your dentures will thank you

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.12.text: How often should dentures be cleaned? At least as often as you brush your teeth, is our answer. Rinse your dentures briefly under running water after every meal. In the evening, thorough cleaning with a brush and cleaning agent is essential.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.13.text: It's also worth doing a more intensive deep clean once a week to reach all the spots that are easily missed in everyday cleaning. A suitable set with a denture brush, cleaning gel and cleaning tablets is available in our prophylaxis shop.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.14.text: Five minutes before bed: how to clean your dentures step by step

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.15.text: Cleaning dentures sounds more involved than it actually is. Once you've got these four steps down, you'll do it in the evening almost without thinking, even after a long day when all you want is your bed.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.17.text: Cleaning dentures sounds more involved than it actually is. Once you've got these four steps down, you'll do it in the evening almost without thinking, even after a long day when all you want is your bed.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.19.text: Use a soft denture brush, not a regular toothbrush. Ordinary bristles are made for enamel, not for plastic. A denture brush is specially shaped to reach every angle and cleans much more gently. If you don't have one yet, you'll find one in our prophylaxis shop.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.2..text: Dentures need to be cleaned daily, but with the right products. Toothpaste, hot water and supposed home remedies such as vinegar or cola do more harm than good to dentures in the long run. Stubborn nicotine and limescale deposits can only be removed to a limited extent at home. Professional cleaning with ultrasound at the dentist's is the better choice here. Caring for your dentures properly not only improves hygiene but also significantly extends their lifespan.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.20.text: Brush the denture thoroughly on all sides: the outer and inner surfaces, the recesses, the base and every area where the denture touches the gums. Use a special denture cleaning gel or a few drops of pH-neutral washing-up liquid as a cleaning agent, but never toothpaste.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.22.text: Rinse the denture under lukewarm water and avoid hot water. Hot water slowly and imperceptibly warps the plastic, until one day the denture no longer fits properly.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.24.text: Place the cleaned denture in a glass of fresh water or a cleaning solution. Overnight, the plastic stays moist, the shape remains stable, and the denture is disinfected at the same time.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.25.text: Have questions? Book an appointment with our KU64 team.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.26.text: Tablets, gel, washing-up liquid: what belongs in the glass, and what doesn't?

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.27.text: Not every cleaning product that sounds effective is actually suitable for dentures. The market offers plenty – from cleaning tablets to antibacterial denture cleaning gel.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.29.text: Disinfecting, gentle, easy to use – our first recommendation for the daily routine

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.3..text: Cleaned daily and still not quite clean?

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.31.text: Specially developed for plastic, not abrasive – ideal for brushing

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.33.text: Grease-dissolving and gentle – a good stopgap when you've run out of cleaning tablets, but please choose one without fragrances or dyes

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.34.text: Well meant, but wrong: the most stubborn myths about cleaning dentures

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.35.text: Many cleaning mistakes don't happen out of carelessness, but out of good intentions. Toothpaste sounds logical, hot water feels more thorough, and everyone has a regular toothbrush to hand. The problem: many of these assumptions sound logical but are wrong. And in the end, you're the one who pays the price. We explain which products and habits really harm dentures, and why they persist so stubbornly all the same.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.36.text: Myth 1: Toothpaste cleans dentures just as well as denture cleaning products.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.37.text: Toothpaste contains abrasive particles designed for tooth enamel, not for denture plastic. It leaves fine scratches on the surface that are invisible to the naked eye. These, however, give bacteria the perfect place to settle in. The result: the denture discolours faster, starts to smell sooner and becomes harder to clean.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.38.text: Myth 2: Hot water cleans more thoroughly.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.39.text: Hot water slowly and imperceptibly warps the plastic. At some point, the denture no longer fits as it should, without any obvious reason. Instead, always rinse your denture with lukewarm water.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.4..text: Many of our patients clean their dentures conscientiously every evening: soaking, brushing, placing them in a glass. Yet during check-ups, discolouration sometimes still shows up that won't brush away. Or the dentures fit noticeably looser than a year ago. In conversation, it often turns out that during a holiday, the cleaning tablets were simply swapped for toothpaste. "I had it to hand anyway," is a common explanation. There's also plenty of cleaning advice online, from vinegar water to bicarbonate of soda, which doesn't always live up to its promises.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.40.text: Myth 3: Soaking is enough, brushing isn't necessary.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.41.text: Cleaning tablets disinfect reliably, but they don't fully dissolve mechanically stuck-on deposits on dentures. A brush remains essential, even alongside an ultrasonic device. Only the combination of both gives optimal cleaning.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.42.text: Myth 4: Vinegar is a natural miracle cure for limescale and stains.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.43.text: Used occasionally and well diluted, vinegar isn't immediately harmful. Regular use, however, attacks metal parts and makes the plastic porous over time. So vinegar is no substitute for special cleaning products.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.44.text: Myth 5: Bicarbonate of soda and baking powder remove stains – so they should work on dentures too.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.45.text: Bicarbonate of soda and baking powder are both mildly abrasive – similar to toothpaste, frequent use leaves fine scratches on the denture surface. Used occasionally and diluted, the risk is low, but they aren't recommended as a routine product.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.46.text: Myth 6: Cola dissolves deposits. You can use it for cleaning too.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.47.text: The acid in cola can indeed loosen deposits. However, the sugar, colourings and acid combined do more harm than good. So you shouldn't use cola as a cleaning product for your denture.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.48.text: Myth 7: The denture can also be stored dry.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.49.text: This is one of the most underestimated mistakes. Plastic needs moisture. Leaving the denture dry risks the material drying out, becoming brittle and cracking. In some cases, the material shrinks and the fit suffers. That's why you should always store your denture in fresh water or a cleaning solution.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.5..text: "Small mistakes sometimes creep into everyday denture cleaning – for example, unsuitable products used on well-meant advice from friends or family. Which products damage dentures in the long run often only becomes apparent once the surface is already affected."

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.50.text: When coffee, red wine and nicotine leave marks despite regular cleaning

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.51.text: Stains on a denture aren't a matter of care. They come from what we consume every day. Coffee, tea and red wine sometimes leave stubborn deposits. If you smoke, you know the problem even better: nicotine and tar stick particularly firmly and don't fully come off with normal cleaning products.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.52.text: 3 tips for getting stubborn stains under control

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.53.text: Tannins and dyes settle into the micropores of the plastic and leave visible stains over time, even if you clean your denture daily. Rinse your denture briefly under lukewarm water straight after eating or drinking, and brush the surface especially thoroughly in the evening. This keeps staining on your denture to a minimum.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.54.text: Nicotine and tar also penetrate deep into the pores of the plastic, making it porous over time and more prone to further deposits. The denture turns yellowish or brownish despite daily cleaning, and the deposits can't simply be brushed away. Special cleaning tablets with enzymes or active oxygen dissolve stains that normal cleaning tablets can't remove. Smokers should use them once or twice a week. A home ultrasonic cleaner provides additional support. As a smoker, it's also best to come to us for professional denture cleaning more often. In the end, no product at home can fully replace that.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.55.text: Limescale builds up particularly where the denture is constantly in contact with saliva. The use of adhesive cream can also contribute to unsightly residue over time. If limescale isn't removed regularly, it hardens into tartar – calcified plaque that can no longer be removed at home. An ultrasonic bath dissolves early limescale deposits especially effectively, even in areas a brush can't reach. For stubborn tartar, come to our practice for cleaning.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.56.text: "Whether it's coffee, nicotine or limescale, in the end it comes down to regular and thorough cleaning. Anyone who consistently does both keeps stains and deposits permanently in check and saves themselves the odd unplanned trip to the dentist."

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.57.text: Our insider tip: deeper cleaning with ultrasound

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.58.text: If you really want to take denture cleaning to the next level, an ultrasonic cleaner is the way to go. Ultrasonic waves create tiny vibrations in the water that reach even the smallest nooks and crannies a brush can't get to. You'll notice the result straight away: less plaque, no staining, significantly fewer bacteria and a denture – all without scrubbing, in just three to ten minutes. Simply fill with water, place the denture inside, and switch on the device. Important: for optimal care, you should still brush your denture daily.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.59.text: At KU64 in Berlin and Potsdam, we offer our patients exactly the right device for this – at a price of 99 euros, suitable for dentures, splints and sports guards. What top athletes have long used for their guards can now be used just as easily at home by denture wearers.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.6..text: Why do dentures need to be cleaned at all?

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.60.text: Denture overnight: take it out or leave it in?

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.61.text: This is a question we're regularly asked in the practice. As a general rule, we recommend taking the denture out at night. Your gums and mucous membrane can recover from the day's pressure, blood circulation improves, and the risk of inflammation and fungal infections decreases. Soaking the denture overnight also cleans it thoroughly at the same time. During the settling-in period, however, it can help to wear the denture at night too at first. This way, your mouth gets used to it more quickly. Once you've fully adjusted, the nightly break is worthwhile – for you, your teeth and your denture.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.62.text: Ultrasonic bath at KU64: clean right to the last corner

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.63.text: Home ultrasonic devices dissolve light deposits – but quickly reach their limits with stubborn tartar, deep nicotine staining or dried-on plaque. At KU64, we clean your denture in an ultrasonic bath: thoroughly, gently and quickly. The surface is then polished, which slows down new deposits and makes the denture noticeably fresher.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.64.text: Use the appointment for a check-up at the same time: Does the denture still fit well? Have any pressure sores developed? Would a reline make sense? Coming to see us once a year can, in some cases, save you an elaborate repair or a new denture. We're happy to give you individual tips on the professional care of your denture, including when it comes to smoking.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.65.text: Book your appointment now at KU64 in Berlin or Potsdam. Or take a look at our Prophylaxeshop. You'll find a wide range of dental care products there. We look forward to seeing you.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.7..text: Even if you wear dentures, there's no getting around daily oral hygiene. Quite the opposite: denture material is more porous than natural tooth enamel. Bacteria and food residue settle on it more quickly, plaque forms more easily, and over time plaque turns into tartar, which can affect how the dentures fit.

beitrag.zahnprothese-reinigen.bloecke.8..text: The consequences of inadequate cleaning are varied: bad breath, gum inflammation, sore spots and, in the worst case, a change in denture fit that makes relining or even a new denture necessary. Oral thrush, medically known as candidiasis, also occurs more often in denture wearers if the dentures aren't cleaned regularly and thoroughly.

beitrag.zahnseide-vorher-oder-nachher.an.text: Dental floss first, then the toothbrush – or the other way round? Many people are unsure about the right order. The good news: with a simple routine, you can clean the spaces between your teeth more thoroughly and support

beitrag.zahnseide-vorher-oder-nachher.bl.text: Dental floss first, then the toothbrush – or the other way round? Many people are unsure about the right order. The good news: with a simple routine, you can clean the spaces between your teeth more thoroughly and support your oral hygiene for healthy teeth and gums. Read what our dentists recommend.
In short
Toothpaste can work better afterwards

If you use dental floss before brushing your teeth, the spaces between your teeth are already free of loosened deposits and food residue. The toothpaste can then reach these areas more effectively. This matters above all because of the fluoride: it supports the remineralisation of tooth enamel and helps make teeth more resistant to decay.
Extra tip: After brushing, it's best to simply spit out the toothpaste or rinse with only a little water, so the fluoride can keep working on your teeth for longer.
What happens if you use dental floss only after brushing your teeth?

Using dental floss after brushing isn't "wrong", and it's certainly better than not cleaning the spaces between your teeth at all. Regular and correct use is more important than the question of whether floss is used in the morning or evening, before or after brushing.

If flossing before brushing doesn't feel right to you, or if your routine has always been the other way round, you don't need to change everything at once. What matters is that you clean the spaces between your teeth gently and every day, to remove food debris and plaque. If you can easily adjust the order, though, you'll simply be making your dental care routine even better.
What does the research actually say?

A frequently cited study on the order of flossing and brushing was carried out with 25 dental students (Mazhari 2016: Comparative Efficacy of Dental Flossing Before or After Tooth Brushing on Interproximal Plaque Reduction and Fluoride Retention in That Area). The researchers compared two sequences: brushing first and then flossing, or flossing first and then brushing. In the phase where participants flossed first, plaque between the teeth and overall was lower. A higher fluoride concentration was also found between the teeth.

This suggests that flossing before brushing may be preferable. At the same time, this finding shouldn't be overstated: a single study with a small group is not sufficient evidence for a general recommendation. That's why a balanced view is important:

“From a dental point of view, flossing before brushing does make more sense – but what matters even more is that you use floss, or another suitable tool for cleaning between your teeth, regularly and correctly. As a simple rule of thumb for everyday life: clean between your teeth once a day, ideally before brushing.”

Use dental floss before brushing your teeth if possible. This loosens plaque and food residue from the spaces between your teeth first. When you then brush with fluoride toothpaste, the loosened deposits are removed, and fluoride can reach the cleaned areas more effectively to fight harmful bacteria.
KU64 Smile & Swiss Smile prevention shop

At our practice on Kurfürstendamm, we've set up the extensive KU64 SMILE prevention shop on the 5th floor for you. Here you'll find a complete range of dental care products, including floss and interdental brushes from the exclusive Swiss premium brands swiss smile and CURAPROX. Advice from trained staff is included!
Morning or evening – when is flossing better?

Whether you floss in the morning or in the evening matters less than doing it regularly. What's most important is that you clean thoroughly between your teeth once a day. For many people, the evening works particularly well: after eating, you remove food debris and plaque from between your teeth, so it can't harm your teeth and gums overnight.

The evening is the perfect moment to round off the day well for your teeth, too. Between breakfast, coffee, lunch and dinner, quite a lot builds up in your mouth over the course of the day – often exactly where you can't see it yourself. A fixed evening routine helps make sure dental care isn't left to chance, but becomes a natural part of everyday life, so your teeth are cleaned thoroughly.
This way, you start the night with a fresh feeling in your mouth and support your dental health as well as possible.
If you tend to be too tired in the evening and end up skipping flossing, the morning may be the better solution for you. What matters is the routine you keep up consistently.
Rule of thumb: better to floss every morning than only occasionally in the evening.
The ideal evening routine: floss, brush, done
Step 1: Clean between your teeth
Why it makes sense to floss before brushing
Start with the spaces between your teeth. Use floss, interdental brushes or another tool such as a water flosser that suits your teeth, as explained in the next section. Work gently and thoroughly.
Step 2: Brush your teeth with fluoride toothpaste

After cleaning between your teeth, brush your teeth thoroughly with fluoride toothpaste. Brush for around two minutes and cover all tooth surfaces: outer surfaces, inner surfaces and chewing surfaces. If you use an electric toothbrush, let the brush head glide slowly from tooth to tooth. With a manual toothbrush, use small, gentle movements from the gum towards the tooth.
Step 3: Spit out the toothpaste, don't rinse heavily

After brushing, it's enough to spit out the toothpaste thoroughly. Try not to rinse your mouth with a lot of water. This way, the fluoride stays on your teeth for longer and can better support the enamel. If you find this difficult, you can use a fluoride mouthwash afterwards instead.
How to floss correctly: step by step

The right technique matters just as much as regular use when it comes to flossing. Pressing too hard or moving the floss abruptly can irritate the gums. Being too cautious, on the other hand, often means plaque isn't removed thoroughly enough. With a few simple steps, you can clean between your teeth gently and effectively – even in places a toothbrush alone can't reach.
How to insert dental floss gently
Break off about 30 to 50 centimetres of dental floss.
Wind the floss around one finger on each hand.
Let the floss slide gently into the gap between your teeth, without pushing it abruptly into the gum.
How to clean both sides of the tooth

When it comes to daily dental care, many people think of the toothbrush first. That's right, but it isn't enough for complete care on its own. The toothbrush mainly cleans the easily accessible outer surfaces, inner surfaces and chewing surfaces of the teeth.
Curve the floss into a C-shape against the tooth.
Move the floss gently up and down, cleaning just below the gum line.
Use a fresh piece of floss for each gap.
Mistakes you should avoid
Applying too much pressure.
'Sawing' into the gum.
Using the same piece of floss for more than one gap.
Only cleaning the front teeth.
Stopping as soon as there's a bit of bleeding.
What does it mean if there's bleeding when you floss?

Slight bleeding when flossing is a warning sign – but not a reason to stop straight away. The gums often bleed when they are inflamed or irritated, for example because plaque has built up in the gaps between the teeth over a longer period. Flossing too hard or incorrectly can also injure the gum.

What matters is this: floss gently and regularly. The gums often settle down once the gaps are cleaned consistently. However, if the bleeding continues over several days, keeps recurring, or is accompanied by pain, swelling or bad breath, you should have it checked by a dentist. This could indicate gum inflammation or periodontitis.
Which tool is best for cleaning between your teeth?

Not every interdental cleaning tool suits every set of teeth. What matters is how tight the gaps between your teeth are and whether you have sensitive gums. If you're cleaning around crowns, bridges, implants or a fixed brace, other tools are often better suited than conventional floss. While floss works well for narrow gaps, interdental brushes often clean larger gaps more easily and thoroughly.

The overview below will help you get an idea of what to use for cleaning between your teeth. Your dentist at KU64 will be happy to show you individually, during your prophylaxis appointment at KU64, which size and tool really suits your teeth.
Table: The best tool for cleaning between your teeth in every situation

The spaces between the teeth in particular are hard for the bristles to reach. Food residue, plaque and bacteria can build up there. In fact, the toothbrush only reaches around 70 per cent of the tooth surfaces, and it's precisely these hard-to-reach spaces between the teeth that are especially prone to tooth decay and gum disease.
Situation
Suitable tool
Why
Very narrow gaps between the teeth
Waxed dental floss or dental tape
Waxed floss glides more easily through tight contact points. Dental tape is broad and flat, making it extra smooth to use.
Normal to tight gaps
Unwaxed dental floss
Unwaxed floss frays more than waxed floss and removes plaque especially well.
Wider gaps
Dental floss loosens deposits your toothbrush can't reach
Interdental brush
The flexible mini brush comes in various sizes and has a handy grip, so it cleans wider gaps more effectively and easily than floss.
Bridges, implants, fixed dentures
Superfloss, interdental brush
Superfloss is a fluffy special floss and, like brushes, works better under bridge sections or around implants than ordinary floss.
Fixed braces
Superfloss, interdental brush, water flosser as an additional option
This special floss, along with brushes and a water flosser, cleans thoroughly around brackets and wires.
Limited finger dexterity
Floss holder or interdental brush

That's why dental floss is such an important addition to brushing your teeth – ideally before brushing with fluoride toothpaste. This way, you first loosen the deposits in the spaces between your teeth and then remove them more thoroughly from your mouth with the toothbrush.
A floss holder makes it easy to hold the floss without using your fingers, so it's just as simple to use as the brushes.
Let us show you the perfect technique

Using dental floss every day is an important step for clean gaps between your teeth and better dental health – your oral hygiene can improve even further if it's precisely matched to your teeth. With Prophylaxe 4.0 at KU64, we professionally clean your teeth in our practice and assess your individual risk of tooth decay and gum disease. Your dentist at KU64 will advise you in detail on which aids are genuinely useful for the gaps between your teeth and how to use them correctly.

Too much pressure can irritate or injure the gums. beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.0.blo.text: Pressure pain in a tooth is a fairly common symptom that can indicate various dental problems. Those affected feel an unpleasant, often sharp or throbbing pain that occurs especially under pressure on the tooth, for example when chewing. The problem affects adults and children alike.

One of the main causes of this toothache is pulpitis, an inflammation of the dental pulp. The pulp is the soft tissue inside the tooth that contains nerves and blood vessels. In pulpitis, an inflammatory reaction occurs – for example due to decay-causing bacteria or cracks in the tooth – which irritates the sensitive nerves in the pulp. This irritation often leads to increased sensitivity to pressure, temperature changes and also sweet or acidic foods.

Pressure pain can occur both temporarily and persistently. Short-term discomfort is often nothing to worry about. However, if the toothache persists, this can be a sign of a deeper inflammation or damage that you should definitely have checked by a dentist. The sooner the cause is identified and treated, the better your chances of becoming pain-free quickly and preserving the affected tooth in the long term. We are here for you weekdays until 8pm and even at weekends and on public holidays!

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.0.tit.text: Pressure pain in a tooth: when touch hurts

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.1.blo.text: When a tooth hurts under pressure, this can have various causes, often indicating problems in the tooth, gums or periodontium. The most common triggers can be divided into bacterial and mechanical factors.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.1.tit.text: Common causes of pressure pain in a tooth

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.10.bl.text: Frequent or long-lasting, throbbing pressure pain can be a symptom of inflammation of the tooth root (pulpitis) or an abscess. In these cases, the inflamed tissue presses on the surrounding area, which causes the pain.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.11.bl.text: Sometimes even light touch is enough to trigger pressure pain. This can indicate acute inflammation or damage to the tooth structure.

If you notice one or more of these symptoms, or if one of your children reports similar toothache, you should see a dentist as soon as possible. The sooner the cause is identified, the better the pain can be relieved and more serious consequences avoided. Our dentists are happy to help – on weekdays even until 8pm!

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.12.bl.text: If you feel pressure pain in a tooth, you shouldn't ignore it. It often points to underlying problems that, left untreated, can have serious consequences for oral health. The most common risks include:

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.12.ti.text: Possible consequences of pressure pain for oral health

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.13.bl.text: If pressure pain is caused by tooth decay or inflammation of the tooth root, the infection can spread without appropriate treatment. The result: worsening pain and possibly the formation of a dental abscess.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.14.bl.text: If damage such as cracks, deep decay or periodontitis is left untreated, the tooth can become so badly damaged that it can no longer be saved. Tooth loss can have far-reaching consequences, such as impaired chewing function or shifting of neighbouring teeth. In this case, dentures are strongly recommended.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.15.bl.text: Pressure pain can indicate gum disease such as gingivitis or periodontitis. Without treatment, these conditions can become chronic and damage the gums, the periodontal tissue, and even the jawbone.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.16.bl.text: Untreated pressure pain often leads people to try to protect the painful tooth by putting more strain on other teeth. This can cause wear, pain and damage to those teeth.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.17.bl.text: In severe cases, infections in the mouth can enter the bloodstream and trigger systemic illnesses, such as cardiovascular problems or complications with diabetes.

Please come to us for regular check-ups and get in touch as soon as possible if you're in pain. Pressure pain is a warning sign that should be taken seriously and examined promptly, to avoid serious consequences.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.18.bl.text: The right treatment for pressure pain in a tooth depends on the underlying cause and can range from simple measures to dental procedures, depending on severity. Here are the most common treatment methods:

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.19.bl.text: For sensitive teeth, for example due to exposed tooth necks, desensitising toothpastes or gels can help calm the nerves in the tooth and ease the pain. An additional fluoride treatment at the dentist strengthens the tooth necks.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.2.blo.text: Tooth decay: one of the most common causes of pressure pain. Decay-causing bacteria attack the tooth enamel and can penetrate as far as the sensitive dental pulp, where they can cause inflammation.
Dental abscess: an advanced infection that shows up as a build-up of pus around the tooth root. The pressure of the abscess on the surrounding tissue causes severe pain.
Tooth infection: bacteria can enter the inside of the tooth through cracks, deep fillings or damaged teeth, causing inflammation there.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.20.bl.text: If receding gums are responsible for the pressure pain, a gum graft can help. Tissue is placed at the affected areas to protect the sensitive tooth necks.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.21.bl.text: Poorly fitting fillings or crowns can cause pressure pain when chewing. Your dentist can renew or adjust these to relieve pressure on the tooth, easing or eliminating the discomfort.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.22.bl.text: If there is inflammation of the tooth pulp (pulpitis), root canal treatment is often necessary. The inflamed tissue is removed, the tooth thoroughly cleaned, and then sealed with a filling to prevent further infection.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.23.bl.text: For pressure pain caused by nighttime teeth grinding (bruxism), a custom-made occlusal splint can help. It protects the teeth from excessive strain, reducing the discomfort.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.24.bl.text: For abscesses or infections, your dentist will clean the affected area, drain the abscess and, if necessary, prescribe antibiotics to fight the infection.

Fast, targeted treatment is essential, not only to relieve the pain but also to prevent long-term damage. Please make an appointment at KU64 Berlin so we can answer all your questions and treat you with the right measures after a thorough examination.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.25.bl.text: Good oral hygiene and a few targeted preventive measures are the best way to avoid pressure pain. Here's how to keep your teeth healthy and pain-free for the long term:

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.26.bl.text: Use a toothbrush with soft bristles to protect your enamel and gums. Brush your teeth with gentle, regular movements to avoid damage caused by scrubbing too hard.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.27.bl.text:
Choose a toothpaste with fluoride, which strengthens the enamel and helps prevent tooth decay.
For sensitive teeth, a special toothpaste that reduces the transmission of stimuli in the dentine is recommended. Complement your care routine with dental floss or interdental brushes to remove food residue and bacteria between the teeth.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.28.bl.text: Visit your dentist for a check-up at least once a year. They can spot and treat damage or inflammation at an early stage. A professional teeth cleaning removes stubborn plaque and helps prevent gum disease.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.29.bl.text: Make sure you eat a balanced diet that strengthens your teeth and gums, for example with foods rich in calcium and vitamins. Wear a mouthguard when doing high-risk sports or other activities, to prevent cracks or fractures in your teeth.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.3.blo.text: When dental implants or other dental prosthetics hurt under pressure, this can have various causes. For example, overloading of the implants through teeth grinding or a poorly fitted crown can cause pain. Inflammations such as peri-implantitis or difficulties during healing, when the implant is not firmly anchored in the jawbone, can also be possible reasons. In any case, you should take pressure pain seriously as a warning sign, especially if it is accompanied by symptoms such as swelling, bleeding gums or pus. Do not hesitate to arrange an appointment with us as soon as possible, so our dentists can determine the cause. With timely treatment, long-term damage can be avoided and dental implants preserved. Please feel free to contact us!

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.30.bl.text: Only consume sugary and acidic foods in moderation, as these can attack tooth enamel. After eating acidic foods, wait around 30 minutes before brushing your teeth, to protect the enamel.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.30.ti.text: 5. Take care with acidic foods and drinks

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.31.bl.text: Pressure pain in a tooth is not just unpleasant for those affected. It is a warning sign that should be taken seriously. The causes can vary, but targeted treatment is always needed. Good oral hygiene and regular dental check-ups can prevent many problems. If you have persistent discomfort, please don't hesitate to contact us early on, so you can soon smile pain-free again!

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.4.blo.text: Exposed tooth necks: receding gums expose the sensitive tooth neck, which can cause pain under pressure as well as on contact with hot and cold liquids or food.
Enamel damage: tooth enamel is the natural protection of the tooth. If it is worn or damaged, the tooth becomes more susceptible to external stimuli.

Cracks in the tooth: small hairline cracks or larger fractures can trigger pressure pain, especially when chewing. The pressure is no longer distributed evenly and is transferred to the sensitive inside of the tooth.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.5.blo.text: Pressure pain can present in different ways, depending on the cause and severity of the underlying problem. Patients most commonly report the following symptoms:

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.5.tit.text: Symptoms: how pressure pain in a tooth shows itself

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.6.blo.text: A typical symptom is a sharp or dull pain that occurs when pressure is applied to the tooth, especially while chewing. This often points to a cracked tooth, tooth decay, or inflammation of the dental pulp.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.7.blo.text: Many people feel a sudden, sharp pain when the tooth comes into contact with cold or hot food and drinks. This sensitivity can be temporary, for instance with exposed tooth necks, or persistent if deeper layers of the tooth are affected.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.8.blo.text: In some cases, pressure pain can be accompanied by swelling of the gums or surrounding tissue, particularly if there is an infection such as a dental abscess.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.8.tit.text: Swelling and a feeling of pressure in the gums

beschwerde.druckschmerz.abschnitte.9.blo.text: After eating certain foods – especially hard, sticky or sweet ones – an uncomfortable pressure pain can linger. This may be a sign of cracks in the tooth, damage to the enamel, or exposed tooth necks.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.einstieg.0.text.text: You may know the situation: you take a satisfying bite of your food, and suddenly a sharp pain shoots through your tooth. What lies behind this kind of toothache? We explain the causes, symptoms and treatment options, so you can smile without pain again soon.

beschwerde.druckschmerz.titel.text: Pressure pain in a tooth: causes, symptoms and treatment

beschwerde.ernaehrung-gesunde-zaehne.abs.text: A radiant smile isn't just a matter of dental care – diet also plays a central role. What you eat and drink every day affects the health of your teeth, gums and entire mouth. The foods you consume provide essential nutrients such as calcium, which strengthen tooth enamel. But they can also encourage the development of tooth decay and gum inflammation.

The biggest danger to a tooth is sugar and acid. Sugar leads to an increase in bacteria in the mouth. These bacteria produce acids that attack tooth enamel. Sweets, sugary drinks and highly processed foods encourage this process in particular. But it's not just sugary foods that are a problem – acidic drinks such as fruit juices or soft drinks can also damage tooth enamel.

The good news is that there are also many foods that actively protect your teeth. Calcium-rich foods such as milk and cheese, kale or broccoli help to remineralise tooth enamel and strengthen bone structure. Chewing nuts and other firm foods also encourages saliva production – and saliva is a natural barrier against bacteria.

A balanced, tooth-friendly diet can reduce the risk of tooth decay and gum disease in the long run. It also brings many other health benefits. A lack of calcium, for example, can lead to osteoporosis. So by eating and drinking mindfully and getting enough calcium, you're not only looking after your smile, but also your bone strength and overall health.
Why is a healthy diet so important for your teeth?

Calcium is the basic building block for firm tooth structure and resilient enamel. Without this essential mineral, no tooth or bone would be stable. The catch is that our bodies can't produce calcium themselves. This means it must be taken in through our diet in sufficient amounts every day. The German Nutrition Society (DGE) recommends 1000 mg of calcium per day as a guideline for adults. Here you'll find a DGE table with recommendations for different age groups.

Good calcium intake doesn't just help prevent tooth decay. It also protects against long-term effects on bone health, above all osteoporosis. People whose bodies need more calcium should pay particular attention to getting enough of this mineral.
Calcium – an essential building block for strong teeth

Fluoride is well known for its protective effect against tooth decay. It strengthens the tooth enamel and makes it more resistant to acids produced by bacteria. Besides fluoride toothpaste, diet can also help with fluoride intake. This nutrient is found particularly in fluoridated mineral water, black tea and certain types of fish.
Our dentists are happy to give you further tips on a tooth-friendly diet during your check-up appointment. Just ask us!
Fluoride – Natural protection against tooth decay

As is so often the case with diet, the theory is the smaller problem. For many people, the real difficulty lies in putting it into practice in everyday life. Fortunately, a few simple changes to your eating and drinking habits can do a great deal of good for the health of your teeth!
A tooth-friendly diet in everyday life – how it’s done

Sugar is one of the main causes of tooth decay. Hidden sources of sugar in processed foods, sweet drinks and sweets are especially risky. Fresh fruit, unsweetened drinks and healthy snacks such as nuts or yoghurt are the better choice for a tooth-friendly diet.
1. Reduce sugar

Fruit juices, soft drinks and some types of fruit contain acids that attack the tooth enamel. If you regularly eat citrus fruits or drink carbonated beverages, for example, it’s best to rinse your mouth briefly with water afterwards. Brushing your teeth straight after acidic foods, on the other hand, is not ideal, as this can further damage the softened enamel. It’s better to wait around 30 minutes and, in the meantime, drink water or chew sugar-free gum to stimulate saliva production.
2. Enjoy acidic drinks and foods mindfully

Water is essential for the whole body, and especially for dental health. It helps rinse food residue and sugar out of the mouth and stimulates saliva production. Mineral water with a high calcium content can also help strengthen your teeth.
3. Drink plenty of water

Reaching for snacks, sweets or sugary drinks frequently throughout the day can damage the tooth enamel, as it is then exposed to acids continuously. It’s better to enjoy main meals mindfully and give your teeth recovery periods between meals.
4. Eating and drinking with structure

Bones and teeth harden every day, especially during intense growth phases. Calcium is essential here, as it supports the mineralisation of tooth enamel and forms the basis for strong teeth and healthy bones. A deficiency can not only lead to insufficient tooth development, but can also increase the risk of osteoporosis later in life.

During pregnancy, overall nutrient needs increase considerably. To build its skeleton and its first teeth, the growing baby needs plenty of calcium above all. If the expectant mother doesn't get enough through her diet, her body draws on its own reserves – particularly from the bones. This can increase the mother's risk of osteoporosis and affect her dental health. That's why getting enough calcium during pregnancy is especially important.

Bone density naturally decreases with age. Women after the menopause are particularly prone to osteoporosis due to hormonal changes, which increases the risk of bone fractures. To counteract this, older people should increase their calcium intake. If the supply is insufficient, the body draws calcium from the bones and teeth, so dental health suffers from a deficiency too. In the long run, this increases the risk of tooth loss.

Children, pregnant women and older people should therefore pay particular attention to a calcium-rich diet to meet their specific needs. Foods such as dairy products, vegetables (e.g. kale and broccoli), nuts or even calcium-rich mineral water can help ensure an optimal supply.
However, not all foods contain the same amount of calcium – and the body's ability to absorb it can also vary. So which foods are particularly helpful for meeting your daily calcium needs?
Who has an increased need for calcium?

With a healthy diet, you can meet your daily calcium needs well – provided you eat the right foods. There are both animal and plant sources that contain particularly high amounts of calcium and thus actively contribute to dental health.

Milk, yoghurt and cheese are among the best-known sources of calcium. Hard cheeses such as Parmesan or Emmental are particularly rich in this important mineral. What's more, the calcium in dairy products is easily absorbed and used by the body. Another benefit: dairy products often also provide valuable protein and support dental health through their positive effect on saliva flow.

Although it's often assumed that only dairy products contain a lot of calcium, there are also numerous plant-based sources. Green vegetables such as kale, broccoli or pak choi contain a considerable amount of calcium. They also contain important vitamins and antioxidants that protect the gums and support oral health.

Almonds, hazelnuts and sesame seeds are excellent sources of calcium. A spoonful of poppy or sesame seeds, for example, can already cover a significant part of your daily needs. Chewing nuts and seeds also promotes the production of saliva, which naturally protects the mouth from harmful acids and bacteria.

It's not only solid foods that contribute to your calcium supply – many mineral waters also contain this vital mineral. When buying mineral water, check the label: some varieties contain a good 500 mg of calcium per litre and can therefore be a valuable addition to your diet – especially if you consume little or no milk and other animal products.

Lentils, beans and soy products such as tofu also provide a good amount of calcium. Calcium-enriched tofu is also available to buy. This is an excellent alternative for anyone following a plant-based diet or looking to reduce their consumption of dairy products without risking a calcium deficiency.

As you can see: if you pay attention to a varied diet and a conscious choice of calcium-rich foods, you can meet your calcium needs optimally every day – for a healthy smile and strong teeth and bones.
Foods rich in calcium

Calcium is essential for strong teeth. However, it's not the only nutrient that plays a role in your dental health. Here are some of the most important nutrients that protect and strengthen your teeth.
Other nutrients for healthy teeth

Without enough vitamin D, the body cannot make optimal use of calcium. With the help of this vitamin, calcium from food can be transported into the bones and teeth. A vitamin D deficiency can therefore indirectly lead to a weakening of the tooth enamel and an increased susceptibility to tooth decay.

Especially during the winter months, when less sunlight is available, you should make sure you get enough vitamin D through your diet. Good sources of vitamin D include fatty fish, eggs and dairy products.
Vitamin D – The key to calcium absorption

Vitamin K supports the storage of minerals in the teeth and bones. It helps to store calcium in the right places in the body while preventing it from being deposited in the arteries. Green vegetables such as kale and broccoli are particularly rich in vitamin K and are therefore a good addition to a tooth-friendly diet.
Vitamin K – Protection for bones and tooth enamel

Vitamin C is essential for healthy gums. It strengthens connective tissue, promotes wound healing and protects the gums from inflammation. A deficiency can lead to bleeding gums and, over time, to periodontitis. Fruits and vegetables such as peppers, oranges, kiwis and berries are particularly rich in vitamin C.
Vitamin C – Strong defence for the gums

Phosphorus plays a crucial role in hardening tooth enamel. Together with calcium, it helps keep teeth stable and reduces damage caused by acids. Good sources of phosphorus include dairy products, fish, meat, eggs and nuts.
Phosphorus – Strengthening the tooth structure

Magnesium is important for tooth mineralisation and supports the strength of the teeth. A deficiency can weaken the resilience of the tooth enamel. Foods rich in magnesium include wholegrain products, nuts, legumes and green leafy vegetables.
Magnesium – For resilient teeth

beschwerde.ernaehrung-gesunde-zaehne.ein.text: [ The best foods with calcium & co. ]
From muesli with fruit in the morning, to a sweet snack with afternoon coffee, to a well-earned dinner and a glass of wine on the sofa: have you ever wondered how your diet affects your teeth?

Our daily eating and drinking habits play a crucial role in dental health. Foods rich in calcium, such as dairy products or nuts, strengthen teeth and enamel, while sugary and acidic foods and drinks increase the risk of decay and gum problems. A balanced diet isn't just good for your overall fitness. It also helps you keep healthy teeth in the long run.
Find out which foods protect your teeth, how to best meet your daily calcium needs, and which other nutrients are important for strong teeth, bones and healthy gums.
Don't forget regular check-ups! Feel free to book an appointment.

beschwerde.ernaehrung-gesunde-zaehne.faq.text:
The food with the highest calcium content per 100 g is poppy seeds. They contain around 1460 mg of calcium per 100 g, making them one of the best natural sources of calcium.
Other foods with particularly high calcium content per 100 g include:

Sesame seeds (unhulled): approx. 975 mg
Almonds: approx. 250 mg
Kale: approx. 210 mg
More information and a table of calcium-rich foods can be found on the website of the German Nutrition Society (DGE).
Which food contains the most calcium per 100 g?

There are many fruits and vegetables that are good sources of calcium. Chewing fresh, especially raw, vegetables also promotes saliva production, which in turn helps protect the tooth enamel.
Some examples of calcium-rich vegetables (per 100 g):
Kale – approx. 210 mg (particularly good for bones and teeth)
Broccoli – approx. 105 mg (easier to digest than other leafy greens)
Pak choi – approx. 105 mg
Fennel – approx. 109 mg
Spinach – approx. 99 mg
Calcium-rich fruit (per 100 g):

Figs (dried) – approx. 200 mg

Mandarins – approx. 37 mg

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.0.blo.text: Not all discolouration is the same. Dentists distinguish between extrinsic discolouration, which appears as deposits on the surface, and intrinsic discolouration, which develops inside the tooth. Both forms affect appearance and have different causes.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.0.tit.text: When a smile develops patina: causes of yellow teeth

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.1.blo.text: Some discolouration doesn’t develop inside the tooth itself but settles on the surface from outside. These deposits gradually change the shade and make the teeth appear darker.

Stimulants: drinks such as coffee, black tea, red wine and white wine, as well as nicotine from cigarettes, contain strong pigments. These gradually settle on the tooth surface and penetrate the enamel.

Food and drink: acidic drinks such as soft drinks (cola, lemonade, etc.) or fruit juices also roughen the enamel and encourage deposits. Balsamic vinegar, strongly coloured foods such as berries, curry or soy sauce, intense spices such as saffron, and even chemically treated chlorinated water can leave visible traces too.

Poor oral hygiene: if plaque is not removed regularly, it hardens over time into yellowish tartar. This can no longer be removed by daily brushing alone and makes the teeth permanently darker until it is professionally removed. Incorrect brushing technique can also wear away the tooth enamel and expose the yellowish dentine underneath.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.10.bl.text: First, your dentist carefully checks whether the discolouration lies within the tooth itself or is caused by external deposits. Your teeth are examined closely for this, if needed with magnifying loupes or an X-ray. This gives you a clear diagnosis showing where the discolouration comes from.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.11.bl.text: After the examination, your dentist explains which factors influence the colour of your teeth. You will get tips on which drinks and foods cause discolouration, how to adjust your brushing habits, and which care products are suitable for you and your children. This way, you learn what you can do yourself to prevent new discolouration.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.12.bl.text: In most cases, surface discolouration can be effectively removed with a professional teeth cleaning. Using special instruments such as ultrasound, powder-jet technology (airflow) and hand tools, the practice team removes plaque, tartar and deposits, even in hard-to-reach spots. Afterwards, the teeth are polished and protected with a fluoride gel, keeping them smooth and resistant. You will notice a fresh feeling straight away and see that your teeth look brighter. To keep your teeth looking healthy, you and your children should have a professional teeth cleaning twice a year.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.13.bl.text: If surface discolouration can no longer be removed by thorough brushing or regular professional teeth cleaning, bleaching is often the right solution. At KU64 Berlin, we offer you various options for this: in-office bleaching, carried out directly at our dental practice, is safe, quick, and shows an immediately visible result. Alternatively, you can choose home bleaching, carried out comfortably at home under dental guidance. In both cases, a special gel is applied that dissolves the colour pigments in the enamel and gently whitens your teeth. Depending on the method, your teeth can be lightened by several shades.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.14.bl.text: If bleaching does not achieve the desired result for yellow teeth, veneers at KU64 Berlin offer you a lasting solution. Your dentist creates ultra-thin ceramic shells, precisely matched to your teeth. These are firmly bonded to the tooth surface and fully cover discolouration. At the same time, they can even out small flaws in the shape or position of the teeth. Veneers are therefore the ideal choice if you want not just whiter teeth, but a harmonious, aesthetic overall solution for a perfect smile.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.15.bl.text: After successful treatment, your smile looks especially fresh and bright again. To help the result last, there is plenty you can do yourself: small everyday routines that prevent new discolouration from settling on your teeth. The following tips will help you keep your teeth shining:
Wait after eating: Don't brush your teeth immediately after eating acidic foods such as fruit or fizzy drinks. Wait about 20 minutes to allow the tooth enamel to re-harden.
Drink enough water: Drinking water regularly rinses away pigments from the teeth and neutralises the mouth. This means acids can do less damage.
Use a straw: For drinks such as cola, iced tea or fruit juices, a straw can help reduce direct contact with the teeth, particularly for children, helping to prevent staining.
Regular care: Brush your teeth thoroughly twice a day, use floss and clean your tongue as well. This gives deposits far less chance to build up.

Whitening toothpaste: A toothpaste with a whitening effect can help in the short term, but it doesn't replace a professional clean and isn't a genuine whitening treatment. Use it only occasionally and after discussing it with your dentist.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.15.ti.text: Keeping your smile bright, day after day

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.2.blo.text: This type of discolouration develops beneath the surface of the tooth. Underneath lies the dentine, a yellowish tooth substance that shows through the enamel. If the enamel becomes thinner or the dentine itself changes, the whole tooth appears darker. Typical causes include:
Genetic factors: some people naturally have a darker tooth shade. This natural tone remains even with careful oral care and makes the teeth appear less white.
Ageing: over time, the tooth substance changes. The enamel becomes thinner, making the yellowish dentine underneath more visible. This makes the teeth appear darker overall.

Medication: certain medicines such as antibiotics can change the colour of teeth even while they are still developing. Tetracyclines, for example, become permanently embedded in the enamel if taken during childhood. Iron-containing preparations, chlorhexidine mouth rinses, excessive fluoride intake or old amalgam fillings can also leave visible discolouration.

Illness: health problems can change the colour of teeth or cause yellow spots on them. Metabolic disorders such as Gilbert's syndrome or jaundice often cause a yellowish tinge. Early-stage decay first appears as a light spot, which can stabilise again through remineralisation. If pigments then become embedded, a yellowish to brownish spot may remain visible.

Dental trauma: a blow or fall affecting the teeth can change their colour. The tooth often appears more yellowish because pigments from the blood enter the dentine or the tooth substance calcifies more quickly after the injury. If the nerve of the tooth is affected, the colour may also shift towards grey.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.3.blo.text: Are you unsure whether your teeth are discoloured by deposits from coffee or tea, or whether causes such as medication or illness have changed the colour of the tooth from within? Our dentists at KU64 Berlin will find out together with you. In a personal appointment, we'll identify the cause and advise you individually on the options for gently removing the discolouration. We'll put together a treatment plan tailored exactly to you, so you can enjoy showing your smile again.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.3.tit.text: Not sure what's causing your tooth discolouration?

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.4.blo.text: Beavers naturally have strikingly yellow teeth. The reason lies in the iron compounds in their enamel, which cause the typical colour. This iron also makes their teeth especially hard and resilient – ideal for an animal that has to gnaw through thick branches and tree trunks every day.

By comparison, human tooth enamel consists only of calcium compounds. While it is the hardest substance in the human body, it isn't as tough as a beaver's teeth. So while yellow teeth are often seen as a cosmetic issue in humans, for beavers this colouring is a clear advantage.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.4.tit.text: Did you know: why do beavers have yellow teeth?

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.5.blo.text: Our dentists at KU64 Berlin are often asked whether yellow teeth can be whitened again with simple home remedies. Home remedies for tooth discolouration often sound like clever tips, but not everything is actually good for your teeth. At best, they can only support professional dental treatment. The overview below puts these home remedies into perspective and shows which ones you're better off avoiding.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.5.tit.text: Which home remedies help against yellow teeth?

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.6.blo.text: Coconut oil: binds bacteria and may support the oral flora.
Dairy products (e.g. cheese): provide minerals, strengthen the enamel and neutralise acids.
Fresh fruit and vegetables (e.g. apples, carrots, celery): clean mechanically while chewing and stimulate saliva flow.
Sugar-free chewing gum: increases saliva flow and supports natural cleaning.
Miswak twigs: a traditional natural remedy with antibacterial properties that supports oral hygiene.
Clove oil: has antibacterial properties and freshens breath, but can irritate the gums and mucous membrane.
Indian basil (tulsi): has antibacterial and antioxidant properties and is traditionally used for oral care.
Fresh sage leaves: can reduce mild plaque build-up and have antibacterial properties.

In summary: these home remedies can usefully support oral hygiene. They stimulate saliva flow, have antibacterial properties, and some can even partly neutralise acid-forming substances. However, they do not produce genuine whitening. They are a support, not a solution for white teeth, as they cannot achieve the effect of professional treatment.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.6.tit.text: Recommended: gentle companions for oral hygiene

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.7.blo.text: Baking soda: strongly abrasive and wears away tooth enamel.
Lemon juice: contains a lot of acid and attacks tooth enamel.
Apple cider vinegar: its acid weakens tooth enamel and increases the risk of tooth decay.
Activated charcoal: scratches the tooth surface and can cause micro-cracks.
Spices such as turmeric: stain strongly and can make teeth look even more yellow.
Fruits such as strawberries: contain fruit acids that can attack tooth enamel.

In short: these home remedies tend to do more harm than good, as they weaken or roughen the tooth enamel. Once the protective layer is damaged, pigments from coffee, tea or red wine settle onto it even more easily. So instead of becoming whiter, teeth can actually end up looking more yellow over time.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.7.tit.text: Not recommended: risks instead of radiance

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.8.blo.text: Slight discolouration on the teeth is often harmless. But there are situations where a visit to the dentist makes sense. If yellow teeth persist despite thorough brushing, the cause should be professionally checked. Caution is also advised if discolouration appears suddenly or affects only a single tooth. In children, newly erupting permanent teeth often appear darker than the milk teeth, as their dentine is more yellowish and shows through more. This difference in colour is usually harmless. Even so, a check-up at the dentist provides reassurance and rules out other causes.

If you also notice pain or sensitivity, please do not hesitate: make an appointment at our practice early on. Together we will find out what is behind the changes and make sure that you or your child can smile freely again.

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.8.tit.text: Yellow teeth: when should you see a dentist?

beschwerde.gelbe-zaehne.abschnitte.9.blo.text: Analysis, advice and modern treatment: your dentist at KU64 takes plenty of time to bring yellow teeth back to a brighter shine. Which method suits your teeth is decided after a thorough examination and based on your personal wishes.
