What do patients say about KU64?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.abschnitte.39.text: From the first white spots to inflammation inside the tooth: tooth decay is not a harmless dental problem, but a progressive condition that, without treatment, penetrates ever deeper into the tooth. It does not heal on its own and can affect people of any age, including children. Anyone who watches for early signs such as sensitivity or discolouration and sees a dentist in good time can avoid more serious damage and keep the tooth. Regular check-ups, good oral hygiene and a mindful diet are the best protection. Act early, before tooth decay becomes a burden.
Conclusion: take symptoms of tooth decay seriously and act early

beschwerde.karies-symptome.abschnitte.4..text: Tooth decay is the most widespread dental disease of all. Around 99% of all adults in Germany are affected by it at some point in their lives. Tooth decay is bacterial damage to the tooth structure, in which the hard surface of the tooth – the enamel – is gradually destroyed. It leads to a loss of tooth substance and, if untreated, can progress into deeper layers of the tooth. Tooth decay is considered a chronic condition that progresses without treatment and can cause pain, inflammation or tooth loss.
More than just a hole in the tooth – what exactly is tooth decay?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.abschnitte.5..text: A thin coating constantly forms in the mouth – known as plaque. It consists of saliva components, food residue and millions of bacteria that settle on the tooth surface. These microorganisms use sugar and other carbohydrates from food as an energy source and convert them into acids. These acids attack the tooth enamel and draw out protective minerals such as calcium and phosphate – a process known as demineralisation. If this state continues over a longer period and the teeth are not cleaned regularly, the damage can gradually deepen.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.abschnitte.6..text: Several factors encourage the development of tooth decay:
Sugary diet: Frequent consumption of sweets, soft drinks or sugary snacks constantly supplies the bacteria with food.
Insufficient oral hygiene: If plaque is not removed regularly, cavity-causing bacteria can multiply undisturbed.
Reduced saliva flow: Saliva protects the teeth by neutralising acids. With a dry mouth, the risk of tooth decay increases considerably.
Hard-to-reach areas: Crowded teeth, gaps between teeth or grooves on the chewing surfaces are difficult to clean and therefore especially vulnerable.
Prolonged acid exposure: Anyone who eats or drinks frequently throughout the day repeatedly exposes their teeth to acid attacks without giving them time to recover.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.abschnitte.7..text: Tooth decay can develop in different areas of the tooth. Depending on the location, different forms are distinguished. What matters is where the bacteria attack the tooth.
What types of tooth decay are there?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.abschnitte.8..text: This form develops in the narrow spaces between teeth, where toothbrush bristles struggle to reach. Without dental floss or interdental brushes, plaque remains there – an ideal breeding ground for bacteria.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.abschnitte.9..text: Decay can also develop beneath crowns as well as old or leaking fillings, for example when the edge of the crown is not completely sealed. In this case, bacteria spread unnoticed beneath the crown and attack the tooth from the inside.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.beschreibung.text: From sensitive teeth to dark spots – spot the symptoms of tooth decay in time to protect your dental health.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.einstieg.0.te.text: Tooth decay is one of the most common dental problems and often goes unnoticed. A sugary diet and poor dental care encourage the attack on tooth enamel. Find out how to spot early signs and protect your teeth.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.0.antwort.text: The early stage of tooth decay, also known as initial caries, can be recognised by white or translucent spots on the tooth surface. As these spots are still quite inconspicuous, these symptoms often go unnoticed and the decay continues to develop unnoticed at first. If the condition is diagnosed at this early stage and treatment begins quickly, the damage can still be reversed.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.0.frage.text: What does early-stage tooth decay look like?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.1.antwort.text: Hidden signs of tooth decay are barely noticeable at first and often cause no pain. They include fine white or dark spots, a slightly rough feeling on the tooth surface, or increasing sensitivity to cold, hot or sweet foods. Bad breath or an unpleasant taste can also indicate developing tooth decay. As these changes are difficult to spot with the naked eye, hidden tooth decay is often only discovered during a dental examination.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.1.frage.text: What are hidden signs of tooth decay?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.10.antwor.text: The cost of treating tooth decay depends on the extent of the damage and the method chosen. A small composite filling is usually covered by statutory health insurance, while higher-quality materials such as ceramic or composite involve out-of-pocket costs. In cases of deeper decay requiring root canal treatment followed by a dental restoration such as a crown, the out-of-pocket costs can be significant depending on the material chosen. Your dentist will advise you individually on the treatment options and the associated costs.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.10.frage.text: What does treating tooth decay cost?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.2.antwort.text:
Not every dark spot on a tooth is automatically tooth decay. Staining is often caused by consuming coffee, tea, red wine or tobacco and usually lies only on the surface of the enamel. It can generally be removed with a professional teeth cleaning.
Tooth decay, on the other hand, changes the tooth substance itself. Typical signs are matte, white or brownish spots that darken over time and are often accompanied by a loss of tooth substance. If you're unsure whether it's tooth decay or harmless staining, a dental examination will provide clarity.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.2.frage.text: Is it tooth decay or just a stain?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.3.antwort.text:
If tooth decay is detected, it's important to act quickly to stop it spreading and to preserve the tooth. Your dentist will first examine the affected area thoroughly to determine the extent of the damage. Depending on how deep the decay has progressed, they will then take targeted measures to contain the inflammation and stabilise the tooth.
It's important to keep the affected area clean and avoid putting extra strain on the tooth. Painkillers can provide short-term relief but do not replace dental treatment. Avoid sugary foods and acidic drinks until the tooth has been treated.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.3.frage.text: What can be done about tooth decay?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.4.antwort.text: As tooth decay usually doesn't heal on its own and good oral hygiene alone isn't enough, you should see your dentist as soon as you suspect you have tooth decay. How quickly tooth decay worsens, or how long it takes to develop, depends on various factors – such as diet, saliva flow and individual dental care. Here too: prevention is better than cure. If you notice typical symptoms, don't hesitate and contact our team at KU64 as soon as possible, so that early tooth decay can be recognised and treated in time.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.4.frage.text: How quickly does tooth decay need to be treated?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.5.antwort.text: If the early stages aren't recognised or treated, the decay gradually penetrates deeper into the tooth and can eventually reach the root and the nerve. How long this takes varies. The process can take anywhere from several months to a few years. To prevent tooth decay from spreading unnoticed, it's essential to recognise the symptoms early and attend regular check-ups.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.5.frage.text: How long does it take for tooth decay to reach the root?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.6.antwort.text: There are various causes of tooth decay, but even children are taught early on: sugar and sweet foods are bad for dental health and encourage the formation of tooth decay. This is because the bacteria in plaque get their energy from carbohydrates in food – mainly easily fermentable sugars. The bacteria in the mouth convert sugar into acid, which decalcifies the enamel and attacks the tooth substance. This process is also known as demineralisation. It makes the enamel porous. Microorganisms can then penetrate the tooth and destroy it from within. For the sake of your teeth, you should therefore only enjoy sweets, cakes, sugary drinks and similar items in moderation. Do you have further questions about tooth decay? Your dentist at KU64 Berlin will be happy to provide further information.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.7.antwort.text: Tooth decay can develop even with regular dental care, for example when certain areas of the mouth are hard to reach or the enamel is naturally more sensitive. Crowded teeth, incompletely removed plaque, or too frequent sugar consumption encourage the formation of acids that attack the enamel. In addition, reduced saliva flow, for example due to medication or stress, can impair the teeth's natural protection.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.7.frage.text: Why does tooth decay develop despite good dental care?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.8.antwort.text: Tooth decay that has already formed cannot simply be brushed away. Once tooth substance has been destroyed, it cannot regenerate on its own. Home remedies or attempts to remove decay yourself are not effective and can even damage the tooth further. Only in very early stages – so-called initial caries – can regular fluoride treatment help remineralise the enamel and stop the process.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.8.frage.text: Can I brush away tooth decay?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.9.antwort.text: Yes, genetic factors often play a role. People with thinner enamel, lower saliva flow, or an unfavourable bacterial balance in the mouth have a higher risk of developing tooth decay. Certain pre-existing conditions or medications can also contribute. However, daily dental care remains the most important protection for your teeth's health, regardless of individual predisposition.

beschwerde.karies-symptome.faq.9.frage.text: Is there a genetic predisposition to tooth decay?

beschwerde.karies-symptome.titel.text: How dangerous is tooth decay? Everything about hidden symptoms, causes, treatment and prevention

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.0.blo.text: They show discolouration, react sensitively to pain and sometimes even chip: chalky teeth (MIH). Around 15 percent of 12-year-olds are currently affected by this common condition. Chalky teeth are caused by poorly mineralised tooth enamel, not by incorrect brushing or an unhealthy diet, and can noticeably affect everyday life for the whole family. The dentists at KU64 Berlin specialise in recognising chalky teeth early, treating them consistently and keeping them free of discomfort in the long term, so your child can eat, drink and smile with ease again.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.0.tit.text: What parents should know about enamel defects and hypomineralisation

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.1.blo.text: Chalky teeth develop when a child's tooth enamel does not harden properly (hypomineralisation). The teeth become softer, porous and more prone to damage and decay.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.10.bl.text: Recurring high fever and infectious diseases in early childhood, such as chickenpox, measles, or respiratory illnesses like bronchitis and asthma, can disrupt enamel formation.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.11.bl.text: Frequent use of antibiotics during the first three years of life can also affect the composition of the tooth enamel and may be a cause of chalky teeth.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.12.bl.text: Pollutants absorbed by the body from the environment can weaken tooth enamel. Environmental toxins such as dioxins, which are absorbed through food, are suspected, as are plasticisers found in food packaging, such as bisphenol A or polychlorinated biphenyl.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.13.bl.text: Illnesses affecting the mother during pregnancy can affect the newborn's dental health. A vitamin D deficiency in the mother or child during the first years of life is also listed as a possible cause of chalky teeth.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.13.ti.text: 4. Illness in the mother during pregnancy

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.14.bl.text: Difficulties during birth, such as lack of oxygen or a caesarean delivery, can contribute to the development of chalky teeth. Research also indicates that premature birth or low birth weight play a significant role in the development of Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation (MIH).

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.15.bl.text: Chronic kidney disease can disrupt the calcium-phosphate balance in the teeth, affecting their stability and health.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.16.bl.text: To recognise chalky teeth in good time, you should have your children's molars checked early on. By the time the permanent teeth come through, at the latest around the age of five or six, it is important for a dentist to professionally examine them. In most cases, the mineralisation defect appears on the first molars and also on the front teeth. The disturbance in enamel formation can affect only small areas of the tooth or the entire crown.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.17.bl.text: Cloudy white or yellow-brown patches: chalky teeth show white-creamy to yellowish-brown patches. Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation (MIH) appears on the chewing surfaces and sides of the teeth. The affected areas are sharply defined.

Increased tooth sensitivity: the enamel defect makes the tooth react more sensitively to mechanical, thermal and chemical stimuli. Brushing teeth, hot, cold or sweet food, even chewing movements or the air jet used by the dentist can cause pain. Those affected are also sensitive when breathing through the mouth.
Uneven tooth surfaces: grooves in the tooth surface, missing cusps or chipped enamel can indicate chalky teeth.

If you notice symptoms of hypomineralised teeth in your child, you should not wait. Contact our practice team at the first signs and arrange an appointment for a check-up with our paediatric dentists.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.17.ti.text: The following signs may indicate chalky teeth:

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.18.bl.text: With chalky teeth, the enamel has not hardened properly and is in places porous. This means external stimuli such as cold, warmth or sweetness can penetrate much more easily to the dentin underneath. Fine channels run through the dentin containing nerve fibres. If these dentinal tubules are exposed due to the damaged enamel, stimuli are passed directly to the nerve. This can be felt as a brief, sharp or pulling pain. It is therefore typical of chalky teeth that everyday situations can trigger pain.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.19.bl.text: Chalky teeth can be more or less pronounced depending on the patient. In mild cases, the teeth are merely discoloured, whereas severe demineralisation can, besides sensitivity, lead to complete loss of enamel and other dental problems. The tooth then becomes less stable and can chip. Depending on the severity, the dentists at KU64 Berlin discuss the appropriate treatment plan together with parents and children.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.19.ti.text: The progression of chalky teeth: from mild to severe

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.2.blo.text: Chalky teeth can be recognised by white-yellow-brown patches, rough surfaces, chipping edges and pain when brushing, eating or drinking.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.20.bl.text: In early stages, only slight changes to the surface are usually visible. The teeth still appear stable on the outside, but may already be slightly discoloured and react more sensitively, for example to sweet food. At this stage, the main focus is on observing whether the patches or sensitivity increase over time.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.20.ti.text: Mild form: first changes in the enamel

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.21.bl.text: As demineralisation increases, initial structural defects appear, such as rough patches, fine cracks or early chipping. The discolouration becomes more noticeable and the teeth react more frequently to temperature stimuli or mechanical strain. At this stage, the risk increases that the enamel layer will weaken further and the damage will spread.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.21.ti.text: Moderate form: visible enamel damage and increasing sensitivity

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.22.bl.text: In severe cases of MIH, the enamel loses its strength, the teeth become generally unstable and can lose larger parts of their surface. In severe cases, chalky teeth are heavily discoloured, badly damaged and often brittle. The affected teeth can even lose parts of the enamel. At this stage, the tooth can hardly fulfil its healthy protective function anymore, which can significantly affect the children's daily life – for example when eating, drinking and brushing their teeth.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.22.ti.text: Severe form: unstable teeth and significant loss of substance

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.23.bl.text: Many parents feel unsure when they notice discolouration or rough patches on their child's teeth. Chalky teeth can easily be mistaken for fluorosis, early tooth decay or ordinary demineralisation, even though the causes and treatment are completely different. The overview below explains the key differences and can help you get a sense of what might be behind the changes:
matte white, symmetrical patches or stripes
whitish at first, later brown to black
intact, smooth, no loss of substance
gradually destroyed, leading to defects and even "holes"
weakened early on, but usually still stable
progressive, up to destruction of the tooth
may improve with care, depending on the stage
protection, fluoridation, sealing, fillings, crowns if needed

So not every case of insufficiently mineralised enamel is automatically molar incisor hypomineralisation. Similar defects can also result from, for example, congenital disorders of enamel formation (such as amelogenesis imperfecta), developmental disorders, dental trauma, inflammation around the tooth, or certain antibiotic treatments (e.g. with tetracycline). As the causes can vary so much, we recommend having any changes to your child's tooth enamel checked at KU64 as early as possible. A check-up appointment helps to clearly identify the condition and start the right treatment.
too much fluoride during tooth development
acids from plaque or diet draw minerals out of the enamel

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.23.ti.text: Distinguishing chalky teeth reliably: how parents can tell the difference from fluorosis, tooth decay and demineralisation

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.24.bl.text: Many people affected ask themselves: how can molar incisor hypomineralisation be got rid of? So far, there is no cure for it. It remains for life. This makes it all the more important to recognise the condition early and stop it progressing as soon as possible. The dentists at KU64 aim to relieve the symptoms and protect the sensitive teeth more strongly against tooth decay. When treating patients with this condition, they take particular care to make the treatment as gentle as possible. KU64 Berlin offers the following methods for children and young people with molar incisor hypomineralisation:

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.24.ti.text: A gentle touch needed: treating molar incisor hypomineralisation with care

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.25.bl.text: The dentists at KU64 Berlin recommend intensive prevention every three to six months, up to four times a year, for patients with a mild form of the condition. Once the tooth has fully come through, it is sealed once with a plastic coating.

In addition, the dentist regularly applies fluoride to the chewing surfaces of the affected teeth. As the surface of these teeth is usually rough and sensitive to pain, they are harder to clean. The affected teeth are more prone to decay. Highly concentrated fluoride protects the demineralised areas from bacteria getting in. At home, you can use fluoride toothpaste and remineralising paste to strengthen the teeth and support mineralisation.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.26.bl.text: Smaller defects in the teeth can be treated with sealing, meaning the application of a covering made of plastic or glass ionomer cement. This protects the damaged areas and prevents further wear. For teeth that are particularly sensitive, desensitising with pain-relieving coatings can also help to smooth the surface and better shield it from stimuli. Veneers, too, can protect the tooth surface and help restore a harmonious tooth colour and smile.

If the structure of the tooth is already affected, fillings or crowns can help stabilise it. For crowns, the dentists at KU64 use materials such as stainless steel or ceramic/zirconia. These not only preserve the function of the tooth but also make it less sensitive to pain. H3: Surgical measures

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.27.bl.text: If the enamel defect is particularly severe, the teeth lose their stability or become very sensitive to pain. If the tooth is badly damaged and cannot be preserved in the long term, it may need to be extracted. The resulting gap can then be closed either with an implant or through orthodontic treatment. For the best possible treatment and short distances, the dental team at KU64 Berlin works closely with the practice's own orthodontists.

Good to know: the usual local anaesthetic only has a limited effect on teeth affected by this condition. Instead, the dentists at KU64 use painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen when treating it. In a preliminary discussion, you will receive further information on the right dosage for your child. If the teeth are especially sensitive to pain, all treatments can also be carried out under partial or general anaesthetic.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.28.bl.text: Our paediatric dentists first examine the affected teeth and assess the severity of the chalky teeth using an MIH index.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.28.ti.text: 1. Severity diagnosis using the MIH index

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.29.bl.text: The dentist then gently checks how strongly your child's teeth react to stimuli such as cold, pressure or air, in order to assess the level of pain as precisely as possible.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.3.blo.text: Early diagnosis, protective varnishes and fluoride treatments, sealants, stable fillings or small crowns, along with close preventive care, help to stabilise chalky teeth and reduce discomfort.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.30.bl.text: Your child then receives a personal treatment and prevention plan that sets out exactly which steps come next and how your child can best protect the sensitive teeth in everyday life.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.31.bl.text: Treatment for chalky teeth varies from child to child. Regardless of how severe the condition is, we recommend that all parents get in touch straight away if they suspect chalky teeth and arrange an appointment with their dentist. During the consultation, the specialists at KU64 give affected children tips for optimal oral hygiene and for preventing tooth decay. As a parent, you will learn how to motivate and support your child with their dental care. The dentist will also discuss the treatment plan together with the patient and clarify any open questions relating to the treatment of chalky teeth.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.31.ti.text: Advice on chalky teeth in children

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.32.bl.text: Prevention – that is, regular check-ups at the dentist – is essential when it comes to chalky teeth. But children and parents can also help in everyday life to protect the permanent chalky teeth and keep them healthy for as long as possible. According to current research, the following tips and measures can help minimise defects caused by demineralisation:

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.32.ti.text: Home remedies and tips: what children with chalky teeth should bear in mind

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.33.bl.text: Daily dental care starts with the very first tooth. As a parent, make sure your child brushes their teeth carefully, ideally after every meal – but at least twice a day. For sensitive chalky teeth, use a soft toothbrush and, ideally, lukewarm water so that brushing doesn't cause additional pain. Until the age of nine, parents should check their children's teeth after brushing and brush again if needed. To reach hidden and deep-lying areas as well, we at KU64 recommend brushing the back teeth with a horizontal motion. To do this, the toothbrush should be moved back and forth at a right angle to the row of teeth. Regular tooth care reduces plaque acids in the mouth and, with them, the risk of tooth decay on the already sensitive chalky teeth.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.34.bl.text: Use an age-appropriate toothpaste containing fluoride for your child's daily oral hygiene at home, as well as weekly applications of highly concentrated fluoride gel, which the paediatric dentists at KU64 Berlin will recommend depending on the findings. In addition to sealants applied by the dentist, these strengthen the enamel and help prevent damage to chalky teeth. This makes the teeth less sensitive and more resistant to decay. Those affected can also use desensitising toothpastes to ease sensitivity in the teeth. These contain active ingredients such as arginine or a compound of casein phosphopeptide and amorphous calcium phosphate (CPP-ACP).

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.34.ti.text: 2. Fluoride and desensitising toothpastes and gels

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.35.bl.text: Plaque acids that cause tooth decay, produced by bacteria in the mouth, mainly result from eating sugary foods. The higher the concentration of plaque acids, the higher the risk of tooth decay. Sweets should therefore be replaced with tooth-friendly foods wherever possible. Fruit purées for young children in soft plastic pouches, so-called squeeze pouches, may be convenient, but in many cases they are real sugar bombs.

A balanced diet also includes healthy drinks such as water or unsweetened tea. For older children, sugar-free chewing gum can also be useful, as it stimulates saliva flow and so helps neutralise acids in the mouth more effectively. Dentists also recommend using fluoridated table salt when preparing meals.

DIY bleaching attempts or homemade cleaning methods using strongly acidic or abrasive substances such as lemon or bicarbonate of soda are not recommended. They can cause further damage to the already sensitive enamel and should be avoided at all costs.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.36.bl.text: Severely affected chalky teeth are often particularly sensitive to pain. The dentists at KU64 therefore make sure to treat patients with chalky teeth as quickly as possible. Please mention this when booking your appointment, so that any waiting time can be kept as short as possible. Even without acute pain, KU64 patients benefit from a wide range of dental services without long waiting times.

Our dental practice is open for you seven days a week. We offer parents and children so-called family appointments on a single day. Get in touch with our specialists for chalky teeth. You can book your appointment at KU64 by email at info@ku64.de or by phone on: 030 86 47 320. Our team will be happy to help with any questions about your dental health.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.36.ti.text: Fast help and family-friendly appointment times

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.37.bl.text: Chalky teeth can be distressing, but today they can be treated well, both medically and cosmetically. What matters is that you take changes in your child's teeth seriously and don't wait. Have any spots, sensitivity or crumbling areas checked early at KU64, so that together we can draw up a suitable protection and treatment plan and help keep your child's teeth stable and as symptom-free as possible in the long term.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.37.ti.text: In conclusion: take chalky teeth seriously, make the most of the options

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.4.blo.text: In the human body, tooth enamel is the hardest substance. It is harder than iron and protects the teeth from outside influences. Chalky teeth develop due to reduced mineralisation of the tooth enamel. Compared to healthy teeth, the enamel of chalky teeth is noticeably softer. As a result, the teeth are less protected, more prone to decay and often as brittle as chalk. The reduced enamel hardness also makes the teeth more sensitive. Chalky teeth react extremely sensitively to outside stimuli. Even daily brushing or eating warm, cold or sweet food can cause pain in those affected.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.5.blo.text: Chalky teeth mainly occur among permanent teeth. Since both the molars and the incisors are affected by the enamel disorder, the condition is also known as molar incisor hypomineralisation (MIH). However, milk teeth can already show enamel changes as they erupt into the mouth. In medical terminology, the development of chalky teeth in the milk dentition is called milk molar hypomineralisation (MMH). Such changes to milk molars are often considered an early warning sign that the permanent teeth may be affected later on.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.5.tit.text: Molar incisor hypomineralisation (MIH): incisors and molars are often affected

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.6.blo.text: The number of children with chalky teeth remains high: according to the Sixth German Oral Health Study (DMS VI, 2025), around 15.3 percent of 12-year-old children in Germany are affected. In cases of MIH, an average of 3.4 teeth per child show the defect. Internationally, the estimated prevalence is around 13 to 14 percent. For comparison, the Fifth German Oral Health Study (DMS V, 2018) found that over 28 percent of 12-year-olds had at least one tooth affected by MIH.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.7.blo.text: Tooth development begins long before the first milk tooth erupts. Even during pregnancy, the teeth are formed in the unborn baby's jawbone. Cells called ameloblasts are responsible for forming the tooth enamel. They secrete proteins that form the framework for the enamel.

Salts such as calcium and phosphate are then deposited into the enamel, mineralising into hydroxyapatite. Healthy tooth enamel consists of 96 percent hydroxyapatite crystals. Their fish-scale-like arrangement gives teeth enormous biting strength. By the age of two and a half, enamel formation for both milk teeth and permanent teeth is complete. The ameloblasts have finished their task. They then die off, and with them the ability to renew the tooth enamel.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.8.blo.text: With chalky teeth, the enamel does not form properly. The function of the ameloblasts is disrupted. Chalky teeth are also referred to as a mineralisation disorder. There is not enough of the enamel-hardening mineral hydroxyapatite. Instead, the enamel of chalky teeth contains significantly more water and protein. This makes the tooth more brittle and more susceptible to decay-causing bacteria. Studies have shown that the enamel of chalky teeth can be up to 90 percent softer than that of healthy teeth.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.8.tit.text: Porous instead of robust: missing minerals weaken tooth enamel

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.9.blo.text: Scientists have been researching what promotes the development of chalky teeth since the 1980s. So far, the causes of this enamel mineralisation disorder have not been clearly established. Despite a tooth-friendly diet and exemplary oral hygiene, children and adolescents can still suffer from extremely soft tooth enamel. Although the causes have not yet been fully researched, several factors have been identified that are thought to contribute to the formation of chalky teeth:

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.abschnitte.9.tit.text: Not a matter of diet: possible causes of chalky teeth

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.beschreibung.text: Recognising chalky teeth in children early: effective methods and holistic advice on treating Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation (MIH)

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.0.antwort.text: Chalky teeth can become visible very early on. In some cases, an enamel defect shows up in babies or toddlers when the first milk teeth come through. This is known as molar hypomineralisation of the milk teeth (MMH). However, chalky teeth are often first noticed when the first permanent teeth erupt, at around six years of age. That's why children's teeth should be checked regularly from the start, so that discolouration, rough patches or sensitivity can be spotted early and treated appropriately.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.0.frage.text: At what age can chalky teeth appear in children?

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.1.antwort.text: Chalky teeth often show a characteristic white, yellowish or brown discolouration and have a rough or uneven surface. The teeth are also frequently sensitive, particularly when brushing or eating hot, cold or sweet foods. If you notice such symptoms in your child, you should see a dentist to get an accurate diagnosis.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.1.frage.text: What symptoms suggest my child has chalky teeth?

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.10.antwort.text: Untreated chalky teeth are prone to decay and can lead to significant tooth damage. The affected teeth are brittle and can easily chip. This causes not only toothache in children but also problems with chewing and speaking. In severe cases, it may be necessary to extract the affected teeth and replace them with dentures.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.10.frage.text: What are the risks of leaving chalky teeth untreated?

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.11.antwort.text: Parents should make sure their child maintains thorough oral hygiene and builds it into everyday life, including brushing daily with a fluoride toothpaste. Regular visits to the dentist for check-ups and professional cleaning are also important. Pay attention to a healthy diet that is low in sugar and generally healthy, and largely avoid sweet snacks and drinks. The children's dentists at KU64 are happy to provide further information on dental care and oral health when it comes to chalky teeth.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.11.frage.text: How can I help my child care for chalky teeth?

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.12.antwort.text: Even though the name suggests otherwise, fruit purée pouches for toddlers are more of a sweet treat than a substitute for an apple or a banana. The sugar and acid content in these purées is often very high. When a child sucks on the pouch for a long time, the teeth are constantly bathed in acid and sugar. Both can make enamel defects worse, increase the risk of tooth decay, and are therefore not healthy.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.12.frage.text: Are fruit purée pouches bad for my child's dental health?

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.2.antwort.text: A vitamin D deficiency can affect tooth mineralisation and is discussed as a possible factor in chalky teeth. In particular, a deficiency in the mother during pregnancy or in the child during the first years of life can impair enamel formation. However, it is not considered the sole or clearly confirmed cause, but rather one of several possible contributing factors for enamel defects.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.2.frage.text: Is vitamin D deficiency a cause of chalky teeth?

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.3.antwort.text: The exact reasons why someone develops chalky teeth are not yet fully understood. Experts believe that several stresses acting together, from late pregnancy through to the first years of life, play a role. This is the period during which tooth enamel is formed and mineralised. Factors such as infections with high fever, developmental disorders, certain medications like antibiotics, possible environmental factors or a disrupted mineral balance can disrupt this enamel formation.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.3.frage.text: Why do so many children have chalky teeth?

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.4.antwort.text: No, adults can no longer develop new chalky teeth. Chalky teeth (MIH) only form during tooth development, that is, from late pregnancy until around the age of three. Adults can, however, still suffer from chalky teeth that have been present since childhood. If similar defects appear later in life, they are usually due to other causes such as decay, acid damage or other enamel defects.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.5.antwort.text: No, chalky teeth cannot heal on their own. As this is a mineralisation disorder, the defect in the tooth enamel remains for life. It is advisable to treat demineralised teeth early on, in order to protect them, relieve pain and minimise the risk of tooth decay.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.5.frage.text: Can chalky teeth heal on their own?

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.6.antwort.text: Chalky teeth can be preserved for a lifetime if they are recognised early and well protected. However, because the enamel in chalky teeth is weakened from the outset, these teeth are more prone to chipping, sensitivity and decay. Still, there is a fair amount that can be done to prevent further damage. With regular check-ups, preventive care and stabilising measures such as sealants, fillings or crowns, their lifespan can be significantly extended. Consistent care from your dentist is essential to keep chalky teeth functional and largely symptom-free in the long run.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.6.frage.text: How long do chalky teeth last?

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.7.antwort.text: Alongside functional treatment, appearance also matters a great deal to many children and parents when it comes to chalky teeth, especially when visible front teeth are affected. Mild to moderate discolouration can often be noticeably improved through gentle polishing or infiltration, without having to remove healthy tooth structure. In this process, a thin resin penetrates deep into the porous areas of enamel, stabilises the structure from within, can slow down early decay and visibly reduce the typical spots, all without drilling. For more pronounced defects, composite veneers can offer an aesthetic solution that also provides stability. Teeth whitening is only advisable when the enamel is stable and not crumbling, and should always be carried out under dental supervision.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.7.frage.text: How can I treat chalky teeth for cosmetic reasons?

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.8.antwort.text:
Many parents are also interested in homeopathic or alternative forms of support for chalky teeth. As a general rule: homeopathic remedies can promote wellbeing, but they cannot repair structural enamel defects, since these already arose during tooth development. They cannot, therefore, replace dental treatment, but can be used alongside it if desired.
At KU64, we're also happy to advise families from a holistic perspective on request. Our dentist for holistic dentistry and naturopath Clara Constanze Meinberg combines conventional dental expertise with complementary naturopathic approaches, helping parents integrate individual additional measures into treatment sensibly and safely.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.8.frage.text: Can chalky teeth be treated homeopathically?

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.9.antwort.text:
As a rule, statutory health insurance (GKV) covers all measures for preventing tooth decay. This includes, among other things, sealing the permanent molars and necessary fillings. This basic care is covered by statutory health insurance. If the chalky teeth are more pronounced, crowns may be medically advisable. Part of this cost is reimbursed by statutory health insurers.
Services such as infiltrations, composite veneers on front teeth, or particularly aesthetic ceramic crowns, on the other hand, are usually private additional services and are generally not reimbursed by statutory health insurers. Patients with statutory insurance bear these additional costs themselves. At KU64, we discuss transparently before every treatment which services are covered by statutory insurance, which are billed privately, and what costs you should expect in your individual case.

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.faq.9.frage.text: Do statutory health insurers cover the cost of treating chalky teeth?

beschwerde.kreidezaehne.titel.text: Treating chalky teeth in children effectively

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.abschnitte.0.text: Perhaps you noticed it while your child was eating: they always chew on one side, tilt their head slightly, or complain of headaches now and then. Perhaps the paediatrician noticed poor posture, or the nursery teacher mentioned that your child often breathes through their mouth or has a slight lisp when speaking. Such signs are easily overlooked in everyday life and put down to other causes, such as stress, growth or a cold. Yet a crossbite could be behind it. As paediatric dentists at KU64, we know that real concerns often lie behind these observations. That's why our orthodontics team takes the time to address your uncertainties and questions, works with you to establish whether a crossbite is present, and supports you and your child sensitively through every step of the orthodontic treatment. And so that even anxious children can start treatment feeling relaxed, our team also uses laughing gas and therapeutic magic tricks.
When your child's jaw is out of balance

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.abschnitte.1.text: Crossbite is one of the more common jaw misalignments in childhood. It usually develops during the mixed dentition phase, when the baby teeth fall out and are replaced by the permanent teeth. The cause is often an upper jaw that is too narrow combined with a lower jaw that is too wide. As a result, individual lower teeth protrude beyond the upper teeth. Depending on which area is affected and how pronounced the misalignment is, different types of crossbite can be distinguished. These can also occur in combination or merge into one another:
What is a crossbite and how does it develop?

The uneven strain on the jaw leads to muscular imbalances, which can show up as tension in the neck or recurring headaches. In some cases, this tension can even trigger migraines. In children, such symptoms are often put down to other causes, without the jaw being considered as a possible trigger.
Recurring headaches and neck pain

An untreated crossbite increases the risk of craniomandibular dysfunction, or CMD for short. This is a functional disorder of the entire chewing system, which can show up in various ways: clicking in the jaw joint, painful tension in the chewing muscles, pain in the face, temples or jaw when opening the mouth or chewing, and difficulty or blockages when opening the jaw. Teeth grinding is also often linked to CMD. What often begins unnoticed in childhood can develop into a serious and hard-to-treat problem in adulthood.
Craniomandibular dysfunction (CMD)

An incorrect bite automatically affects and shifts neighbouring teeth as well. The uneven strain leads to premature tooth wear, especially on the back teeth. In the long run, this can make fillings or even dentures necessary. Problems biting into food are also possible if the front teeth do not meet correctly.
Tooth wear and consequential damage

A crossbite can affect tongue movement and thereby disrupt speech development. The tongue takes on an incorrect position when speaking, because the jaw does not give it the space it needs. Children may struggle to form certain sounds cleanly, such as 's', 'z' or 'sh', and lisp instead. Other sounds that require precise tongue placement can be affected too. As children are developing and consolidating their speech during this phase, an untreated misalignment usually has long-term effects on pronunciation. Speech therapy can help, but it does not solve the underlying problem.
Impaired speech development

An upper jaw that is too narrow constricts the airways and impairs nasal breathing. This encourages mouth breathing and snoring, which noticeably worsens the child's sleep quality. Poor sleep has a direct effect on concentration, mood and school performance.
Sleep, breathing and concentration

Especially with a one-sided crossbite, visible facial asymmetry can develop over time, as the upper and lower jaw grow unevenly. One side of the face may then appear fuller or wider than the other. The longer a crossbite remains untreated, the more pronounced these changes become. This affects the self-confidence of children and teenagers, who may feel embarrassed about their appearance, smile less often and avoid social situations. Particularly during puberty, this can have far-reaching effects on social and emotional development.
Facial asymmetry and psychological wellbeing

The right time for treatment depends on which stage your child's teeth are at. As a general rule: the earlier a crossbite is spotted, the more gently and effectively it can be treated with children's orthodontics. This is because the jaw is still growing in childhood and is therefore much more mouldable than in adulthood.
Baby teeth or permanent teeth: when is the right time for treatment?

A crossbite can already be identified and treated in baby teeth. At this age, the jaw is especially mouldable, and even small corrections can positively influence later growth. If, for example, a baby tooth is lost too early, a space maintainer can help prevent a crossbite: it keeps the space open for the permanent tooth and stops neighbouring teeth from tilting into the gap and affecting the position of the teeth unfavourably.
Crossbite in baby teeth (from around 3 years)

The phase in which baby teeth fall out and permanent teeth grow in is considered the ideal window for treatment. The jaw is still actively growing, and orthodontic appliances can guide this growth in a targeted way. Treatment during this phase is usually less involved than at a later stage.
Crossbite during the mixed dentition stage (from around 6 years)

If a crossbite was not treated in childhood, correction is still possible in adolescence or adulthood. However, the jaw is no longer growing at that stage, which makes treatment more involved. In severe cases, jaw surgery may become necessary in adulthood.
Crossbite in the permanent dentition

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.abschnitte.2.text: With a unilateral crossbite, one side of the bite is normal, while on the other side the teeth meet incorrectly. This is often caused by tilted teeth or unfavourable tooth positions. The lower jaw often shifts towards the affected side, which can lead to a visible facial asymmetry over time.

A crossbite is not always obvious at first glance. At KU64, diagnosis begins with a thorough clinical examination of the teeth, jaw and bite position. Our orthodontists look not only at the teeth themselves, but also at jaw movements, facial symmetry and your child's posture. If needed, we supplement the examination with digital 3D X-rays, which provide a precise picture of the jaw and tooth roots. Based on this data, we work with you to create an individual treatment plan that determines the right orthodontic therapy, so your child is treated as gently as possible.
Clarity through diagnosis: how KU64 identifies a crossbite

If your child's upper jaw is too narrow, it can be widened specifically with a palatal expansion appliance. The orthodontist attaches the appliance to the back teeth. Parents turn a small screw in the centre of the appliance daily, which gradually widens the palate. Since the palatal suture in children has not yet fused, the treatment can be carried out purely orthodontically, without surgery. In adults, however, the palatal suture has already fused, which means the appliance can only be used after a surgical procedure. A pleasant side effect: many children breathe noticeably better through the nose after treatment.

The quad helix is a fixed wire appliance with four loops, attached to the first permanent molars using metal bands. The orthodontist fits it under tension, so that from the start it pushes the upper teeth outwards and widens the dental arch. During regular check-up appointments, the appliance is adjusted as needed and the current data on jaw development is evaluated. Because it is fixed in place, its effectiveness does not depend on the child's cooperation. As a rule, the quad helix remains in the mouth for around six months, until enough new bone has formed and the crossbite is corrected.

A removable brace is individually made from plastic and wire and is used mainly during the early growth phase. It applies gentle forces to the rows of teeth, encourages growth of the upper jaw, corrects mild tooth tilting and stabilises the bite position at an early stage. Because it can be taken out, it makes oral hygiene easier and reduces the risk of tooth decay. However, the effectiveness of removable braces depends heavily on the child's cooperation. It is often also used to prepare for later treatment with a fixed brace. A special type of removable brace is the activator, which covers both jaws at once. It sits loosely in the mouth and uses the natural movements of the mouth and facial muscles during speaking and swallowing to specifically stimulate jaw growth.

Active plates are a special type of removable brace and consist of individually made, removable plastic plates. They are used particularly during the mixed dentition stage, when the jaw is still pliable. A built-in expansion screw is turned regularly to widen the plate and stimulate jaw growth. Specific springs also push individual misaligned teeth into the correct position, while clasps hold the plate securely in place on the teeth. Because it is removable, oral hygiene remains straightforward.

For more pronounced misalignments, or when permanent teeth are already present, fixed braces are often used. The brackets are bonded directly to the teeth and connected by an archwire, which guides the teeth specifically into the correct position. Unlike removable appliances, they change not only the position of the individual tooth but also the position of the tooth root. They can only be removed by the orthodontist, which ensures a consistent effect regardless of the child's cooperation.

Transparent aligners can be used for a crossbite, though with limitations. They are particularly suitable for milder misalignments or for fine-tuning at the end of treatment, once larger corrections have already been made using other orthodontic appliances. Aligners are individually made, clear plastic trays that are removable and barely visible in everyday life. Because they can be taken out, this makes oral hygiene easier. However, if the crossbite is severe or affects the jawbone itself, aligners are usually not sufficient.

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.abschnitte.3.text: Sometimes it simply runs in the family. An upper jaw that is too narrow, or a comparatively wide lower jaw, can be inherited, as can certain features of tooth position.

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.abschnitte.4.text: Baby teeth are not just for chewing. They also hold the space open for the permanent teeth. If a baby tooth is lost too early, the neighbouring teeth can drift into the gap and affect the position of the teeth later on.

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.abschnitte.5.text: Children who regularly grind their teeth or clench them firmly put constant, unnatural pressure on the jaw. Over time, this can change the bite and encourage or worsen a crossbite.

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.abschnitte.6.text: A shortened tongue tie, malformations of the palate, or congenital conditions such as a cleft lip and palate can cause the upper jaw to develop too narrow, resulting in a crossbite.

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.abschnitte.7.text: Falls or injuries to the jaw or face can affect tooth position or jaw growth unfavourably and, as a result, cause a crossbite.

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.abschnitte.8.text: Parents don't always notice a crossbite straight away in everyday life. Sometimes it shows as a crooked bite when chewing, sometimes as a slight lisp when speaking. In other cases, parents only notice on closer inspection that their child's face looks slightly asymmetrical. The following signs may point to a crossbite and should be checked by an orthodontist:
Crooked rows of teeth, especially around the back teeth
A preference for chewing on one side
Asymmetrical jaw movements or a slight shift when closing the mouth
Lisping or difficulty pronouncing certain sounds
Clicking or limited movement in the jaw joint when chewing or speaking
A crossbite does not go away on its own. The earlier it is spotted, the more gently it can be treated with children's orthodontics.
How can you tell if your child has a crossbite?

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.abschnitte.9.text: If your child consistently bites unevenly, they unconsciously adjust their head position. The head tilts to one side, the shoulders follow, and over time this can lead to poor posture or even a misalignment of the spine. Paediatricians and physiotherapists often notice such signs without linking them to the jaw.
Postural problems and a curved spine

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.beschreibung.text: Crooked chewing, a lisp or headaches? Find out all about the causes, types and treatment of crossbite in children. ✅ Book an appointment at KU64 now

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.einstieg.0.t.text: A crossbite in children is more common than many parents think, and has more far-reaching consequences than it might seem at first glance. If left untreated, it can put a strain not only on the teeth and jaw but on the whole body – from posture to sleep. The good news: with the right treatment at the right time, a crossbite in children can be corrected very well.

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.faq.0.antwor.text: In most cases, the answer is clear: no, a crossbite rarely corrects itself on its own. Dentists and orthodontists therefore recommend acting as early as possible, ideally before the age of ten, to make specific use of natural jaw growth and prevent the condition from worsening. Based on current data on your child's jaw development, our paediatric orthodontics team at KU64 will work with you to determine the optimal time for treatment. If this point has been missed, there's still no need to hesitate: a crossbite can still be treated in older children, adolescents and adults.

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.faq.0.frage.text: What does early-stage tooth decay look like?

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.faq.1.antwor.text: An untreated crossbite can have far-reaching consequences that go well beyond the teeth. These include visible facial asymmetry due to uneven jaw growth, jaw joint problems up to craniomandibular dysfunction, chronic headaches and neck pain caused by muscular imbalances, as well as postural problems and a curved spine. In addition, there is premature tooth wear, an increased risk of tooth decay due to hard-to-reach spaces between teeth, impairments in speech development such as a lisp, and sleep and breathing problems caused by an overly narrow upper jaw. Finally, an untreated crossbite can also affect the self-confidence and social development of children and adolescents. So act early: paediatric orthodontics at KU64 offers the right treatment for every age.

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.faq.1.frage.text: What consequences can a crossbite have for children?

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.faq.2.antwor.text: Depending on the findings, various appliances are used: removable braces, active plates, functional orthodontic devices such as the activator, palatal expansion, the quad helix, fixed braces or transparent aligners. Which method is right depends on the age, severity and type of crossbite. In our paediatric orthodontics practice, we determine the appropriate treatment for our young patients after a thorough examination.

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.faq.2.frage.text: What types of braces are available for children with a crossbite?

beschwerde.kreuzbiss-kinder.titel.text: Crossbite in children: causes, types and treatment – what you can do before it gets worse

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.0.blo.text: A hole in the tooth is often caused by decay, but fractures, defects at the neck of the tooth, wear or leaking old fillings can also lead to a loss of tooth structure.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.0.tit.text: Tooth decay isn't the only cause of a hole in a tooth

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.1.blo.text: A hole in the tooth can appear on the chewing surface, between the teeth, at the neck of the tooth or under an older filling, and places different demands on treatment depending on its position, size and depth.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.1.tit.text: Not every defect is in the same place

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.10.bl.text: Most often, a hole in the tooth is caused by tooth decay: bacteria in plaque convert sugar into acids that attack the hard tooth substance, leading to a defect. This process is mainly encouraged by a sugar-rich diet and insufficient oral hygiene. Individual factors such as dry mouth, the composition of saliva, tooth structure, tooth enamel and genetic factors can also play a role in the development of tooth decay.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.11.bl.text: A hole in the tooth becomes visible when tooth substance is lost through fine cracks, chipped edges or fractures. This can be triggered, for example, by biting on very hard foods such as ice, nuts, sweets or bones. Accidents or direct impact, such as falls or blows, can also be a cause. Bacteria can enter the tooth more easily through the crack or fracture site and lead to tooth decay.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.12.bl.text: A hole in the tooth can also appear around an older filling. This can happen, for example, if a filling becomes leaky over time or a gap forms between the filling and the tooth. A filling that has partially or completely fallen out also leaves an open hole in the tooth at that spot.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.13.bl.text: Wear and erosion can damage the tooth to such an extent that a hole remains. Anyone who frequently comes into contact with acids – for example through fruit, juices, soft drinks or stomach acid from reflux and vomiting – can gradually lose tooth substance. Mechanical influences, such as brushing too hard, a toothbrush that is too firm or abrasive toothpastes, can also encourage holes in the teeth.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.14.bl.text: A lack of important minerals and vitamins can weaken the resistance of the teeth. If the body lacks sufficient vitamin D, calcium or phosphate, for example, the hard tooth substance is less stable and reacts more sensitively to acids and bacteria.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.15.bl.text: Tooth substance is also lost through clenching or grinding the teeth. This often happens unnoticed during sleep. Stress and inner tension are considered important triggers here. Repeated heavy strain gradually wears the teeth down. This encourages fine cracks or further defects.

A hole in the tooth should always be treated by a dentist. Make an appointment with the dentist as soon as the first symptoms appear. This allows us to preserve your dental health and the natural appearance of your tooth as best as possible.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.16.bl.text: A hole in the tooth can form in several places. Where the hole is located plays an important role in treatment, as it can be recognised, reached and treated with varying degrees of ease depending on the location. Areas where plaque settles more easily or that are harder to clean in everyday life are particularly often affected.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.16.ti.text: Where a hole in the tooth can develop

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.17.bl.text: In the gaps between the teeth, a hole often goes unnoticed for a long time, because this area is neither easy to see in the mirror nor fully reachable with a toothbrush. Especially if dental floss or interdental brushes are not used regularly, food remnants and plaque can easily build up there and lead to tooth decay. This is why the gaps between the teeth are among the most common places for a hole in the tooth. A hole between the teeth is often only reliably visible on X-rays, digital scans and photos. Compared with clearly visible tooth surfaces, treating decay between the teeth is often more demanding. The defect is harder to access, and the shape of the tooth as well as the contact with the neighbouring tooth must be reconstructed with particular precision.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.18.bl.text: On some chewing surfaces, fine grooves and indentations form natural niches where plaque can settle more easily and remain longer. If these areas are not cleaned thoroughly, the tooth substance there can gradually be attacked by decay. When a defect develops on the chewing surface, this is known as fissure caries.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.19.bl.text: The tooth is particularly sensitive at the tooth neck, because the enamel is thinner there than on other surfaces. If gum recession due to periodontitis also occurs, these areas become more exposed and react more sensitively to external influences. A hole at the tooth neck therefore affects a sensitive transitional area between the crown and the root of the tooth. Loss of tooth substance is also frequently seen at the tooth neck with incorrect brushing technique or strong pressure from grinding. Treatment here must be particularly gentle and provide a tight seal.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.2.blo.text: A hole in the tooth does not heal on its own. So please arrange a dental appointment as early as possible. KU64 will advise you on suitable filling materials, treatment options and costs.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.2.tit.text: A hole in the tooth needs professional treatment

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.20.bl.text: A hole under an older filling, an inlay, a crown or a bridge is often caused by what is known as secondary caries: this develops when the edges of dental restorations become leaky over time, for instance because the filling material changes. At the edge of a crown or bridge, leaky spots can become a problem, for example if the cement washes out over the years or the restoration becomes loose. During treatment, your dentist will usually remove the old filling or restoration completely to properly assess the extent of the damage. Your dentist will then restore the tooth so that it is sealed and stable again.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.21.bl.text: Tooth structure can also gradually be lost on the smooth outer and inner surfaces of the teeth. Misaligned or crowded teeth can make daily cleaning more difficult, increasing the risk of caries in these areas. In the front tooth area especially, a hole in the tooth often becomes visible earlier, because even small changes affect the natural look. This makes it all the more important to choose a restoration that stabilises your tooth functionally and blends in visually with your smile.

The best way to deal with a hole in a tooth is to have it professionally closed with a filling by your dentist. This replaces the lost tooth structure, seals the tooth again and preserves its natural function when chewing. A hole in a tooth cannot be treated safely or permanently by yourself. At KU64, we will advise you in detail on the right treatment, suitable filling materials and which costs your health insurance will cover.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.22.bl.text: Not every hole in a tooth is treated in the same way. Which type of filling makes sense depends on how much tooth structure has been lost, where the damage is located, and what demands the tooth needs to withstand in the long term. At KU64, our aim is always to treat the tooth so that it remains functionally stable, is treated as gently as possible, and – especially in visible areas – blends in aesthetically. The following criteria play a role in choosing the right filling:

Size of the damage 
Small areas of damage can often be treated directly and gently with a filling, for example a tooth-coloured composite filling. For larger areas of damage, a simple filling is not always enough. In these cases, inlays or other precisely fitted restorations may be needed to stabilise the tooth permanently.

Depth of the hole
If the damage already reaches the inside of the tooth or the nerve is affected, a normal filling is often no longer enough. In this case, root canal treatment may be needed first, before the tooth is permanently restored.

Everyday chewing load
Molars and chewing surfaces have to withstand high forces every day, for example when chewing nuts, bread crusts or raw vegetables. In these areas, the tooth therefore needs a restoration that can withstand chewing pressure and fits precisely into the natural shape of the tooth, so it functions reliably in everyday life.

Condition of the tooth structure
The more healthy tooth structure that remains, the more gently the tooth can usually be treated. If the tooth walls are already thin, unstable or badly damaged, the restoration must also support the tooth and protect it from further loss of structure.

Aesthetic requirements
In visible areas, it matters not only that the tooth is sealed and stable again, but also that its shape, colour and surface look natural. In the front tooth area in particular, the restoration should blend in as unobtrusively as possible with your smile.

Type of damage
Depending on how it developed, the restoration must not only close the hole in the tooth but also take into account the underlying weak point of the tooth. If, for example, a tooth is weakened at the neck due to incorrect brushing technique or receding gums, the restoration should not just seal the area tightly but also protect this sensitive spot gently.

Personal circumstances
Pregnancy, breastfeeding, known intolerances or very sensitive tooth necks place particular demands on treatment. Durability, aesthetics and cost also play an important role when choosing the right restoration.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.22.ti.text: Which criteria matter when choosing a filling

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.23.bl.text: With the right care and regular check-ups, you can do a lot to prevent a hole in a tooth:
Brush your teeth thoroughly twice a day: this removes plaque and bacteria before they can attack the tooth structure.
Clean the spaces between your teeth too: dental floss or interdental brushes help in places your toothbrush can't reach well.
Use fluoride toothpaste: fluoride strengthens the enamel and makes it more resistant to acids and therefore to caries.
Watch your sugar intake: frequent sugary snacks and drinks encourage bacteria to produce acids, which leads to caries.
Drink water rather than soft drinks: this protects your teeth from extra strain caused by acid and sugar.
If you grind your teeth, use an individually fitted grinding splint: this takes the strain off your teeth and protects them from further wear.
Have your teeth checked regularly: this often means early changes are spotted before an actual hole develops.
Make use of professional prevention: regular professional teeth cleaning helps remove stubborn plaque and lowers your risk of caries.
Protect your fissures with a sealant: this helps prevent caries forming in hard-to-reach grooves on the chewing surfaces.
Seek individual advice if you have an increased risk: for sensitive teeth, crowded teeth or frequent problems, a tailored prevention plan is particularly worthwhile.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.23.ti.text: How you can prevent a hole in your tooth

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.24.bl.text: Do you have symptoms from a hole in your tooth, would you like the cause checked, or would you like to arrange a treatment appointment? Then you're in the right place at KU64. We'll advise you personally on the next steps, on suitable care, on appropriate filling materials, and on which costs your health insurance will cover.
Short waiting times and a pleasant, relaxed atmosphere make your visit to KU64 as comfortable as possible.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.24.ti.text: Contact and appointments for a hole in the tooth

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.28.bl.text: A hole in the tooth is not a minor matter – it's a defect that usually keeps growing and deepening without treatment. The earlier the cause is checked by a dentist and the tooth is treated appropriately, the more of your natural tooth structure can be preserved. With good oral hygiene, regular check-ups and an early appointment with your dentist, you can help prevent greater damage and more extensive treatment.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.28.ti.text: In summary: a hole in the tooth should be treated early

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.29.bl.text: You should have a hole in your tooth treated as early as possible, even without any toothache. The sooner the defect is treated by a dentist, the greater the chance of preserving the tooth with a comparatively simple and gentle treatment. If you wait too long, the hole can deepen and the tooth structure can be weakened further. This often means more extensive treatment is needed. An early appointment therefore not only helps avoid discomfort, but often also helps keep your tooth stable in the long term.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.29.ti.text: How quickly does a hole in the tooth need to be treated?

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.3.blo.text: Some people first notice only a rough spot or a dark mark, others become sensitive to cold, hot or sweet stimuli, or feel pain when chewing. A hole in the tooth may be behind this. It can develop in quite different places, for example in a front tooth, a back tooth, between the teeth or at the neck of the tooth. Especially in the early stages, a hole in the tooth often goes unnoticed at first and is neither easy to spot in the mirror nor reliably felt with the tongue. Once initial symptoms appear, the defect has usually already progressed and should be treated by a dentist. Which type of filling and material is suitable then depends on the position and size of the hole in the tooth. The sooner you come to us with your symptoms, though, the more gently we at KU64 can preserve your tooth.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.3.tit.text: When a hole in the tooth causes discomfort

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.30.bl.text: A hole that has already formed in the tooth doesn't heal by itself. Once the tooth surface has broken down – for example due to tooth decay – the lost tooth structure doesn't naturally rebuild. This is only different in very early stages: if the enamel is already affected but no real hole has formed yet, the process can in some cases be stopped or partly reversed with fluoride and good oral hygiene. With an actual hole in the tooth, however, dental treatment is needed so the decay doesn't deepen further and the tooth can be preserved. To do this, your dentist needs to clean the affected area, remove the decay by drilling, and then seal the tooth again with a filling.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.30.ti.text: Can a hole in the tooth heal on its own?

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.31.bl.text: No, a hole in the tooth doesn't always cause toothache straight away. Especially at the start, many defects go unnoticed for a long time and cause no symptoms, or only very mild ones, at first. Pain often only appears once deeper layers of the tooth are affected, or when the tooth becomes sensitive to cold, heat, sweet food or pressure. This is exactly why regular check-ups are so important: a hole may already be present even though you don't yet feel any clear pain.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.31.ti.text: Is a hole in the tooth always painful?

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.32.bl.text: Yes, not every hole in the tooth is caused by tooth decay alone. Fractures or erosion from acids can also lead to a loss of tooth structure and cause a defect. That's why it's always important to establish exactly what's behind the hole before treatment. Depending on the cause, your tooth will need a different treatment and different protection against further loss of substance.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.32.ti.text: Can a hole form in the tooth without tooth decay?

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.33.bl.text: Hormonal changes, more frequent cravings for sweet or sour foods, and vomiting with stomach acid can make teeth more prone to decay and holes during pregnancy. Even during pregnancy, a hole in a tooth should be treated so that the defect does not deepen and inflammation is avoided. For treatments that can be planned, the second trimester – weeks 13 to 27 of pregnancy – is often considered particularly favourable, as the baby's early organ development is already complete by then. Many pregnant women feel physically more stable during this phase than at the start or end of pregnancy. However, acute problems are treated at any stage of pregnancy. Modern, well-tolerated filling materials can be used for treatment. Local anaesthetic is usually possible, and X-rays are only taken when medically necessary.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.34.bl.text: With tooth decay, the dentist usually has to drill the affected area to remove the damaged tooth substance and then fill the hole. If larger holes are present or the tooth is badly damaged, dental restorations may be needed instead of a filling.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.34.ti.text: How is a hole in a tooth repaired?

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.35.bl.text: If a hole in a tooth is left untreated, it will grow larger over time and reach deeper into the tooth. This can first cause sensitivity, then pain, inflammation, and eventually even an abscess. The longer you wait, the higher the risk that the tooth will need more extensive treatment. In the worst case, the tooth is lost and you will need dental restorations.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.35.ti.text: What happens if I don't have a hole in my tooth treated?

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.36.bl.text: A hole in a tooth cannot be permanently repaired by yourself. In an emergency, you can use dental repair putty from a pharmacy to cover the area briefly and protect the tooth a little until your dental appointment, for example if a filling has fallen out. However, this is no substitute for dental treatment, as it neither removes the cause, such as decay, nor seals the tooth permanently.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.36.ti.text: How can I temporarily close a hole in a tooth?

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.4.blo.text: A hole in the tooth forms once solid tooth structure has already been lost. A hole in the tooth can have various causes and is not always solely the result of decay. The further the defect spreads into the interior of the tooth, the more the tooth loses in stability, protection and load-bearing capacity. Since lost tooth structure does not build itself back up, a hole in the tooth should always be checked and treated appropriately by your dentist.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.4.tit.text: What is a hole in the tooth?

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.5.blo.text: Not every hole in the tooth is immediately obvious as such. Often the tooth first changes only slightly before a visible defect develops. Depending on the stage, the colour, surface and firmness of the tooth structure can become noticeable in different ways.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.5.tit.text: How to recognise a hole in the tooth

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.6.blo.text: In the early stage, often only small changes appear on the tooth surface. These include white, chalky spots, slight brown discolouration or a dull surface. Some people also notice slight sensitivity, even though no clear hole is visible yet.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.7.blo.text: If the defect has progressed further, dark spots, small dips or a damaged area on the tooth may be visible. In some cases, the enamel there feels rough, uneven or brittle.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.8.blo.text: A hole in the tooth is not always noticeable straight away. At first, there may be no symptoms at all. In other cases, further, rather subtle symptoms accompany the visible changes, for example:
Sensitivity to stimuli: hot or cold drinks, sweets or acidic foods trigger a twinge, sting or unpleasant feeling in the affected tooth.
Sensitivity to pressure: the tooth becomes sensitive as soon as pressure is applied to it, for example when biting down or brushing.
A rough feeling on the tooth: a spot on the tooth feels unusual, sharp or uneven to the tongue.
Food keeps getting stuck: food repeatedly lodges in the same spot.
Dental floss catches or tears: when cleaning between the teeth, the floss keeps catching or fraying in the same spot.
Recurring gum irritation: the gum repeatedly reacts sensitively, becomes irritated or slightly inflamed in the same spot.
An unfamiliar feeling when chewing: the tooth feels different from usual while eating.
An unpleasant taste in the mouth: an unusual or bothersome taste is noticeable in the mouth.
Bad breath: an unpleasant smell remains in the mouth despite brushing your teeth.
Pulling or throbbing toothache: repeated pulling or throbbing pain occurs, even without a clear trigger.

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.8.tit.text: Symptoms: these signs may indicate a hole in the tooth

beschwerde.loch-im-zahn.abschnitte.9.blo.text: A hole in the tooth doesn't always develop in the same way. Very different triggers can lie behind the loss of tooth substance – from classic tooth decay to mechanical stress or already damaged areas of the tooth.
