beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.abschnitte.text: Some people have it constantly, for others it only appears now and then: bad breath. The causes are varied and can be found in food, dental care or more generally in the mouth or body. KU64 can help you if you want to understand and treat bad breath rather than just cover it up.
Tips, questions and answers from the halitosis clinic
Bad breath can be caused by bacterial deposits in the mouth, inflammation and illness in the body, or by diet and stimulants.
Causes of bad breath

Bad breath and unpleasant breath are usually caused by inadequate oral hygiene. If you only brush and floss irregularly, you create a breeding ground for odour-causing bacteria. They collect on tooth surfaces, between teeth and in gum pockets. Your tongue, with its grooves, is also an ideal place for them to settle.

There is a link between tooth decay and bad breath, particularly when decay occurs in hard-to-see areas. This includes the spaces between teeth, as well as areas under existing or damaged fillings or ill-fitting dentures, where so-called hidden decay can develop. Bacteria collect in these damaged tooth structures and release unpleasant odours. Because decay in such areas rarely causes early symptoms, it can progress unnoticed and remain the cause of persistent bad breath until your dentist identifies and treats it.

Bad breath is considered an early sign of gum inflammation (gingivitis). This causes redness, swelling and bleeding of the gums. If left untreated, the inflammation can develop into periodontitis, in which gum pockets form. Bacteria multiply particularly strongly in these pockets and release odour-active metabolic products, which cause persistent unpleasant breath. As with tooth decay, this inflammation develops gradually and often goes unnoticed for a long time. In advanced stages, the bacteria spread along the tooth root and damage the jawbone.

A dry mouth can be caused by, among other things, insufficient fluid intake, breathing through the mouth at night, snoring, certain medications, stress, hormonal changes or disorders of the salivary glands. It is a common cause of bad breath. When there is not enough saliva, the mouth can no longer clean itself naturally. Bacteria, dead cells and other residues remain in the mouth for longer and can multiply unchecked. In this dry environment, odour-active substances form, leading to persistent bad breath. Bad breath is often less noticeable after eating, because saliva flow is briefly stimulated. The increased saliva dilutes odour-active substances and temporarily flushes them out of the mouth.
Causes within the mouth

Bacterial infections of the nose, throat and pharynx can also cause bad breath. Infections in these areas often lead to a build-up of secretions, bacteria and dead cells. These release odour-active substances that can be noticeable both when breathing out through the mouth and through the nose. Bad breath therefore often occurs alongside colds, chronic nasal congestion, acute or chronic sinus infections (sinusitis) or throat infections (pharyngitis). Chronic inflammation of the throat can also cause you to notice an unpleasant smell from the mouth over a longer period of time.

Tonsil stones, also known as tonsilloliths, are small, usually yellowish-white deposits that form in the deep grooves (crypts) of the tonsils. They consist of a mixture of bacteria, dead cells, mucus and food debris that collect there and break down. This process produces odour-active sulphur compounds. They can cause pronounced bad breath that persists despite thorough oral care.

As someone affected, you won't notice tonsil stones straight away. You feel healthy and usually have no pain. Instead, you may notice persistent bad breath, an unpleasant taste, repeated throat clearing or a feeling of something stuck in your throat. Tonsil stones can occur regularly, especially if the tonsils are enlarged or have a jagged surface. If you experience recurring symptoms, have them checked by a doctor.

In some cases, bad breath points to metabolic conditions such as diabetes mellitus, as well as conditions affecting the digestive or respiratory system. With these conditions, metabolic processes or the composition of exhaled air changes, which can show up as noticeable bad breath. Liver conditions such as hepatitis or blood disorders such as leukaemia can also contribute to bad breath, as they affect how the body breaks down metabolic products.

Many patients suspect a gastrointestinal condition behind their bad breath and hope a gastroscopy will help. In most cases, however, bad breath is not a sign of a condition affecting the digestive tract. According to current findings, around 90 per cent of all cases of bad breath originate in the mouth, nose or throat. Conditions of the stomach or intestines, such as gastro-oesophageal reflux, are rarely involved. These should mainly be considered if you also notice typical symptoms such as heartburn, acid reflux or stomach problems. Without such accompanying symptoms, the cause of bad breath is usually much closer to home.
Causes outside the mouth

Many people are familiar with the unpleasant taste or breath that follows eating onions, garlic or other foods. The breakdown products involved enter the bloodstream and can be noticeable in your breath for a while. This is usually not a case of chronic bad breath, but a temporary effect that disappears on its own after some time.

Cigarettes, coffee or alcohol can also affect your breath in the short term. Smoking leaves its own odorous substances in the mouth, while coffee and alcohol dry the mouth out further. This creates more favourable conditions for odour-causing bacteria, so bad breath can become stronger or last longer.

Certain medications can also lead to bad breath, as they affect metabolic processes or change the composition of the oral flora. These include antibiotics, antidepressants, antihistamines and medication for Parkinson's disease, among others.

Ongoing stress affects the autonomic nervous system and hormone balance. This can throw your saliva flow, digestion and eating habits out of balance. Studies also show that psychological factors such as stress, anxiety or low mood can heighten the perception of bad breath, even when only mild odours are actually present.
Is bad breath affecting your everyday life and do you suspect one of the causes mentioned above? Our team at KU64 is happy to help. Book an appointment for the halitosis consultation.
Everyday factors

Children can suffer from bad breath too. As with most adults, the causes often lie in the mouth – for example, brushing too rarely or not thoroughly enough. Enlarged adenoids can also be a cause of bad breath, as they restrict breathing through the nose. Affected children breathe through the mouth and sometimes snore. In this case, it makes sense to have the child examined by an ENT doctor.
Bad breath in children: possible triggers

People affected by bad breath rarely notice it themselves. A common approach is to breathe into your hands and smell them to try to detect bad breath. In fact, you're more likely to smell your skin's own scent than your breath. Guides recommend the following tests to reliably check for bad breath:

Spoon test: Press your tongue against a clean spoon and let the saliva dry. Then smell the spoon. The smell of the spoon gives you an idea of your breath odour. If you don't have a spoon to hand, you can use your wrist instead.
Floss test: Use dental floss to clean between your teeth, then smell it afterwards. An unpleasant smell is a clear sign of bad breath.

Spit test: The smell of your saliva can also tell you something about your breath. Spit several times into an empty container and cover it for a few minutes. If the contents smell unpleasant when you open it, this points to bad breath.
Recognising bad breath: tips that can help

Bad breath is an unpleasant companion. Those affected want to get rid of it as quickly as possible. For most causes of bad breath, there are simple methods that support a healthy oral flora and promise a quick effect against unpleasant breath. The dentists at KU64 recommend only turning to anti-bad-breath tablets or other medical products if hygiene measures alone don't bring improvement. The specialists at KU64 Berlin are happy to advise you and put together an individual treatment plan against bad breath:
Regular oral care: Brush your teeth after meals for at least three minutes. Sugar-free dental chewing gum is a good option on the go, when you can't brush your teeth.
Clean between your teeth: Use dental floss and interdental brushes as part of your daily oral care.
Clean your tongue: Remove any coating from your tongue thoroughly, ideally with a tongue cleaner or tongue scraper.
Change your toothbrush: Replace your toothbrush regularly, every six to eight weeks. This helps prevent bacteria that cause bad breath from multiplying on the brush.

Use mouthwash: Use mouthwash to prevent bacteria from settling in. A simple home remedy for bad breath is a natural mouthwash made from water with baking soda or lemon juice. It has an antibacterial effect and freshens the breath.

Balanced diet: Reduce your consumption of protein-rich foods, onions and garlic, as well as stimulants such as coffee, alcohol and tobacco. Instead, eat plenty of fruit and vegetables and make sure you have a healthy balance of vitamins and minerals.
Diets in moderation: Avoid extreme low-carb diets or strict fasting. Both can encourage bad breath.
Less sugar: For the sake of your health, reduce your sugar consumption. This deprives odour-causing bacteria of their food source while also protecting your teeth.
Drink enough: Make sure you drink enough fluids throughout the day. Ideally, drink at least two litres of water or unsweetened tea.
Chew herbs: Herbs such as peppermint, sage, eucalyptus, chamomile and parsley are effective against bad breath and healthy too. Doctors recommend chewing the fresh herbs for around ten minutes.
What helps against bad breath: useful tips and home remedies

Special dental care products can help eliminate bad breath. Zinc-containing toothpaste, for example, binds sulphur-containing odour particles in the mouth. Tin fluoride also has an antibacterial effect. Whether mouth sprays, deodorant capsules, pastilles or chewing gum: the dentists at KU64 Berlin will be happy to put together a list of the best products for fresh breath. You can then buy your new hygiene products directly on site in our prophylaxis shop on the fifth floor.
Buy oral hygiene products for your teeth on site

Dental care products such as mouthwashes, chewing gum and sweets only help against bad breath temporarily. What's needed instead is a thorough clean to eliminate the local causes of bad breath. In addition to regular prophylaxis appointments, dentists recommend thorough, regular professional teeth cleaning.

During a professional teeth cleaning, the dental hygienists and specialised prophylaxis assistants at KU64 Berlin attend to your entire mouth: the teeth, the spaces between them, the gums and the tongue. This tackles the most common causes of bad breath. With the help of magnifying loupes, nothing goes unnoticed. This allows us to give you tailored advice for your daily oral hygiene routine and show you what helps in your particular case against unpleasant breath odour. We are here for you with our years of experience in oral hygiene. This way, you can be sure that fresh breath and healthy teeth won't remain just a brief pleasure.
What to do about bad breath: professional teeth cleaning

KU64 Berlin offers a professional halitosis consultation for patients with bad breath complaints. Our halitosis specialists, dental hygienist Michaela Kunkel and prophylaxis assistant Nicole Dickhoff-Kranz, guide you sensitively on the path to fresh breath: from diagnosis to treatment. In doing so, they work closely with dentists, ENT specialists, internists and dental physicians.
Goodbye bad breath: the halitosis consultation at KU64 Berlin

During the consultation, our specialists first determine whether halitosis is actually present and what the possible causes are. Together with the patient, they discuss the extent to which medication, oral hygiene, diet or existing illnesses may be contributing to the bad breath. To identify the individual causes of the bad breath, our experts examine you closely. They check fillings, crown margins and coating on the tongue. The teeth are also examined for signs of decay.

To assess the breath and its odour intensity, our dental hygienists use a halimeter. The device measures the sulphur content of the breath and provides a reliable diagnosis of bad breath. Once all the examination results are available, our halitosis specialists draw up a detailed treatment plan and give you tips and information on proper dental care and diet. Treatment options for persistent, pathological bad breath vary from person to person and depend on the underlying causes.
How the halitosis consultation works
Bad breath is often noticeable through a persistent unpleasant taste, coating on the tongue, a dry mouth, or comments from people around you.
Noticing bad breath
The patient's ongoing cooperation is crucial to the treatment of bad breath and begins even before the first consultation. We therefore ask our patients to follow these guidelines:
no antibiotics for three weeks before the appointment
no onions, garlic, alcohol or coffee for 48 hours before the appointment
on the day of treatment, no mint products or mouthwash, no smoking, no cosmetics or perfume
no oral hygiene four hours before the appointment, no eating and at most a little water to drink
Requirements for successful treatment

Have you already made an appointment for the halitosis consultation? For a thorough consultation, please fill in the halitosis questionnaire in advance and bring it with you to the appointment. You can download the questionnaire in German and English:
Halitosis questionnaire (DE) – download
Halitosis Questionnaire (EN) – download
Halitosis questionnaire for download
As a rule, one to two sessions about a week apart are enough to get bad breath under control for the long term. The cost is 170 Euro for both sessions.
Fast help guaranteed: cost and duration of treatment
If you would like to treat bad breath specifically, KU64's specialised halitosis clinic can help identify the causes and find the right treatment.
Treating bad breath

Bad breath is more than a medical issue: it can noticeably affect everyday life. Many people feel insecure in conversations, keep their distance or avoid closeness, worried that others might notice the smell. This often leads to feelings of shame, even though the causes are usually harmless and treatable. When bad breath becomes a constant companion, it affects not only self-confidence but also social contacts and personal wellbeing. This makes it all the more important to clarify the cause. In KU64's specialised halitosis clinic, we support you in doing exactly that.
When bad breath becomes a burden

Bad breath is an unpleasant smell on the breath that arises when the natural balance of the oral flora is disturbed. In a healthy mouth, there is a balance between aerobic bacteria, which need oxygen, and anaerobic bacteria, which live without it. When this balance is disrupted, anaerobic bacteria multiply excessively. These feed mainly on protein-rich food residues such as dairy products, fish, meat and eggs. In doing so, they produce what are known as volatile sulphur compounds (VSC). When these sulphur compounds are present in higher concentrations, they cause the typical unpleasant, sometimes rotten smell that we perceive as bad breath.
How does bad breath develop?

In everyday language, the terms bad breath, foetor ex ore and halitosis are often used to mean the same thing. Medically, however, there are differences that matter for correct classification and treatment. What matters here is whether you notice the smell only from the mouth, or also when breathing out through the nose.
Not all bad breath is the same: how to tell the difference
Foetor ex ore describes bad breath that is only noticeable when speaking or breathing out through the mouth. The causes are usually found in the mouth or throat.
Foetor ex ore

Unlike foetor ex ore, people with halitosis can also notice it when breathing out through the nose. In many cases, this smell also originates in the mouth, nose or throat, but it can also point to underlying causes.
Halitosis

Bad breath has many different causes. Short-term bad breath after certain foods or stimulants is usually harmless. However, if the unpleasant smell persists, there is often a specific trigger behind it that should be identified by your dentist.
What can cause bad breath?

The dentists at KU64 will be happy to show you, step by step, what to pay closer attention to in your oral hygiene during a check-up appointment.

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.0.frag.text: Why do I have bad breath despite brushing my teeth?

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.1.antw.text: Bad breath can point to various conditions, including gum inflammation, periodontitis, tooth decay, inflammation of the nose and throat, tonsil stones, and, less commonly, liver, respiratory or metabolic diseases such as diabetes. In most cases, however, the cause lies in the mouth and can be identified, treated and prevented through targeted diagnosis.

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.1.frag.text: Which illnesses cause severe bad breath?

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.2.antw.text: Only rarely. In more than 90 percent of cases, bad breath originates in the mouth, nose or throat. A connection with the stomach, for example through reflux, is usually only relevant if additional symptoms such as heartburn also occur.

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.2.frag.text: Can bad breath come from the stomach or bowel?

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.3.antw.text: A lack of certain nutrients can also play a part in bad breath, though it is rarely the sole cause. A deficiency in zinc, vitamin C, vitamin D or iron can weaken the gums and oral mucosa and encourage inflammation. More often, however, bad breath is caused by bacteria in the mouth, for example through plaque or inflammation.

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.3.frag.text: What deficiency leads to bad breath?

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.4.antw.text: No. Bad breath has different causes, so there is no one-size-fits-all solution. It often cannot be resolved through surface measures alone, such as chewing gum or mouthwash. An effective treatment depends on a targeted diagnosis.

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.4.frag.text: Is there a remedy that works 100 percent against bad breath?

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.5.antw.text: Persistent bad breath requires an analysis of the underlying cause. Depending on the findings, options include professional teeth cleaning, treatment of inflammation, periodontitis therapy, or checking for tonsil stones or conditions such as diabetes. At KU64, this takes place in the halitosis consultation.

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.5.frag.text: What helps with persistent or long-lasting bad breath?

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.6.antw.text: Mouthwash usually only masks odours temporarily. The actual cause – such as plaque, inflammation or bacterial build-up in the mouth – remains if you do not treat it directly.

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.6.frag.text: Why does mouthwash often only help with bad breath in the short term?

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.7.antw.text: Stimulating saliva flow, time and thorough oral hygiene help best. The smell of garlic usually disappears on its own once the breakdown products have left the body. Certain foods such as apples, salad or fresh herbs can help, as they bind odour-active substances or encourage saliva flow. You can help prevent it by drinking enough after eating and thoroughly cleaning your teeth and tongue, so that odour-active substances are removed more quickly.

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.7.frag.text: What neutralises bad breath after eating garlic?

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.8.antw.text: Bad breath is usually harmless, but should be taken seriously if it persists, is very strong, or comes with other symptoms. In these cases, get in touch with your dentist. Or have the causes checked by your doctor.

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.8.frag.text: Is bad breath a concern for dental health?

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.9.antw.text: If bad breath persists despite regular oral care, or keeps coming back, an examination by your dentist is advisable. This way, hidden causes can be identified and treated specifically. For persistent symptoms, KU64 also offers a specialised halitosis consultation, in which possible triggers are systematically investigated and treated individually. You will also receive valuable information on caring for your teeth and tongue.

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.faq.9.frag.text: When should I get bad breath checked despite good oral care?

beschwerde.mundgeruch-was-tun.titel.text: A delicate subject: bad breath – what can you do about it?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.abschnitte..text: Oral thrush is a yeast infection of the mucous membrane in the mouth. It often shows up as whitish patches, redness and a burning sensation on the tongue, inside of the cheeks or on the palate.
How to recognise oral thrush
Babies, older people, pregnant women and people with a weakened immune system or after a course of antibiotics are particularly likely to be affected.
Who is particularly at risk

Yes, oral thrush can be painful, but it doesn't have to be. Some people feel only slight discomfort, while others experience considerably stronger pain, especially when eating or swallowing. How severe the pain is depends on how pronounced the inflammation of the mucous membrane is.
Is oral thrush painful?

Not every white change in the mouth is automatically a fungal infection. Oral thrush can easily be mistaken for other conditions, as similar symptoms also occur with other changes to the mucous membrane.
White patches in the mouth – not always oral thrush

Mouth ulcers (aphthous ulcers) are small, painful lesions on the mucous membrane that usually appear yellowish-white and are surrounded by a reddish rim. Unlike oral thrush, they tend to occur as isolated spots rather than as a widespread coating. Mouth ulcers often heal on their own within one to two weeks.
Mouth ulcers and „white blisters“ in the mouth

White patches that cannot be wiped away and persist over a longer period may also indicate what is known as leukoplakia. This is a chronic change to the mucous membrane that occurs more frequently in smokers or through alcohol consumption. Such changes should always be checked by a dentist, as they – unlike oral thrush – are not caused by an infection.
Leukoplakia and other white changes

So-called „COVID tongue“ is also not the same as oral thrush. COVID tongue usually describes inflammatory changes or swelling associated with a viral infection. The tongue appears whitish-coated, patchy, swollen, or shows enlarged papillae, and thus differs in cause and appearance from fungal oral candidiasis.
If you are unsure whether you have oral thrush or another change to the mucous membrane, have the cause checked by a dentist and book an appointment at KU64 now.
COVID tongue

Oral thrush usually does not result from a single trigger, but from the interplay of various factors that affect the delicate balance of the oral flora. Certain situations or habits can weaken the defences of the oral mucosa and encourage the growth of yeast fungi. The most common causes include:

Weakened immune system: Reduced defences, for example due to chronic illness, immunosuppressive medication, radiotherapy or chemotherapy, older age, or significant physical strain, encourage the growth of the yeast fungus in the mouth.
Dry mouth: When there isn't enough saliva, the mouth's natural cleaning and protective function is impaired, making it easier for fungi to settle and spread.
Smoking and alcohol consumption: Nicotine and alcohol can irritate the oral mucosa and impair its defensive function, thereby encouraging the development of oral thrush.
Chronic illness: Conditions such as diabetes mellitus, HIV infection, or cancer can have a lasting effect on the immune system or metabolism and weaken the defences in the mouth.
Taking antibiotics: Oral thrush caused by antibiotics occurs because they disrupt the bacterial balance of the oral flora, giving yeast fungi room to multiply.

Inhaled corticosteroid sprays (asthma sprays): Oral thrush caused by asthma or corticosteroid sprays can occur when residue of the active ingredient remains in the mouth and weakens the local immune defences.
Prolonged stress: Ongoing psychological or physical stress can weaken the immune system and is therefore one of the factors that can increase the risk of oral thrush.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Oral thrush occurs more frequently during pregnancy, as hormonal changes and an altered immune state can increase the risk.
Possible causes and contributing factors

Oral thrush can develop unnoticed under dentures, as yeast fungi attach particularly well to plastic surfaces. Often, the infection only becomes visible once the denture is removed. Pressure points or ill-fitting dentures can also encourage local inflammation. Thorough, daily cleaning of removable dentures is therefore especially important.
Please note: dentures increase the risk of oral thrush

Oral thrush occurs relatively often in babies and infants, as their immune system is not yet fully developed in the first months of life and the oral flora still needs to stabilise. As with adults, even minor changes in the balance of the oral mucosa can allow yeast fungi to multiply more strongly.

In general, oral thrush in babies is not dangerous and usually runs an uncomplicated course. It becomes a concern mainly when your child is barely drinking or shows signs of dehydration. In such situations, you should have your child examined promptly. At KU64, we take your child's symptoms seriously and provide quick clarity and reassurance through a gentle examination.
What parents should look out for: oral thrush in babies, infants and young children

If you notice unusual white patches in your baby's mouth for the first time, it's natural to wonder: What does oral thrush look like in babies? How can I tell the difference from harmless milk residue?

Similar to adults, oral thrush in babies shows up as pale, firmly adhering patches in the mouth. These whitish to cream-coloured deposits are usually found on the tongue, the palate or the inside of the cheeks. Unlike harmless milk residue, these patches cannot simply be wiped away. The mucosa underneath may appear red or irritated. Changed breath odour can occur, but doesn't always. In infants, the affected areas of the mouth are often larger than in adults.
How can I recognise oral thrush in my baby?

When a baby has oral thrush, this is often noticeable in everyday life, especially during feeding. Oral thrush is painful for babies. But since infants cannot express their pain in words, they usually show discomfort indirectly.

If your child repeatedly pulls away during breastfeeding or feeding, turns their head away, or becomes unusually restless, this may indicate that the inflamed oral mucosa is reacting painfully. Some babies also become more sensitive to touch around the mouth or seem generally more irritable than usual.
How does a baby with oral thrush behave?
An early check-up by a dentist or doctor allows targeted treatment with local solutions and gels, and lowers the risk of the thrush spreading to the throat or oesophagus.
Why you should act in good time

Unlike babies, where the still-immature immune system plays the main role, oral thrush in toddlers and older children often occurs in connection with antibiotic treatment or a temporarily weakened immune defence. The symptoms are similar to those in adults and should also be clinically assessed at this age.
Oral thrush in toddlers and children

Pregnant patients often ask our dentists at KU64: Does oral thrush occur more often during pregnancy? In fact, hormonal changes and an altered immune status during pregnancy can make the mucous membranes react more sensitively. This slightly increases the risk of excessive growth of yeast fungi.
A special phase, special attention: oral thrush during pregnancy and breastfeeding

During breastfeeding, mutual transmission between baby and mother can occur. If the child has oral thrush, yeast fungi can also settle around the nipple. This is known as nipple thrush. Conversely, an infection on the breast can be passed on to the baby.
In the mother, common signs include:
intense itching or burning of the nipples
sharp pain during or after breastfeeding
reddish, shiny or flaky skin on the nipple and areola
small cracks (fissures) or pinpoint blisters
It's characteristic that the pain can be pronounced even though only minor changes are visible on the surface.

Quite often, the baby shows symptoms of oral thrush or nappy thrush at the same time. Nipple thrush is encouraged by small injuries to the nipple, a warm, moist environment, for example from rarely changed breast pads, as well as by the general risk factors already known to play a role in oral thrush.
In such cases, you and your baby should be examined together. If necessary, we treat you and your child at KU64 in parallel to prevent repeated mutual infection.
Breastfeeding: how mother and baby transmit oral thrush
Yeast fungi of the Candida genus can generally be passed between people. Whether this actually leads to oral thrush depends on how resilient the affected person's oral mucosa and immune system are.
Infection: how is oral thrush transmitted?

Infection usually happens through direct contact with mucous membranes or through shared objects. However, transmission does not automatically lead to symptoms. Often the fungus remains without causing any complaints.
Transmission can occur through, among other things:
intensive kissing
oral sex
shared cutlery or drinking vessels
licking a dummy or bottle clean in everyday family life
breastfeeding between mother and baby
Within partnerships or families, mutual transmission can therefore occur.
Typical routes of transmission in everyday life

If you have visible symptoms and have not yet started treatment, the risk of passing on oral thrush is increased. Once you are undergoing treatment and the symptoms have noticeably improved or fully healed, the risk of infection usually drops significantly.
How long you should avoid close contact

Which doctor is responsible for oral thrush depends on age and symptoms. In most cases, the dental practice is the first point of contact, since oral thrush affects the oral mucosa and can be properly assessed here.
GPs or ENT doctors can also make the diagnosis and start treatment. For babies and young children, a paediatrician should be consulted to assess the situation appropriately for their age.
The right point of contact for oral thrush

At KU64, our dentists can identify oral thrush in many cases through a thorough examination of the oral mucosa alone. Typical coatings and signs of inflammation can usually be assessed directly, without the need for extensive tests.
How KU64 identifies oral thrush

If there is any uncertainty during the examination, or if symptoms return despite treatment, our dentists at KU64 take a further step: in such cases, we take a swab of the affected mucosa if needed. This is examined in a laboratory to clearly confirm the fungus and adjust the treatment accordingly.
Terms such as “oral thrush test”, “mouth fungus test” or “tongue fungus test” usually refer to exactly this kind of swab. A special rapid test is usually not required.
Oral thrush test: when is a swab useful?

The course of oral thrush varies from person to person and depends on the cause as well as your general immune defences. In mild cases, the infection stays limited to the oral mucosa and causes mainly local symptoms. Without treatment, however, oral thrush can persist for a longer period.

For treatment, you will usually be given medication against yeast fungi, known as antifungals. Commonly used active ingredients include nystatin or amphotericin B. These inhibit the growth of the fungi or fight them directly. They are often prescribed as a liquid solution that you apply directly in the mouth. Depending on the situation, lozenges or – if the lips are affected – an ointment may also be useful. In very rare cases where the oral thrush pathogens spread beyond the oral mucosa into the bloodstream, treatment with medication given via a vein is required.
Treatment and duration of oral thrush

A whitish coating in the mouth, a burning tongue or pain when swallowing – oral thrush can make itself clearly felt in everyday life. What at first seems minor quickly becomes a noticeable burden for many people. This is especially true when the symptoms don't clear up on their own. Eating suddenly feels uncomfortable, hot food and drink sting more than usual, and even brushing your teeth can become sensitive.

Because the symptoms aren't always clear-cut, they can quickly cause worry. Many patients first wonder whether it's just a harmless irritation or an infection that needs treatment. For babies, the worry grows if their feeding habits change or they become unusually unsettled.

You should take such signs seriously. A dental examination will clarify whether it is oral thrush or another cause. The good news: in most cases, oral thrush can be treated well – what matters is getting the right diagnosis early and following a clear approach. At KU64, we treat oral thrush professionally and with care.
When your mouth feels “furry” and oral thrush affects daily life

Before applying the medication, you should gently remove the visible coating so that the active ingredients can reach the affected areas properly. How often you apply the medication and how long the treatment lasts depends on the prescription – usually around seven to fourteen days. The aim of treatment is to stop the infection in the oral tissue specifically and prevent it from spreading further. Even if symptoms noticeably improve after two to three days and the signs of inflammation have subsided, yeast fungi can settle again. It is therefore important to treat an oral thrush infection consistently and complete the prescribed course fully, in order to avoid relapses as far as possible.

It is also crucial whether your doctor identifies and treats possible triggers – such as medication, dentures or a weakened immune system. If there is no clear improvement, or if symptoms recur, you should see a doctor again. For babies and people with a weakened immune system, an early assessment by a doctor or dentist is especially important.
How to apply the medication correctly and avoid relapses

If you are suffering from oral thrush, adjusting your diet can help to protect the oral mucosa and avoid making symptoms worse. In our consultations, we are often asked what to avoid eating with oral thrush and what tends to make it worse. This is because certain foods can put additional strain on already irritated mucosa or are thought to encourage fungal growth.
Diet and daily life: what you should avoid
very hot, spicy or strongly seasoned food
alcohol
sweets, cakes and sugary drinks
white bread and heavily processed white flour products
dried fruit and fruit juices
products containing yeast
Best avoided for now:
Lukewarm, soft food
Vegetables and potatoes
Wholegrain products
Meat and fish
Natural yoghurt
plenty of water or unsweetened herbal teas (e.g. sage or chamomile)

With oral thrush, deliberately cutting down on sugar and heavily processed products can be helpful as a supportive measure. It is important to note that diet can complement medical treatment, but it does not replace it. Thorough oral hygiene also remains a central part of the therapy.
If you are unsure what to eat with oral thrush or which habits might be affecting your symptoms, we are happy to advise you individually at KU64.
Recommended:

Although oral thrush cannot always be completely prevented, you can significantly lower the risk with a few targeted measures. The key is to support the balance of the oral flora and to avoid known triggers. Regularly removing coating from the tongue can help make it harder for yeast fungi to settle. Well-maintained dentures reduce irritation and help prevent a new infection. This also avoids leaving residues of active substances that could unnecessarily strain the mucosa.
Prevention: how to reduce the risk of oral thrush
Brush your teeth regularly and thoroughly.
Gently clean your tongue as well, to reduce coating.
Take care to look after the oral mucosa gently but consistently.
Thorough oral hygiene
Clean removable dentures thoroughly every day.
Have the fit checked regularly.
If possible, take dentures out at night so the mucous membrane can recover.
Looking after dentures and other dental prosthetics properly
After using a corticosteroid or asthma spray, rinse your mouth thoroughly with water.
Clean any inhalation devices you use on a regular basis.
Using inhalation sprays correctly
Clean or sterilise dummies, teething rings and bottle teats regularly.
Pay attention to careful breast hygiene while breastfeeding.
If infections keep recurring, have mother and child examined together.
Extra hygiene for babies and during breastfeeding

Oral thrush is a fungal infection of the mucous membrane in the mouth. It is caused by the yeast Candida albicans, which is part of the natural oral flora in many people. As long as the balance between bacteria, fungi and the immune system remains stable, this organism causes no problems. But if this balance is disturbed by a weakened immune system, the fungus can multiply excessively, leading to the typical symptoms such as white patches and a burning tongue.
Oral thrush tends to appear in certain places:
on the tongue
on the palate
on the inside of the lips and cheeks
on the gums
less often on the outside of the lips

In healthy people, this fungal infection, also called oral candidiasis, usually stays superficial and is easy to treat. In people with a weakened immune system, however, it can be more pronounced and spread from the mouth into the throat or further into the oesophagus.
What is oral thrush?

Typical signs of oral thrush are whitish, sometimes creamy-looking patches on the mucous membrane that can't easily be wiped away. If you try to remove them, the mucous membrane underneath may look red or slightly bloody – a sign of inflammation.
Recognising oral thrush: what it looks like
On the tongue, oral thrush often clearly changes its surface: it looks patchy, coated and less pink than usual.
What does oral thrush look like on the tongue?
The early stage of oral thrush is often barely noticeable. Many patients initially notice only slight changes. Common signs include:
fine, initially isolated white spots
redness and shiny patches
a furry feeling
a slight burning sensation in the mouth
dry mouth
a changed or unpleasant taste
cracked corners of the mouth
Early signs of oral thrush
As oral thrush progresses further, it can lead to:
creamy, widespread patches
inflammation in the mouth and throat
burning
bad breath
pain when eating, drinking and speaking
an impaired or altered sense of taste
a feeling of tightness
increased sensitivity of the oral mucosa
swollen lymph nodes in the neck
Oral thrush at an advanced stage
If the thrush is in the throat, additional symptoms can occur. Typical signs of thrush in the throat include:
pain or a burning sensation when swallowing
a scratchy feeling or the sensation that something is stuck in the throat
increased difficulty swallowing
occasional dry cough

If you have pronounced symptoms such as difficulty drinking or pain when swallowing, have this checked by a doctor promptly. Left untreated, oral thrush can persist in the mouth for months or even years, or in rare cases spread further towards the oesophagus. If the immune system is severely weakened, there is also a risk that the fungal infection spreads further and affects deeper tissue layers. Very rarely, the pathogen can enter the bloodstream and cause a severe systemic infection (sepsis).
Oral thrush in the throat

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.beschreibun.text: White patches, burning or trouble swallowing? Find out about the causes, contagiousness and treatment of oral thrush. ✅ Book an appointment at KU64 now

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.einstieg.0..text: White patches in the mouth, a burning tongue or pain when swallowing? Oral thrush often develops when the immune system is weakened or after taking antibiotics, and it can also affect babies. At KU64, we identify the cause, explain it to you clearly and start the right treatment.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.0.antwo.text: In its early stages, oral thrush, also known as oral candidiasis, often shows only slight changes to the oral mucosa. A fine, whitish coating is typical, appearing initially in small patches and not easily wiped away. A mild burning sensation or increased sensitivity in the mouth may also occur alongside it. Because symptoms are usually mild at first, they are often underestimated or mistaken for harmless mucosal irritation.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.0.frage.text: What does oral thrush look like at the start?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.1.antwo.text: Oral thrush is caused by an excessive growth of the yeast fungus Candida albicans. The fungus is generally harmless and can be detected in the mouths of around 50 to 75 per cent of healthy people without causing any symptoms. Only when the balance of the oral flora is disturbed, the immune defences are weakened, or chronic illnesses such as diabetes or HIV are present can Candida multiply more strongly and trigger an infection.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.10.antw.text: During an acute oral thrush infection, dummies, teething rings and bottle teats should be cleaned thoroughly every day and sterilised regularly. Consistently caring for these items helps prevent reinfection through contaminated objects. Also make sure not to put the dummy in your own mouth, to avoid passing the infection back and forth.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.10.frag.text: How often should I sterilise a dummy during oral thrush?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.11.antw.text: If oral thrush persists despite treatment, various factors may play a role. Contributing causes such as antibiotics, ill-fitting dentures, a weakened immune system or reinfection within the family are often responsible for oral candidiasis. Stopping treatment too early can also allow the yeast to multiply again.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.11.frag.text: Oral thrush won't go away: what could be the reason?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.12.antw.text: Very hot, spicy or heavily seasoned foods can put additional strain on the irritated oral mucosa. Alcohol and foods high in sugar should also be reduced as far as possible during the acute phase. Lukewarm, soft foods and adequate fluid intake are recommended.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.12.frag.text: What should you avoid eating with oral thrush?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.13.antw.text: In most cases, oral thrush is straightforward. It becomes a concern when severe difficulty swallowing occurs, babies barely feed, or there is a pronounced immune deficiency. In such situations, you should have the symptoms checked promptly at KU64, so that we can identify any spread early and treat it in a targeted way.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.13.frag.text: When does oral thrush become dangerous?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.2.antwo.text: Stress alone does not cause oral thrush, but it can weaken the immune system. This increases the risk that existing yeast fungi will multiply more strongly.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.3.antwo.text: Yes, using corticosteroid-containing asthma sprays can encourage oral thrush. The corticosteroid they contain locally weakens the immune defences in the mouth and throat and can also cause dry mouth. This creates an environment in which yeast fungi can multiply more easily. Here is how you can help prevent oral thrush: after each use of the asthma spray, rinse your mouth thoroughly with water and spit it out. Brush your teeth as soon as possible afterwards, or eat or drink something, to remove any remaining active substance. Using a so-called spacer can also help reduce the amount of active substance in the mouth and throat.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.3.frage.text: Can asthma sprays or corticosteroid sprays give me oral thrush?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.4.antwo.text: During pregnancy, hormonal changes and a shifting immune balance can make the mucous membranes more sensitive. This can slightly increase the risk of oral thrush.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.4.frage.text: Is oral thrush more common during pregnancy?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.5.antwo.text: Oral thrush can be transmitted through direct contact with mucous membranes, for example through intense kissing. Shared items such as cutlery, cups or dummies can also play a role. However, transmission does not automatically mean the other person will become ill. A strong immune system can often prevent an infection from developing.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.5.frage.text: How can I catch oral thrush?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.6.antwo.text: As long as symptoms are visible and treatment has not yet begun, you should avoid intense mucosal contact, particularly kissing. Once targeted treatment has started, the risk of transmission usually drops noticeably within a few days. Many people are symptom-free after seven to fourteen days of treatment. If you are unsure when close contact is safe again, feel free to ask us at KU64.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.6.frage.text: How long should I avoid kissing if I have oral thrush?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.7.antwo.text: Yes, oral thrush (oral candidiasis) can be transmitted through oral sex. If a partner has an active genital or anal yeast infection, yeast fungi – usually Candida albicans – can be passed into the mouth during oral sex and trigger an infection there. Although Candida is part of the natural flora for many people, transmission is possible where an infection is already present. Protective measures such as condoms or dental dams can reduce the risk, and an existing fungal infection should be fully healed before further intimate contact.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.7.frage.text: Can oral thrush be transmitted through oral sex?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.8.antwo.text:
If you suspect oral thrush, you shouldn't ignore the symptoms. As fungi occur naturally in many people but can cause problems in certain illnesses or with a weakened immune system, a professional assessment is advisable. Antifungal medication – often in the form of a gel – is usually used to treat the infection in a targeted way.
Also pay attention to thorough but gentle oral hygiene. Clean your teeth regularly and remove plaque carefully, without irritating the mucous membrane further. Good care of the mouth supports healing.
When eating, choose lukewarm, soft foods such as vegetables, potatoes, wholegrain products, natural yoghurt, as well as plenty of water or unsweetened herbal teas. It is also important to identify and address possible triggers. Only then can the oral mucosa stabilise again and a healthy oral flora be restored.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.8.frage.text: What should I do about oral thrush?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.9.antwo.text: As with adults, oral thrush in babies usually requires medical treatment. As the infection is often painful, can affect feeding, and may spread through the digestive tract or lead to nappy thrush, prompt treatment is important. If you notice signs of oral thrush in your baby, please have this checked early at KU64 or by your paediatrician.

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.faq.9.frage.text: Can oral thrush in babies go away on its own?

beschwerde.mundpilz-mundsoor.titel.text: Oral thrush: what helps against fungal infection in the mouth?

beschwerde.mundschleimhautentzuendung.ab.text: A burning sensation, blisters, redness and swelling in the mouth that turn eating or drinking into a painful challenge: inflammation of the oral mucosa, also known as stomatitis or mouth rot, can be a real burden in everyday life. The painful symptoms are especially noticeable when eating hot or acidic foods. Accompanied by bad breath, the inflammation can make social interaction uncomfortable and affect self-confidence. Do these symptoms sound familiar? Then don't hesitate to contact the dental specialists at KU64 Berlin. We will help you clarify the causes and find a suitable treatment together.
Discover effective treatments at KU64 Berlin

The oral mucosa plays a crucial role for your health, as it forms a protective barrier against bacteria and viruses. As part of the immune system, it protects the body from infections. Numerous nerve endings in the oral mucosa provide a sensitive sense of pain, and thanks to its high regenerative capacity, wounds in the mouth heal quickly. In addition, the oral mucosa is involved in taste perception and supports saliva production, which in turn is essential for digestion and cleaning the mouth. An intact oral mucosa is therefore a fundamental shield for your oral health and for a healthy life.
More than just protection: the importance of the oral mucosa

Simple stomatitis is a mild form of mouth inflammation. It is often accompanied by respiratory infections. Feverish illnesses, insufficient oral hygiene, and excessive alcohol or nicotine use can also encourage it to develop. Those affected are often pregnant women or people with anaemia. Simple stomatitis is usually temporary and can be treated well with suitable measures.
Simple stomatitis
Certain medications, such as painkillers, antibiotics, or drugs used to treat cancer or depression, can also cause stomatitis. In this case, it is known as stomatitis medicamentosa.
Medication-related stomatitis
Stomatitis angularis, also known as angular cheilitis, mainly affects the corners of the mouth. It shows up as painful cracks or inflammation in this area and occurs mainly in older people.
Angular stomatitis
Mouth inflammation does not develop overnight. It is often a combination of several factors that encourage stomatitis to develop. The most common causes are:
Causes of mouth inflammation: what your mouth is telling you
Viruses such as herpes, chickenpox or measles viruses, as well as bacteria and fungi, can cause inflammation in the mouth.
Infections
Injuries from sharp foods, dentures or dental treatments can damage the oral mucosa and cause inflammation.
Mechanical injuries
Allergies to certain foods, medications or oral care products can also lead to stomatitis.
Allergic reactions
A lack of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, folic acid or iron, can weaken the oral mucosa and encourage inflammation.
Nutrient deficiency

Chronic conditions such as diabetes, HIV/AIDS or autoimmune diseases can increase the risk of stomatitis. Hormonal fluctuations, such as those occurring during puberty, pregnancy or the menopause, can promote stomatitis, as can anaemia, blood clotting disorders or leukaemia.
Illnesses
Psychological stress can weaken the immune system and thereby lead to inflammation in the mouth.
Stress

A healthy oral mucosa is normally pink and covered with clear saliva. In inflammation of the oral mucosa, also known as stomatitis or mouth rot, one or more painful ulcers develop on the mucous membrane in the mouth or on the gums (gingiva). These can occur either in a limited area or over a wider area. Children and adults are affected equally. In many cases, gum inflammation (gingivitis) triggers the condition of the oral mucosa. It usually heals within one to two weeks.
Inflammation of the oral mucosa: when your mouth shows the “red card”
Insufficient, but also excessive, oral care can lead to bacterial infections and thus to stomatitis.
Inadequate oral hygiene

Toxins such as mercury, lead or arsenic can encourage stomatitis by irritating or damaging the oral mucosa. Toxins can slow down wound healing in the mouth, thereby worsening existing inflammation and encouraging new cases of stomatitis.
Toxins
Unhealthy substances such as alcohol, as well as nicotine, very hot drinks and food, or spicy seasonings, can irritate the oral mucosa and lead to inflammation.
Diet

Inflammation of the oral mucosa can show itself through various uncomfortable symptoms. Sore patches often develop on the inside of the lips, inside the cheeks or on the tongue. The accompanying discomfort affects not only oral health but also general wellbeing. Brushing your teeth often causes pain when the mucosa is inflamed. The most common symptoms of an inflamed oral mucosa include:
How to recognise inflammation of the oral mucosa
Inflamed areas in the mouth appear noticeably red, often more intensely than the surrounding tissue. This redness shows that the tissue is irritated or damaged.
Redness

The swelling that occurs with an inflamed oral mucosa can be limited to one spot or spread over a larger area. The affected tissue may appear thicker or raised and often feels soft. Sometimes the swelling is so pronounced that it changes the normal shape of the oral mucosa.
Swelling

In some cases, blisters or small greyish-white pustules the size of a millet grain, known as aphthae, can form on the reddened and swollen areas. They cause pain when touched. The open areas and small ulcers can sometimes bleed as well.
Painful blisters or pustules
A yellow, greasy coating on the oral mucosa also points to inflammation. Swollen lymph nodes, fever and increased salivation are also common accompanying signs.
Coating
Inflammation of the oral mucosa is often accompanied by a burning or stinging sensation, which occurs particularly when eating hot or acidic foods.
Burning sensation and tingling
Bad breath is, in many cases, an accompanying symptom of an inflamed oral mucosa. The unpleasant smell occurs when bacteria in the mouth get the upper hand.

If the symptoms of an inflammation of the oral mucosa are severe, this often affects the entire ear, nose and throat area. Those affected frequently complain of ear, tooth and cheek pain. Eating and drinking can feel unpleasant and communication becomes difficult. In some cases, difficulty swallowing and numbness may be accompanied by a loss of taste. Occasionally, the inflammation of the oral mucosa may also be accompanied by fever.
Bad breath
There are various forms of oral mucosa inflammation, depending on the cause, appearance and symptoms. The most common forms include the following:
The different types of oral mucosa inflammation

The symptoms are usually so pronounced that those affected notice themselves that they have stomatitis. As a rule, the inflammation and pain disappear on their own within a few days. If the symptoms persist for longer, please contact your dentist for a thorough clinical examination, including laboratory tests.

During the examination, the dental specialists at KU64 Berlin carefully inspect the oral cavity and assess the symptoms of the inflammation, such as redness, coating, swelling or ulcers. Sometimes further tests may be necessary to determine the exact cause of the inflammation. This is the case if the inflammation of the oral mucosa is caused by an infection, an allergy or a systemic condition such as diabetes, arthritis or a thyroid disorder.
Diagnosing inflammation of the oral mucosa: when should you see your dentist?
Also read our article on “Recognising and preventing gum disease in good time”.
Tip:

The treatment of stomatitis depends on the cause and severity of your symptoms. In most cases, therapy focuses on relieving discomfort and promoting the healing of the oral mucosa. Painkillers such as topical gels or mouth rinses can help here. If the stomatitis was caused by an infection, antiviral or antibacterial medication can stop the inflammation.

A tried-and-tested remedy is rinsing with a mild saltwater solution, which reduces inflammation and disinfects the oral mucosa. Chewing on chamomile or sage tea can also have a soothing effect, as these herbs have anti-inflammatory properties. Peppermint oil and sea buckthorn pulp also have anti-inflammatory effects. Also, make sure to drink enough to keep the oral mucosa moist. Brush your teeth regularly with a soft toothbrush and pay attention to thorough oral hygiene with mouthwash and dental floss. This can also help prevent future inflammation and infections in the mouth.
Treatment options for stomatitis: relief for your oral mucosa

With the right diet, you can relieve the symptoms of an inflammation of the oral mucosa and specifically support healing. Soft, mild foods are ideal, as they cause less irritation. These include pureed soups, yoghurt, porridge and soft fruit such as bananas or peeled apples. Avoid spicy, acidic or hot foods, as these can further irritate the sensitive mucosa. Crunchy and hard foods such as crisps or nuts can also cause pain. Drink plenty of fluids in the form of water or mild teas. This will keep the oral mucosa moist and relieve discomfort. A balanced diet rich in vitamins and minerals also supports healing.
Dietary tips for inflammation of the oral mucosa: what supports healing
Stomatitis allergica is triggered by an allergic reaction in the mouth. It can be caused by certain foods, medications or oral care products and causes redness and swelling.
Allergic stomatitis

Herpetic stomatitis, also known as stomatitis herpetica, is – as the name suggests – caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV). It leads to painful blisters in the mouth and can bring on fever and general malaise. This form of mouth inflammation is also called gingivostomatitis herpetica, as it often shows on the gums as well. It occurs mainly in children up to the age of five and is highly contagious. The herpes viruses are transmitted through direct contact with skin or saliva.
The widespread term “mouth rot” is another everyday name for stomatitis herpetica or gingivostomatitis herpetica.
Herpetic stomatitis

Stomatitis diphtherica is caused by the bacterium Corynebacterium diphtheriae. It occurs in connection with a diphtheria infection and is a serious illness. Unlike other forms of mouth inflammation, stomatitis diphtherica also affects the tonsils.
Stomatitis diphtherica
Stomatitis ulcerosa is also caused by a bacterial infection. The term “ulcer” describes a deep-seated, festering sore. Left untreated, it can lead to severe tissue damage and even bone loss.
Ulcerative stomatitis

Stomatitis aphthosa is a general term for mouth inflammations. These are marked by recurring, painful blisters known as aphthae (mouth ulcers). The blisters usually appear on the inside of the cheeks, the tongue or the lips.
Aphthous stomatitis
Fungal stomatitis is also known as oral thrush. It develops from an overgrowth of yeast fungi (usually Candida albicans) and shows up as yellowish coatings and patches in the mouth.
Fungal stomatitis

beschwerde.mundschleimhautentzuendung.be.text: Do you have painful inflammation of the oral mucosa? Find out more about causes, symptoms, diagnosis and treatment options. Book an appointment now!

beschwerde.mundschleimhautentzuendung.fa.text: There are various measures you can take to relieve the symptoms of an inflamed oral mucosa and support healing. Rinse your mouth with a mild saltwater solution or use pain-relieving gels or ointments. Choose your food consciously when eating. Avoid spicy, hot or hard foods and drinks as far as possible, as these can further irritate the mucosa. Pay attention to good oral hygiene and adequate fluid intake to keep the oral mucosa moist. If your inflammation is caused by a nutrient deficiency, dietary supplements may help to restore balance to the mucosa. See a doctor or dentist if the symptoms persist or worsen. This way, the cause of your inflammation of the oral mucosa can be quickly identified and an appropriate treatment chosen.
What can I do about an inflamed oral mucosa?

In the case of mild inflammation of the oral mucosa, home remedies such as homemade mouth rinses can bring relief. Rinse your mouth several times a day with saltwater. The saltwater reduces inflammation and kills bacteria. Chamomile tea also has anti-inflammatory properties and can be used as a mouth rinse once cooled. Aloe vera gel and honey also support healing. Eat probiotic yoghurt to help restore the balance of your oral flora. A well-known remedy against inflammation in the mouth and for removing toxins is oil pulling with coconut oil. Numerous articles on the internet provide information on which home remedies may offer relief for mild inflammation of the oral mucosa. Please note: for pronounced inflammation of the oral mucosa with severe pain, home remedies can help but cannot replace professional medical treatment. If symptoms persist or worsen, it is advisable to see a doctor or dentist.
Which home remedy helps against inflammation in the mouth?

The duration of an inflammation of the oral mucosa depends on the cause and your individual health and immune system. In most cases, acute inflammation of the oral mucosa heals on its own within one to two weeks, especially if it was caused by temporary factors such as minor injuries or irritation.
However, if the inflammation is caused by infections, systemic conditions or other serious causes, healing can take longer and last several weeks. In such cases, it is important to identify the underlying cause. Only then can you start appropriate treatment that relieves the symptoms and speeds up healing.
If your symptoms last longer than two weeks or worsen, please contact a doctor or arrange an appointment with your dentist at KU64 Berlin. In a thorough examination, we can determine the cause of your inflammation of the oral mucosa, rule out complications and discuss a tailored treatment. Timely treatment of the inflammation is crucial to protect your teeth as well.
How long does an inflammation of the oral mucosa last?

The causes of inflammation of the oral mucosa, stomatitis or mouth rot, are varied. In most cases, it is triggered by viruses, bacteria or fungi, such as the herpes simplex virus or the Candida albicans yeast fungus. Mechanical injuries, for example from sharp foods or dental treatments, can also cause inflammation of the oral mucosa. Allergic reactions to food or dental care products also increase the risk of inflammation of the oral mucosa. An inflammation of the oral mucosa often occurs when the immune system is weakened. This can happen due to chronic conditions such as diabetes and autoimmune diseases. Stress and poor oral hygiene also play a role in the development of stomatitis. Often, several factors are responsible for the outbreak of an inflammation of the oral mucosa. Therefore, see a doctor or dentist at the first signs of stomatitis to get the right diagnosis and treatment early on.

An inflamed oral mucosa can also indicate a nutrient deficiency in the body. A lack of folic acid can affect the oral mucosa. An iron deficiency can lead to anaemia, which increases the risk of inflammation of the oral mucosa. A vitamin C level that is too low can also make the tissue more susceptible to inflammation. A balanced diet rich in these nutrients helps keep your oral mucosa healthy while also protecting your teeth.
Which deficiency leads to inflammation of the oral mucosa?

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.0..text: With dry mouth, medically known as xerostomia, the salivary glands in the mouth do not produce enough saliva. Yet saliva plays a central role in the mouth: it protects the teeth from decay, supports digestion and makes speaking and swallowing easier. Disrupted saliva production over a longer period therefore has a negative effect on oral health, the teeth and general wellbeing. This can lead to various complaints and even long-term damage to teeth and gums.

In medicine, dry mouth is generally not regarded as a condition in its own right, but rather as a symptom or consequence of other health conditions or influences. It is important to notice the signs of dry mouth early, so that it can be treated if necessary and any further damage avoided.

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.1..text: The effects of dry mouth vary widely, and so do its causes. These can be divided into three main categories:
Causes of xerostomia: what leads to dry mouth?

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.16.text: Early detection and treatment: Regular dental check-ups help to spot signs of dry mouth early and take targeted action. At KU64 Berlin, we're happy to advise you on which special products or therapies are best suited to prevent dry mouth in your case.
Advice on medication: If you develop dry mouth as a result of medication, talk to your GP or dentist early on about alternative treatment options or additional preventive measures.

As you can see, a few simple measures can help preserve natural moisture in the mouth and prevent dry mouth. Building new routines may feel like an effort at first, but it's guaranteed to be worth it!

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.17.text: The right treatment for xerostomia depends on the causes and severity of the symptoms. In mild cases, simple home remedies can help; in others, professional treatment methods are needed.
Treating xerostomia: what helps against dry mouth?

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.18.text: Saliva substitute products: There are special saliva substitutes available as gels, sprays or mouth rinses that moisten the mouth and replace the missing saliva flow. They have a soothing effect on the mucous membranes and can also be used over a longer period of time.

Moisturising sprays for on the go: For quick relief in between, there are moisturising sprays that immediately hydrate the mouth. They're especially useful in situations where drinking or eating isn't possible.

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.19.text: Regular visits to the dentist: Regular check-ups are particularly important for chronic dry mouth. Your dentist can spot impending dental damage early and recommend targeted treatments, such as special fluoride treatment to help prevent tooth decay.

Therapies for specific underlying conditions: For conditions such as Sjögren's syndrome, diabetes or other chronic illnesses, treatment should involve close cooperation between GP, dentist and, where needed, a specialist, to address the underlying cause of dry mouth as effectively as possible.

Medication to stimulate saliva: Your doctor may prescribe special medication that stimulates saliva production. These medications require a prescription and are generally only used for severe xerostomia.

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.2..text: Illnesses: Conditions such as diabetes, Sjögren's syndrome or Parkinson's disease are common triggers of dry mouth. These conditions affect the salivary glands directly or indirectly, reducing saliva production. Autoimmune conditions in particular often lead to persistent dry mouth.

Medication: A number of common medicines have dry mouth as a side effect. These include antidepressants, antihistamines, diuretics, blood pressure medication and painkillers, which either inhibit saliva production or increase fluid loss. People taking several medications – particularly older people – are especially affected.

Medical treatments: Radiotherapy to the head and neck area can damage the salivary glands and impair their function. Chemotherapy can also alter the composition and production of saliva, which often leads to dry mouth.

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.20.text: Sugar-free chewing gum and sweets: Chewing and sucking stimulates saliva production. Sugar-free chewing gum and sweets can have a positive effect on the oral flora and lower the risk of tooth decay.

Diet: Drinking frequently throughout the day keeps the oral mucous membranes sufficiently moist. Make sure to drink water especially after meals and between meals. Fresh fruit and vegetables can also help stimulate saliva production naturally.
Mild toothpaste and alcohol-free mouth rinses: Use dental care products suitable for sensitive mucous membranes that don't contain alcohol, as this can further dry out the oral mucosa.
Moisturising gel: These products can be applied directly to the mucous membranes and provide a moisturising effect for hours. Some products also contain anti-inflammatory and soothing ingredients.

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.21.text: Dry mouth is a common problem that can be caused and made worse by various factors, ranging from illnesses to individual lifestyle and dietary habits. Simple measures such as drinking regularly, using special oral care products and home remedies can often provide good relief. If you have chronic xerostomia, contact your doctor or dentist for professional treatment. Feel free to book an appointment at KU64 Berlin, so we can help you enjoy your everyday life without worry again soon!

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.3..text: Insufficient fluid intake: Not drinking enough means the body produces less saliva. Older people in particular tend to drink too little, which can make dry mouth worse.

Diet: Foods high in sugar or salt draw fluid from the body and can cause or worsen dry mucous membranes. Substances such as alcohol and caffeine have a diuretic effect and can also contribute to dry mouth.
Smoking: Nicotine and other substances in tobacco damage the oral mucosa and reduce saliva production. Smokers are therefore particularly prone to dry mouth.

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.4..text: Stress and anxiety: Prolonged stress and anxiety affect how the salivary glands function. In stressful situations, the body switches into “fight or flight” mode. It gathers and focuses its energy on dealing with the (perceived) danger – functions such as saliva production are not a priority in this state.

Hormonal changes: Hormonal changes, particularly during the menopause and pregnancy, can also cause dry mouth. Fluctuations, especially in oestrogen levels, affect the moisture of the mucous membranes and can inhibit saliva production.

All these causes of dry mouth can occur alone or in combination, briefly or over a longer period. Identifying and understanding the specific causes is the first step towards prevention and treatment. Feel free to ask us what we can do for you! Our dentists at KU64 Berlin will provide you with all the important information and take the time to get to the bottom of the causes of your dry mouth and treat them specifically – so you can soon be smiling through life again.

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.5..text: Dry mouth, or xerostomia, presents with a range of typical complaints that can vary in severity depending on the cause and extent of the reduced saliva. Watch out for the signs, and feel free to arrange an appointment at KU64 Berlin so our dentists can check whether you need treatment and which option would suit you best.
Symptoms of dry mouth: how do you recognise xerostomia?

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.6..text: Dry, sticky mouth: Those affected often describe a dry or sticky feeling in the mouth, which is only briefly relieved by drinking.
Frequent thirst: Because the mouth is permanently dry, a constant feeling of thirst can develop, which is often felt to be particularly troublesome at night.
Chapped lips and dry mucous membranes: Besides the mouth itself, the lips and the mucous membranes in the mouth and throat are often dry and prone to cracking, dryness or even inflammation.

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.abschnitte.7..text: Problems with chewing and swallowing: Saliva is important for softening food and making swallowing and digestion easier. When saliva is lacking, chewing and swallowing can become uncomfortable, difficult or even painful, especially with dry or firm food.

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.einstieg.0.te.text: A long, hot day, no water to hand – most people know the unpleasant feeling of a dry mouth. However, persistent dry mouth (xerostomia) is more than just unpleasant: it can seriously harm your teeth and your general health. Xerostomia often causes problems with swallowing and speaking. Those affected also suffer more often from tooth decay and gum disease.

beschwerde.mundtrockenheit.einstieg.1.te.text: We explain the causes of dry mouth, how we treat it at our practice in Berlin, and what you can do yourself to prevent it from developing in the first place.

beschwerde.schiefe-zaehne.abschnitte.0.t.text: Say goodbye to crooked teeth – our treatment options

beschwerde.schiefe-zaehne.abschnitte.1.b.text: For a long time, fixed braces were associated – at least in people's minds – with large metal wires and a look that wasn't particularly appealing. These days, however, there's a wide range of discreet methods available to correct misalignments. Removable, visible or invisible, there are many types of braces for both children and adults. With gentle pressure, they gradually move the teeth and jaw, straightening out misalignments. Depending on the type and severity of the misalignment, your orthodontist will decide which options are suitable for you.
Our team at KU64 is happy to inform you about the features, costs and benefits of the various types of braces. Simply arrange an appointment at our practice in Berlin-Charlottenburg.

So-called fixed braces are probably the best-known type of orthodontic appliance and consist of brackets, bands and wires. While the brackets are usually attached to the front of the teeth and connected by wires, the bands are fitted to the back teeth.

These are similar to classic braces and give you straight teeth without being visible. Lingual braces are fitted to the inside of the teeth, so they're hidden and can't be seen. Although it can take patients a little while to get used to having something in their mouth at first, the results speak for themselves.

Correcting misaligned teeth is also possible without classic braces. Invisalign® achieves excellent results when correcting gaps in the front teeth and crooked teeth, and is barely visible. Two removable trays, known as aligners, are made and swapped for a new pair every two weeks, gradually moving the teeth into the desired position. KU64 has over 15 years of experience with Invisalign® and holds ELITE partner status. If you have any questions, please get in touch with our KU64 team.

Once an active course of orthodontic treatment has finished, a retainer keeps the new tooth position stable in the long term. Whether fixed or removable, retainers come in various forms. They're suitable for any age group, though they're usually recommended for minor misalignments. Retainers are typically used to stabilise straight teeth and their position after orthodontic treatment.

beschwerde.schiefe-zaehne.abschnitte.10..text: A pronounced overbite, underbite or crossbite often leads to problems with chewing or speaking. If this is ignored for a long time, with no visit to a dentist or orthodontist, it can also lead to premature wear and an increased sensation of pain in the mouth. But crooked teeth don't just cause pain in the mouth – they can also affect other areas of your health:

More and more orthodontists are convinced that there is often a connection between severe headaches or back pain and misaligned teeth. At KU64 too, we see clear interactions between the two, and this is why we always take a holistic view of our patients' health. Even minor jaw misalignments can cause severe pain and, in the worst case, even chronic health problems.
full mouth restoration, amalgam removal). This includes small fillings in the desired tooth shade, laboratory-made ceramic veneers, and even a full ceramic restoration of the damaged dentition.
