beschwerde.zahnarzt-schwangerschaft.absc.text: During pregnancy, changing hormone levels increase blood flow to the gums, making them more sensitive and prone to inflammation. These hormonal changes can lead to pregnancy gingivitis, a mild form of gum inflammation marked by redness, swelling and bleeding of the gums. If left untreated, this condition can progress to a more severe form, periodontitis, which can damage the jawbone and teeth.
The importance of dental care during pregnancy

Dental problems during pregnancy can have a significant impact on the health of both mother and unborn child. Studies have shown that poor oral health can be linked to premature birth and low birth weight. Inflammation in the mouth can raise inflammatory markers throughout the body, increasing the risk of complications during pregnancy. It is therefore essential to identify and treat dental problems early, to protect the health of both mother and child.
How dental problems can affect pregnancy

During pregnancy, dental health plays a vital role in the overall wellbeing of the expectant mother and unborn child. Hormonal changes bring an increased risk of gum inflammation and other oral health issues. This makes regular dental check-ups and appropriate dental treatments especially important. This section discusses which dental treatments are safe during pregnancy.

Regular dental check-ups and cleanings are not only safe during pregnancy but essential. They help prevent gum inflammation and tooth decay, which can be made more likely by hormonal changes. 
Professional dental cleanings remove plaque and tartar, the main causes of gum problems, and support oral health. Regular cleaning is essential in preventing periodontitis in particular and maintaining oral health during pregnancy. Periodontitis, a serious gum inflammation, can be effectively avoided through thorough cleanings and good oral hygiene.
For pregnant women, it is therefore advisable to schedule these routine check-ups, dental treatments and cleanings particularly during the second trimester, as this is the safest and most comfortable time for dental procedures. This helps prevent gum inflammation or tooth decay.

Dental treatments, routine check-ups and professional cleanings are safe and highly recommended during pregnancy. These measures help prevent gum inflammation and tooth decay, which can be encouraged by the hormonal changes of pregnancy. A thorough cleaning removes plaque and tartar, the main causes of gum problems.
The ideal time for pregnant women to visit the dental practice is the second trimester (months 4–6), as most early pregnancy symptoms, such as nausea, have usually eased by then, and the belly is not yet so large that it affects comfort. In the first trimester, it is recommended to carry out only necessary treatments, as this is the most critical phase of foetal development. In the third trimester, lying back in the dentist's chair for long periods can be uncomfortable and should therefore be avoided unless urgently necessary.

Local anaesthetics such as lidocaine are safe during pregnancy and can be used when needed. Studies have shown that these agents have no adverse effects on the mother or unborn child when used in the recommended doses. Nevertheless, the dentist should always be informed of the pregnancy so that the safest anaesthetic option can be chosen.
Risks and precautions when using anaesthesia
Although local anaesthetics are safe, some precautions should be observed. Epinephrine, often used together with local anaesthetics to prolong their effect, should be used in minimal amounts, as it can affect blood flow to the placenta. In addition, extensive dental procedures requiring general anaesthesia or sedation should, where possible, be postponed until after the birth to avoid any risks.
During pregnancy, it is important to avoid or postpone certain dental treatments to safeguard the wellbeing of both the expectant mother and unborn child. Here are some key points to bear in mind:

X-rays should be avoided during pregnancy where possible, as radiation exposure can potentially harm the unborn child. If an X-ray is absolutely necessary, special safety measures are taken, such as wearing a lead apron to protect the abdomen and minimise radiation exposure.

Major dental surgery, such as removing wisdom teeth or extensive implant procedures, should be postponed until after the birth where possible. These treatments can cause stress and pain, which should be avoided during pregnancy.
Dental treatments to avoid during pregnancy

beschwerde.zahnarzt-schwangerschaft.besc.text: Pregnancy & hormonal changes increase the risk of dental problems. How to protect your dental health & which steps are recommended.

beschwerde.zahnarzt-schwangerschaft.eins.text: During pregnancy, it's especially important to pay attention to oral health. Hormonal changes can increase the risk of gum inflammation and other dental problems. Regular dental check-ups help minimise these risks and safeguard the health of both mother and child.

At KU64, we offer specialised care for pregnant women to ensure safe and effective dental treatment during this particular time. Let the experts at KU64 advise you and benefit from comprehensive care and the most up-to-date treatment methods.

beschwerde.zahnarzt-schwangerschaft.faq..text: Yes, emergency dental treatment is safe during pregnancy and often necessary to avoid infections and pain. Urgent procedures, such as treating severe toothache or infections, should not be postponed, as untreated dental problems can increase the risk of pregnancy complications. It is important to inform the dentist of the pregnancy so that the safest treatment methods can be used.
Can I have emergency dental treatment during pregnancy?

Yes, fillings and root canal treatments can be carried out safely during pregnancy. The local anaesthetics used are generally considered safe and help avoid pain. The second trimester is the best time for such treatments, as the risk of complications is lowest during this phase.
Are fillings and root canal treatments safe during pregnancy?

During pregnancy, it is important to use a fluoride toothpaste to help prevent tooth decay. Fluoride is safe and helps strengthen teeth and protect them against acid damage. It is advisable to choose toothpastes that also contain gentle ingredients and avoid harsh chemicals, to support oral health.
Which toothpaste should I use during pregnancy?

Toothache itself is not passed on to the baby, but untreated dental problems can have indirect effects. For example, dental infections or severe gum inflammation can increase the risk of premature birth and low birth weight. That's why it's important to treat toothache and other dental problems promptly during pregnancy, to protect the health of both mother and child.

beschwerde.zahnerosion-behandeln.abschni.text: Tooth erosion refers to the gradual loss of tooth hard substance through direct contact with acid. Over time, the tooth enamel can be worn away so severely that the dentine underneath is exposed. Dentine is softer and less mineralised than enamel. This makes it more prone to damage and sensitivity.

Healthy tooth hard substance is essential to protect your teeth from mechanical and chemical influences such as acids. That's why it's important to recognise the signs of tooth erosion early and take appropriate action.

The causes of tooth erosion are varied: alongside acidic foods, stomach acid can also play a role. Children and adults who regularly suffer from issues such as heartburn or vomiting are therefore particularly at risk.
What is tooth erosion?

Tooth erosion develops through repeated contact between the teeth and acids, which attack the tooth surface and dissolve minerals from the tooth hard substance. Unlike tooth decay, which is caused by bacteria, tooth erosion occurs without the involvement of microorganisms. Acids attack the tooth surface directly and dissolve minerals from the enamel, the outer protective layer of our teeth. This weakens it, and its protective function diminishes.
How does tooth erosion develop? Causes and risk factors you should know
Dental restorations for advanced tooth erosion
With these simple measures, you can help prevent tooth erosion and contribute to stable, healthy tooth substance in the long term. Why not book a check-up at our Berlin practice today?
Many foods and drinks we consume daily contain acids that can attack the teeth. These include, in particular:
Acidic drinks such as lemonade, fruit juices and energy drinks.
Foods containing citric acid, such as citrus fruits.
Vinegar-based foods, such as salad dressings or pickled foods.
Regularly consuming such products can significantly weaken the protective function of the tooth enamel.
External causes: acids from food and drink
External factors aren't the only ones involved in the development of tooth erosion – stomach acid can also cause significant damage to the teeth. This is often the case with:
Heartburn (reflux), where stomach acid rises into the mouth.
Vomiting, for example due to eating disorders or during pregnancy.
Aggressive stomach acid is particularly harmful, as it acts directly on the teeth and quickly attacks the enamel.
Internal causes: stomach acid
Certain groups of people have an increased risk of tooth erosion:
Children and young people, whose tooth enamel has not yet fully matured.
People with unhealthy eating habits, such as frequent consumption of acidic drinks.
People with conditions such as reflux, chronic heartburn or bulimia.

If several of these factors apply at once, erosion can develop even more quickly and cause serious damage. If you are at increased risk in particular, you should attend regular dental check-ups so that problems can be identified and treated early.
Risk groups for tooth erosion

Tooth erosion often develops gradually and in many cases goes unnoticed for a long time. Even so, it can have far-reaching consequences if it is not treated in time. Take signs such as sensitive teeth or visible changes to the tooth surface seriously. The earlier the problem is recognised, the better the progress of the erosion can be stopped and the affected tooth protected.
Symptoms and consequences of tooth erosion: why you should protect your teeth early
The first symptoms of tooth erosion are usually subtle changes that can become more pronounced over time:
Tooth sensitivity: as the protective layer of enamel becomes thinner, the dentine underneath reacts sensitively to hot, cold or sweet food and drinks.
Changes to the tooth surface: teeth may appear smoother or shinier, as the outer layer of enamel is worn away.
Colour changes: when the yellowish dentine beneath the enamel is exposed, the teeth appear darker.
Rounded edges and flattening: visible signs of wear appear especially on the chewing surfaces or cutting edges of the teeth.
Good to know: how to recognise tooth erosion
Untreated tooth erosion, which places increasing strain on the hard tooth substance, can have far-reaching consequences for your dental health:
Increased risk of decay: as the protective function of the enamel weakens, bacteria can penetrate the tooth more easily and cause decay.
Damage to the dentine: when the dentine is exposed, not only does sensitivity increase, but so does the risk of further tooth damage, as it is softer and more vulnerable than enamel.
Need for dental restorations: in cases of advanced erosion, it may be necessary to restore the damaged teeth with dental restorations such as crowns, inlays or veneers.

At our practice on Kurfürstendamm in Berlin, we offer thorough preventive care. This allows your dentist to identify and treat possible problems early, before the tooth is damaged to the point where a dental restoration becomes necessary.
Long-term effects of tooth erosion

The right treatment for tooth erosion depends on how far the breakdown of the enamel has already progressed. The aim is always to protect the enamel, stabilise damaged areas and prevent further erosion. Alongside professional measures carried out by your dentist, regular dental care and an adapted lifestyle also play a crucial role.
Gentle care for your teeth: treating tooth erosion
The first step in treating tooth erosion is to protect and strengthen the remaining enamel. At KU64 Berlin, we use the following measures for this:
Fluoride treatments: high-dose fluoride gels or varnishes applied by your dentist support remineralisation of the tooth surface and make the teeth more resistant to acids.
Mineralising toothpastes: special toothpastes containing calcium or phosphate compounds can also help strengthen the hard tooth substance.

Minimising contact with acids: alongside proper dental care, you should reduce your consumption of acidic food and drinks and avoid brushing your teeth straight after eating, as the enamel is particularly sensitive at that time.
How to protect and strengthen your tooth enamel

beschwerde.zahnfleischbluten.abschnitte..text: Symptoms of bleeding gums can vary, but here are the most common signs to look out for:
Symptoms of bleeding gums
If you notice your gums bleeding while brushing your teeth or using dental floss, this could indicate inflammation.
Blood while brushing or flossing

Brush your teeth at least twice a day for two minutes to remove dental plaque and prevent the build-up of plaque and tartar. Use a gentle, circular technique and a soft toothbrush so as not to injure your gums. This removes food residue and prevents the growth of harmful bacteria. If your gums bleed after brushing, this is often due to your brushing technique or your toothbrush.
Brushing your teeth with a system
Using dental floss or interdental brushes every day to clean between your teeth is good for your dental health. This removes bacteria and food particles that can be responsible for inflammation.
Dental floss as a faithful companion
An antibacterial mouthwash can complement your daily oral hygiene routine and help prevent inflammation.
Mouthwash for extra protection
A balanced diet rich in vitamins and minerals supports the health of your gums. Vitamin C and vitamin K in particular are important for oral health.
Nutrition for healthy teeth
Arrange regular check-up appointments with your dentist so that any problems can be spotted early and treated in good time.
Regular dental check-ups
Smoking encourages gum disease and bleeding gums. Stopping smoking can help reduce the risk of gum problems.
Stopping smoking

Stress can indirectly contribute to bleeding gums by weakening the immune system, which encourages bacteria to build up. Try to reduce stress by bringing relaxation techniques such as yoga, meditation or exercise into your daily routine.
Reducing stress

Regular professional teeth cleaning by your dentist or a hygienist can effectively help remove plaque and tartar that build up despite good oral hygiene. This can reduce the risk of gum inflammation and, in turn, bleeding gums.

By following these tips, you lay the foundation for healthy gums and effectively help prevent bleeding gums. If problems do occur, please don't hesitate to visit us at our practice – we're here to help you and to restore your bright smile together.

Bleeding gums are a common phenomenon that can have various causes. To identify the culprit, an accurate diagnosis is needed. Here are some common causes of bleeding gums:
If brushing and flossing are not carried out sufficiently or regularly, plaque and tartar can build up. These can cause inflammation of the gums (gingivitis).
At our practice, we take the time to identify your individual needs and find the best treatment for your bleeding gums.
Pregnancy, puberty or hormonal contraceptives can make the gums more sensitive and cause bleeding.
Brushing too hard or incorrectly can injure the gums and lead to bleeding.
Bleeding gums can also be a symptom of general conditions such as diabetes or viral and bacterial infections.

Untreated gingivitis can lead to a more serious condition, periodontitis. Here, the inflammation affects not only the gums but also the jawbone and the tissue that holds the teeth in place. In the worst case, this can lead to tooth loss.
Certain medications, such as blood thinners, can increase the risk of bleeding gums.
A lack of vitamin C or vitamin K can contribute to bleeding gums.
Saliva plays an important role in maintaining oral health and is one of the body's natural defences against germs and pathogens.

To determine the exact cause of your bleeding gums, it is important to see a dentist. Often, the symptoms can already be resolved through changes in oral hygiene or brushing habits. If a serious condition is present, such as gum inflammation, it needs to be actively treated. Otherwise, the inflammation can become chronic and develop into periodontitis. This chronic inflammation can lead to tooth loss.
Causes of bleeding gums – more than just poor brushing

Gum inflammation, also known as gingivitis, is one of the main causes of bleeding gums. When plaque, a sticky layer of bacteria, builds up on the teeth, it can irritate the gums. This irritation shows up as redness and swelling of the gums, as well as bleeding.

Plaque consists of harmful bacteria that feed on food residue and sugar and produce acids. These acids can attack the tooth and the surrounding tissue, triggering an inflammatory response in the gums. Ignoring chronic bleeding gums or gingivitis often leads to more serious conditions such as periodontitis.

Periodontitis is an advanced form of gum inflammation that affects not only the gums but also the surrounding tissue and bone. Bacteria can settle below the gum line and cause chronic inflammation. This can lead to tissue loss, loosening of the teeth and, ultimately, tooth loss.

Bleeding gums also point to problems with your periodontium, the complex system that anchors your teeth in the jawbone. The periodontium consists of the gums, the jawbone and the periodontal ligament, which holds the tooth in the bone. If your gums are inflamed and bleeding, this could be a sign that other parts of the periodontium are affected too, such as inflammation of the jawbone (periodontitis). It is important to recognise and treat these symptoms early to avoid more serious consequences such as tooth loss. This is why regular dental check-ups should be carried out and any changes in the mouth should be watched for. At KU64 Berlin, we are here to support you with professional advice and treatment to keep your periodontium healthy.

At KU64, we take gum inflammation and bleeding gums seriously. Our experienced dentists specialise in diagnosing the underlying causes of your gum problems and developing effective treatment plans. Through thorough examinations and professional dental cleanings, we effectively remove plaque and bacteria from your teeth and gums. Let us help you keep your teeth and gums in top condition. Book an appointment at KU64 today to improve your gum health and get your bright smile back.
Gum inflammation – the most common cause of bleeding gums

If you occasionally have bleeding gums, this is not yet a reason to worry. What matters is that the bleeding subsides quickly and does not occur too often. However, bleeding gums can also be a symptom of a serious condition. At KU64, we are happy to help you get to the bottom of your symptoms and ease your worries. We examine your teeth and gums and determine whether the bleeding is harmless or whether treatment is needed. Gum conditions can often be treated with medication, without the need for a dental procedure. It is important to us that you can relax without worry and with a full smile.

beschwerde.zahnfleischentzuendung.abschn.text: Gingivitis is the medical term for gum inflammation, a condition that occurs quite frequently. It often develops due to insufficient oral hygiene, when bacteria in the mouth form a coating known as plaque on the teeth and especially on the gums, allowing germs to multiply. If gingivitis is left untreated, it can even develop into periodontitis. In this case, the entire tooth-supporting structures in the mouth become inflamed, threatening the health of the teeth and, in the worst case, even leading to tooth loss.
Gingivitis – when harmful bacteria take over

So how do you recognise gingivitis? One of the most common signs of gum inflammation in most people is blood in the saliva and the typical reddish toothpaste foam. Less commonly, brushing too harshly or using a toothbrush that is too hard can cause bleeding gums. Inflamed gums are also often red and swollen.

If the gum inflammation has been present for some time, the gums can recede, exposing the tooth necks. While there is usually not yet much pain at the start of the inflammation, many people with chronic gum inflammation also experience acute toothache.

Other possible symptoms indicating gum inflammation include bad breath, the formation of pus, or the development of further conditions such as gingivostomatitis, the associated inflammation of the oral mucosa, or periodontal disease.
Typical symptoms of gum inflammation
Gum inflammation that does not clear up on its own after a few days, or that is not treated by a dentist in more severe cases, can have serious consequences.
Gingivitis – an inflammation with consequences

If gum inflammation is not treated, this often has painful consequences for those affected. If the gums recede as a result of inflammation, the tooth necks become exposed. So-called gum pockets form. These are gaps between the tooth and the gum. These pockets provide a hiding place for further bacteria. This allows them to easily reach the tooth root and break down the bone. Over time, the teeth become increasingly loose and can even fall out as the condition progresses.
Gum inflammation can lead to periodontitis

With suitable measures, gum inflammation subsides after a few weeks, whereas periodontitis is irreversible. The gum pockets that have formed, however, remain. If you do not recognise the inflammation in time and do not stop it from spreading, the bacteria can even enter your bloodstream and lead to cardiovascular disease. This is why it is important to recognise gum inflammation early and to have it properly treated by a dentist.

Are you showing the typical symptoms of gum inflammation? It is then important to act quickly and get in touch with your dental practice as soon as possible. Our team at KU64 Berlin has the routine and experience to take care of your concerns, relieve your pain, and ensure that the gum inflammation subsides.

Periodontitis is usually treated by dentists with medication such as antibiotics. Patients at KU64 Berlin can also opt for an alternative treatment with EmunDo. This involves a coloured substance that is applied to the teeth and activated by laser, effectively combating bacteria even in stubborn cases.
You can find out more about treatment with EmunDo at our practice from our dentists, on our website, or by phone on 030 8647320. Get in touch with our team now.
Gum inflammation – a condition with further consequences

Plaque that is not removed can also lead to the formation of tartar. This happens when minerals from saliva combine with plaque and harden into tartar. Bacteria can settle even more easily on the rough surface of tartar. This, in turn, promotes the development of gum inflammation.

Tartar can be recognised, for example, by a whitish-yellow colouring on the teeth, which in smokers can even appear brownish to black. If you run your tongue over the affected area, it also feels somewhat rough. Even though most of the bacteria that have settled in tartar are rendered harmless through calcification, the rough surface on the tooth now creates ideal conditions. This can encourage gum inflammation, and the risk of tooth decay is also increased.
For this reason, regular check-ups with a dentist and regular professional teeth cleaning are essential. This can help prevent gum inflammation from developing.
Inflammation of the oral mucosa

If gum inflammation is not treated, it can lead to further conditions such as inflammation of the oral mucosa. With stomatitis, the oral mucosa is affected, and it usually develops when the gums are already inflamed. Here too, the cause is usually poor oral hygiene or a deficiency. Typical symptoms are swelling and redness in the mouth, as well as severe pain.

To prevent inflammation of the oral mucosa and, as a result, inflammation of the gums, those affected should see a doctor immediately if the gum inflammation has not subsided after four to five days. Are you suffering from gum inflammation? Then book an appointment today at one of our dental practices in Berlin and Potsdam.
full mouth rehabilitation, amalgam removal). This includes small fillings in the desired tooth colour, laboratory-made ceramic veneers, and even full ceramic rehabilitation of a damaged set of teeth.

Poor oral hygiene allows bacteria to multiply increasingly, leading to tooth decay. These bacteria convert carbohydrates, particularly sugar, into acid, which causes demineralisation of the tooth enamel. The decay-causing bacteria attack the enamel, making it less robust. If a tooth is affected by decay, the bacteria can, in the worst case, also attack the nerve. A root canal treatment is then usually the most effective way to save the tooth. Regular assessment of decay risk is essential to prevent this.
Further risks of poor oral hygiene:

Good oral hygiene is essential when it comes to gingivitis. Caring for the teeth and gums is enormously important, both for prevention and treatment. If inflammation is suspected, it is advisable to see a doctor straight away.

At our KU64 practice in Berlin, we have a range of state-of-the-art technical equipment to diagnose various conditions. Regular dental check-ups are one way of detecting gingivitis. A special periodontitis examination can also help with diagnosis. In this examination, all gum pockets are checked using a so-called periodontal probe. In most cases, however, a visual assessment by the dentist is sufficient. If periodontitis is suspected, X-rays can be used to determine whether bone loss has already occurred.

Thorough and regular oral hygiene is essential for patients if treatment of gum inflammation is to succeed. If this does not help, those affected should definitely see a dentist to have the inflammation treated. At the KU64 Berlin practice, our dentists can take professional care of the health of your teeth.
Even simple measures can help prevent gum inflammation and thereby avoid pain and further complications.
Whether it's removing plaque / biofilm, regularly cleaning the spaces between teeth, or general dental care, the following measures are considered helpful in preventing gum inflammation:
Brushing: brush your teeth at least twice a day
Dental care: use dental floss once a day
regular check-ups with a dentist
professional teeth cleaning by dentists

Don't forget: regular check-ups at KU64 Berlin! The best precaution against gum inflammation is regular preventive appointments with your dentist. In a personal conversation, you will also receive further helpful tips and information on preventing gum inflammation.

Thanks to the use of EmunDo, our dentists at KU64 are able to fight inflammation even more effectively. Using the colour substance EmunDo together with a laser, plaque and bacterial pathogens are destroyed without endangering the root substance of the patient's teeth.
The EumunDo dye is applied locally and specifically only to the inflamed areas. When activated by the laser, EmunDo effectively kills only those bacteria responsible for the gum inflammation.
Treatment with EumunDo has the advantage that it is a selective therapy that acts specifically on the inflamed tissue, causes no side effects, shows a quick treatment result, and is pain-free.
Gum inflammation: prevention is better than cure
If the pain from the inflammation is severe, the following home remedies can help ease gingivitis:
Chamomile and sage: Rinse your mouth several times a day with chamomile or sage tea to make use of its disinfecting and soothing effect.

Apple cider vinegar: This stimulates saliva flow and has an antibacterial effect. Mix a glass of water with two spoonfuls of apple cider vinegar and gargle with it half an hour before brushing your teeth.
Massage: Gently massage your gums with a toothbrush to stimulate blood circulation.
Ginger: This spice plant also has antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties. Gargle with or drink ginger tea several times a day.
Medication: If you suffer from severe pain, medication can help relieve it.
If the inflammation has not gone away on its own after two to five days, it is advisable to see a dentist for professional treatment. Book an appointment at KU64 Berlin for this!

Gingivitis symptoms

Bacteria in our mouths are completely normal and usually don't cause any problems. In fact, our oral flora as a whole contains over 1,000 different types of bacteria, which have specialised in particular areas such as the oral mucosa, the tongue or the gums. These germs feed on food residue and form a biofilm on the tooth surface or at the point where tooth and gum meet. This is known as plaque, and you can generally remove it through simple brushing and adequate oral hygiene, such as regular professional teeth cleaning or cleaning between the teeth with dental floss.

However, if you don't brush your teeth thoroughly enough, there is a risk that bacteria will multiply to an unhealthy degree in the mouth. The toxins they release can then reach the gum tissue and cause inflammation. The so-called sulcus in particular – a shallow groove where the gum meets the tooth – provides a suitable point of attack for germs. If bacteria get into this area, your body responds with inflammation of the gum, putting the health of your teeth at risk.
What to look out for: causes of gum inflammation

A lack of oral hygiene is often a relevant factor in the development of gum inflammation, but it's not the only one. While for some people even a small amount of plaque can lead to gum inflammation, others show no symptoms even with heavy tartar build-up. Gum inflammation can have several causes. For example, in rare cases, a lack of vitamin C (scurvy) can lead to gum inflammation. Hormonal changes or viral infections can also be causes of inflammation.
The following factors increase the risk of gum inflammation:
Stress
Smoking
Chronic illnesses such as diabetes
A weakened immune system
Genetic predisposition
Hormonal fluctuations (puberty, pregnancy or menopause)
Vitamin C deficiency
Poorly fitting dental restorations (bridges, implants, crowns or fillings)
Factors that promote gum inflammation
Just as varied as the causes of this condition – gingivitis – are, so too are the different types of gum inflammation:
Types of gum inflammation
Chronic gum inflammation is one of the most common forms of inflammation in the human body. Here, the bacteria have advanced from the gum line into the jaw, where they damage the periodontium.
Chronic gum inflammation

This form of gum inflammation is characterised by the fact that the gum tissue between the teeth is also infected. An unhealthy lifestyle involving stress, nicotine or alcohol is often the cause. Foul-smelling breath, fever and severe pain are typical symptoms.
Acute necrotising and ulcerative gingivitis (ANUG)

Hormonal gum inflammation occurs particularly during puberty, pregnancy, or as a result of taking the contraceptive pill. While this form of inflammation is usually only temporary, in the worst case it can develop into hormonal periodontitis. For this reason, particular attention should be paid to possible inflammation during pregnancy.
Hormonal gum inflammation

Desquamative gingivitis is very rare. In most cases, it occurs during menopause. A strong burning sensation in the mouth, deep red gum tissue, blistering, and severe pain are typical and common symptoms of this condition.
Desquamative gingivitis

beschwerde.zahnfleischrueckgang.abschnit.text: Gum recession, also known as gingival recession, describes the gradual pulling back of the gums from the teeth. This increasingly exposes the tooth neck, which can lead to greater tooth sensitivity. Gum recession is a serious issue for oral health, as the exposed dentine becomes more prone to decay and periodontitis. In the long term, receding gums can also cause the affected teeth to loosen or even be lost.
What is gum recession?
Gums pulling back
Exposed tooth necks
Sensitive teeth (e.g. to heat, cold, sweetness)
Bleeding gums (especially when brushing)
Swollen or red gums
Teeth appearing longer than usual
Pain or discomfort in the gums
Loose teeth
Formation of gum pockets
Increased risk of decay at the exposed tooth necks

Do you have these symptoms and suspect that your gums are receding? Early treatment is essential to avoid serious consequences and to preserve the appearance of your teeth. Get in touch with our team at KU64 today and arrange an appointment at our practice. We take time for your concerns and treat you professionally.
Signs of receding gums

Gum recession goes beyond oral health and also has significant effects on general health. Numerous studies have shown that gum disease is linked to a range of systemic health problems, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, respiratory conditions and even pregnancy complications.
General health

Gum recession also has significant aesthetic effects, which can affect self-confidence and general wellbeing. When the gums recede, the teeth appear longer than they actually are, which can make a smile look unnatural. This change can be particularly noticeable when several teeth are affected, and often leads to dissatisfaction with one's appearance.
In addition, the exposed tooth necks can become discoloured, as they are less protected by enamel and therefore more prone to staining from food, drinks or tobacco products. This further adds to the aesthetic impact and can make those affected feel self-conscious and less inclined to show their smile.
Aesthetic effects

Early diagnosis of gum recession is crucial to stop the condition from progressing and to prevent serious consequences. Dentists use a range of techniques and instruments to accurately assess the condition of the gums and develop suitable treatment plans.
Diagnosing gum recession

During a dental examination, the dentist will first carry out a visual inspection of the mouth to identify obvious signs of gum recession. This includes assessing the gum line, checking for exposed tooth necks, and looking for redness, swelling or bleeding of the gums.

An important part of the diagnosis is measuring pocket depth. Here, the dentist uses a special instrument, called a periodontal probe, to measure the depth of the gum pockets between the tooth and gum. Normal pockets are usually between 1 and 3 millimetres deep. Deeper pockets can indicate advanced periodontitis, which requires more intensive treatment.

Dentists use X-rays to assess the condition of the bone around the teeth. These images help to determine the extent of bone loss and visualise how far the gum disease has spread. X-rays are particularly useful for determining the extent of the condition and enabling accurate treatment planning.

By diagnosing gum recession, the dentist can determine whether bone resorption has occurred. This is a critical factor, as significant bone loss can affect the stability of the teeth and increase the risk of tooth loss.
In some cases, the dentist may carry out a bacterial analysis to identify the specific bacteria causing the inflammation. This allows for targeted therapy aimed at combating the bacteria responsible.

In addition, the dentist will also take the patient's medical and dental history into account, in order to identify possible risk factors such as smoking, diabetes or genetic predisposition that could contribute to gum recession. Combining these diagnostic techniques allows the dentist to determine the exact condition of the gums and supporting tissue, and to develop a tailored treatment that meets the patient's individual needs.
Dental examination and diagnostic techniques
Gum recession requires targeted treatment to stop the condition from progressing and to restore gum health. The choice of treatment depends on the severity of the recession and the underlying causes.
Treatment options for gum recession

Regular professional dental cleaning and good preventive care are a fundamental step in preventing and treating gum recession. During a professional cleaning, the dentist or dental hygienist thoroughly removes plaque and tartar that have built up despite regular brushing. This reduces the bacterial load and lessens gum inflammation.
In addition to cleaning, signs of gum recession and periodontitis can be identified during this treatment, allowing for early intervention. Regular professional cleanings are essential for improving oral hygiene and minimising the risk of gum recession.
Professional dental cleaning
In more advanced cases of gum recession, specific periodontal treatment is required. These treatments aim to control the inflammation and restore the health of the tooth-supporting tissue.
Periodontal treatment
Deep cleaning procedures, in which plaque and tartar are removed above and below the gum line. The tooth surfaces are smoothed to promote healing.
Use of lasers to remove inflamed tissue and reduce the bacterial population. This method is gentler and less invasive than traditional procedures.
Use of antibiotics or antiseptic solutions to fight infection and reduce inflammation. Medication can be applied locally or taken orally.
Surgical procedures to correct gum recession and restore bone structure. Techniques such as bone augmentation and soft tissue grafts are used.
Further treatment options for gum recession:

Receding gums can be caused by a variety of factors, both mechanical and biological in nature. The most common causes range from incorrect oral hygiene to serious gum disease such as periodontitis. Gum recession is not just an aesthetic issue – it also has a significant impact on dental health. Without the protective gum tissue, the sensitive tooth necks become exposed, which can lead to increased sensitivity, decay and, in the worst case, tooth loss.
Causes of receding gums

Another myth is that gum recession is exclusively a problem for older people. In fact, gum recession can affect people of any age, including young adults. Factors such as incorrect oral hygiene, genetic predisposition, smoking and certain medical conditions can increase the risk of gum recession even in younger people. It is important to maintain good oral hygiene and attend regular dental check-ups regardless of age, so that gum problems can be identified and treated early.
Gum recession is only a problem in old age

Recognising early warning signs and seeing a dentist in good time are essential to prevent the consequences of gum recession and to preserve oral health in the long term. It is important to watch for the signs of gum recession and to see a dentist promptly if these symptoms occur.
When should you see a dentist?
Bleeding gums: Gums that bleed regularly when brushing or flossing can be a sign of inflammation and gum recession.
Redness and swelling: Swollen or reddened gums indicate inflammation and may point to early-stage periodontitis.
Exposed tooth necks: Visible recession of the gums and exposure of the tooth necks are clear signs of gum recession.
Tooth sensitivity: Increased sensitivity to hot, cold or sweet food and drinks can indicate exposed tooth necks.
Loosening of teeth: If teeth move or feel less firmly anchored in the jaw, this can indicate advanced gum recession and bone loss.
Pain and discomfort: Pain in the gums or affected teeth can be a sign of inflammation and infection.

If you notice one or more of these symptoms, you should arrange a dental appointment as soon as possible. Early diagnosis and treatment can help stop gum recession and prevent serious consequences such as tooth loss and systemic health problems.

The team at KU64 in Berlin is available to you every day of the week. Our experts offer thorough consultations and diagnostic options for dental problems, as well as individual treatment options. Feel free to call us on 030 864 73 20 or email us at info@ku64.de to arrange your appointment.
Recognising early warning signs
Gum recession describes the process by which the gums pull away from the teeth, exposing the tooth necks. This can lead to sensitivity, aesthetic concerns and, in the long term, even tooth loss.
What is gum recession?

The most common causes include periodontitis (gum inflammation), incorrect brushing technique with too much pressure, genetic predisposition, smoking, and poor oral hygiene. All of these factors can weaken the gums and lead to recession.
What are the main causes of gum recession?

Yes, gum recession can be stopped or slowed down if action is taken early. Gentle oral hygiene, professional teeth cleaning and treating underlying issues such as periodontitis can help stabilise the condition. Healthy habits such as not smoking and reducing stress also support healing. However, receded gum tissue does not grow back on its own, which is why surgical procedures are sometimes necessary.
Can I stop gum recession?

No, gums cannot regenerate on their own. Once gum tissue has receded, it usually remains permanently affected. In some cases, however, surgical measures such as gum grafts can help restore the gum tissue.
Can gums grow back on their own?

One of the most common causes of receding gums is incorrect brushing technique. Many people tend to brush their teeth too vigorously, often assuming that intensive brushing leads to better cleaning. This is a widespread misconception, however. Scrubbing too hard, especially with a hard-bristled toothbrush, can injure the gums and gradually push them back. Constant mechanical strain from incorrect brushing causes the gum tissue to wear down and recede.
Use a soft toothbrush: hard bristles can irritate the gums. A soft brush cleans gently and thoroughly.
Brush your teeth with gentle, circular movements: avoid vigorous scrubbing. Small, gentle circular movements along the gumline are most effective.
Keep the right angle: hold the toothbrush at a 45-degree angle to the gumline to remove plaque and bacteria without injuring the gums.
Clean tooth by tooth: focus on each tooth individually to ensure thorough cleaning.
Don't apply too much pressure: press the brush only lightly against your teeth and gums to avoid injury.
Brush twice a day: clean your teeth in the morning and evening for at least two minutes to ensure optimal oral hygiene.
Use additional aids: dental floss or interdental brushes help clean the spaces between your teeth and protect the gums.

In addition, poorly fitting dental restorations, such as dentures or bridges, as well as teeth grinding (bruxism), can put additional pressure on the gums, leading to gum recession. It is important to visit the dentist regularly to make sure all dental restorations fit correctly and do not cause mechanical strain.
1. Incorrect brushing technique and mechanical strain
Gum recession can be prevented through correct and gentle oral hygiene, regular dental check-ups, a healthy diet and avoiding harmful habits such as smoking.
How can gum recession be prevented?

Yes, untreated gum recession can lead to tooth loss, as the periodontal structures weaken and the bone around the teeth breaks down. This destabilises the teeth and leads to their loss in the long term.
Can gum recession lead to tooth loss?

Although gum recession is often associated with age, young people can be affected too, particularly through incorrect brushing techniques or genetic factors. Early signs can also be noticeable in teenagers, which is why a timely dental check-up is important.
Is gum recession common in young people?

Periodontitis, an advanced form of gum inflammation, is the most common cause of receding gums. This bacterial infection affects the entire periodontium, including the gums, bone and the fibres that anchor the teeth in the jaw. 
If periodontitis is not treated in time, it leads to chronic inflammation of the gums that gradually destroys the tissue. As a result of this inflammation, the gums recede and so-called gum pockets form, in which bacteria settle and the disease worsens further.
Gum recession caused by periodontitis is particularly dangerous, as the inflammation can also attack the underlying bone. This can cause the teeth to become loose and eventually lead to tooth loss. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential to stop the progression of periodontitis and minimise gum recession. Regular professional teeth cleaning and thorough oral hygiene at home are important preventive measures.
2. Periodontitis as a main cause

Genetic predisposition plays a significant role in the development of receding gums. Some people, due to their family history, have an increased risk of developing gum problems such as periodontitis, which in turn can lead to gum recession. Certain genetic markers can mean a higher susceptibility to inflammation of the gums and the periodontium. Although this genetic predisposition cannot be prevented directly, it is important to pay particular attention to thorough oral hygiene and regular dental check-ups if there is a family history of gum disease, in order to counteract it early on.
3. Genetic factors

Poor oral hygiene is one of the main causes of gum recession. If plaque, a soft biofilm of bacteria, is not removed from the teeth regularly, it hardens into tartar. This tartar builds up along the gumline and irritates the tissue, which can lead to inflammation and, ultimately, receding gums. Untreated plaque and tartar deposits allow bacteria to accumulate, gradually destroying the gum tissue. Regular brushing, the use of dental floss and professional teeth cleaning are therefore essential to prevent plaque and tartar and to keep the gums healthy.
4. Poor oral hygiene

Smoking is a significant risk factor for receding gums. Tobacco use weakens the immune system, impairing the body's ability to fight infections such as periodontitis. In addition, smoking reduces blood flow to the gums, which slows healing and increases the risk of gum problems. Studies show that smokers have a significantly higher risk of gum recession and tooth loss than non-smokers.
In addition to smoking, other harmful habits such as excessive alcohol consumption, an unbalanced diet and stress can also increase the risk of gum disease. These factors impair overall oral health and weaken the gums, which can lead to recession in the long term.
5. Smoking and other risk factors

Untreated gum recession can have far-reaching consequences that go beyond immediate oral health. The progressive damage to the gums can not only lead to tooth loss, but also cause aesthetic impairments and increase the risk of serious systemic diseases. This section highlights the main consequences that can arise from untreated gum recession.
Consequences of untreated gum recession

Gum recession is often an early sign of serious periodontitis, an advanced form of gum disease. When the gums recede, the underlying structures of the tooth-supporting tissue, including the bone, become exposed and more vulnerable to infection and breakdown. This progressive bone loss means the teeth are less firmly anchored in the jaw and can become loose.
In the long term, this can lead to tooth loss, as the support from bone and gum is insufficient to hold the teeth in place. The loss of individual teeth not only affects chewing function, but can also destabilise the surrounding teeth, leading to further tooth loss. In addition, losing teeth negatively affects jawbone growth, which can lead to changes in facial structure and a reduced quality of life over time.
Tooth loss and loosening of the teeth

beschwerde.zahnfleischtaschen.abschnitte.text: Gum pockets are small gaps or recesses that form between the gums and the teeth. They occur when the gums detach from the teeth, often triggered by inflammation or bacteria in the mouth. These pockets provide an ideal breeding ground for bacteria and, if left untreated, can lead to serious gum disease such as periodontitis.

Gum pockets form when the gums detach from the tooth due to bacterial plaque or inflammation. Normally, the gums fit snugly against the tooth, but with inflammation they can pull back and form a pocket between the tooth and the gum. Bacteria collect in these pockets, further intensifying the inflammation and causing long-term damage to the tissue.
What are gum pockets?
Bleeding gums (especially when brushing your teeth)
Bad breath
Pain in the gum area
Gums that are sensitive to touch
Receding gums (teeth appear longer)

These symptoms are a sign that a dental examination is needed to prevent more serious consequences.
full mouth rehabilitation, amalgam removal). This includes small fillings in the desired tooth colour, laboratory-made ceramic veneers, right through to full ceramic rehabilitation of a damaged set of teeth.
Symptoms of gum pockets

Careful oral hygiene is the foundation for preventing periodontal pockets. Brushing regularly – at least twice a day – helps remove bacterial plaque and tartar, the main causes of periodontal pockets. Dental floss or interdental brushes should also be used daily to clean the spaces between the teeth, where bacteria often accumulate. Electric toothbrushes and mouthwashes can also make a positive contribution to preventing periodontal pockets.
Proper oral hygiene

A balanced diet plays a central role in gum health. Foods rich in vitamins and minerals, such as fresh fruit, vegetables and dairy products, help strengthen the immune system and prevent inflammation. Vitamin C in particular promotes gum healing and health, while avoiding sugary foods helps reduce the growth of tooth decay and plaque, which can contribute to the formation of periodontal pockets.
Healthy diet

Regular check-ups with your dentist are essential for detecting and treating gum pockets at an early stage. During these visits, your dentist can also carry out a professional teeth cleaning, which removes plaque and tartar more thoroughly than is possible at home. These check-ups should take place at least once a year, or more often if your risk is increased, to prevent inflammation and maintain oral health.
Regular dental check-ups

Untreated gum pockets can have far-reaching consequences for oral health and general wellbeing. They not only lead to serious dental disease but can also increase the risk of systemic health problems. Neglecting treatment of these pockets can ultimately result in tooth loss and a decline in quality of life. There is also growing scientific evidence linking periodontitis to various chronic conditions, which underlines how important early intervention is.
Consequences of untreated gum pockets

Untreated gum pockets are a leading cause of tooth loss. The progressive inflammation destroys the connective tissue and bone that support the teeth, causing them to become loose and eventually fall out. In addition to the loss of individual teeth, larger sections of the dentition can be affected, causing not only aesthetic but also functional problems, such as difficulty chewing and speaking.

Untreated gum pockets can also lead to the formation of abscesses, which are painful and require further medical treatment. These complications can have a considerable impact on daily life and general health. We offer solutions for a wide range of dental restoration, including small fillings in the desired tooth colour, laboratory-made ceramic veneers and full-ceramic restoration of a damaged dentition.
Tooth loss and other complications

The link between periodontitis and systemic disease is well documented and highlights how important oral health is for overall wellbeing. Studies have shown that chronic inflammation in the mouth can increase the risk of heart disease, stroke and high blood pressure. There is also a two-way link between periodontitis and diabetes: people with diabetes have a higher risk of gum disease, while untreated periodontitis can make blood sugar control more difficult. Other health effects include respiratory conditions and increased susceptibility to certain types of cancer.
These links show that caring for your oral health is an essential part of general healthcare.
Effects on general health

With an experienced team and the latest treatment methods, we offer comprehensive solutions for gum pockets and periodontal disease. Our approach is designed to preserve your oral health in the long term and improve your quality of life.

The latest treatment methods

Periodontal pockets form when the gums detach from the teeth, creating deepened spaces between tooth and gum. These pockets provide an ideal breeding ground for bacteria, which can lead to inflammation. The main causes of periodontal pockets are poor oral hygiene, untreated gum inflammation and certain lifestyle factors such as smoking.
Causes of periodontal pockets

Bacterial plaque is the main cause of periodontal pockets. Plaque forms from food debris and bacteria that build up on the teeth and along the gum line. If these deposits are not removed regularly through thorough brushing and the use of dental floss, they harden into tartar. The tartar irritates the gums, leading to inflammation and eventually periodontal pockets
Bacterial plaque and tartar

If gum inflammation (gingivitis) is not treated in time, it can develop into periodontitis. Periodontitis is an advanced form of gum disease in which the inflammation spreads to the bone and connective tissue that support the teeth. This leads to periodontal pockets, as the tissue is destroyed and the gums recede. Left untreated, periodontitis can lead to tooth loss.
Periodontitis and gum inflammation

Besides bacterial plaque, there are other risk factors that encourage the formation of periodontal pockets. Smoking is one of the main factors, as it reduces blood flow to the gums and slows down healing processes. Genetic predisposition can also play a role: some people are more prone to gum problems. Other factors such as diabetes, stress or a weakened immune system can also increase the likelihood of periodontal pockets.
Further risk factors

Periodontal pockets require targeted treatment to maintain oral health in the long term. Depending on severity, various treatment methods can be used to relieve inflammation and stop the disease from progressing. Treatment usually begins with a thorough cleaning and can extend to surgical procedures if conservative measures are not sufficient. Here you can find out which treatment options are available and when they are used.
How are periodontal pockets treated?

Periodontal pockets require targeted treatment to maintain oral health in the long term. Depending on severity, various treatment methods can be used to relieve inflammation and stop the disease from progressing. Treatment usually begins with a thorough cleaning and can extend to surgical procedures if conservative measures are not sufficient. Here you can find out which treatment options are available and when they are used.
Professional teeth cleaning

Periodontal therapy is the next step when periodontal pockets have progressed further. This involves a deeper cleaning of the periodontal pockets, also known as scaling and root planing. Scaling removes plaque and tartar located below the gum line. Root planing helps smooth the tooth surfaces so that new bacteria cannot settle. These measures reduce the depth of the periodontal pockets and promote healing of the gums.
Periodontal therapy

In particularly severe cases where non-surgical treatments do not have a sufficient effect, surgery may become necessary. A commonly used method is flap surgery. Here, the gum is folded back to allow a better view of the tooth roots. The inflamed tissue is removed, and the roots are thoroughly cleaned. The gum is then repositioned and secured. This surgical measure helps reduce deep periodontal pockets and stabilise the teeth in the long term.
Surgical measures

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.10.bloec.text: A reliable diagnosis begins with a thorough examination of your mouth and a detailed analysis of possible triggers. We use the following methods for this:
Imaging techniques: X-rays and digital volume tomography (DVT) help identify dead teeth, decay and hidden inflammation.
Testing for markers of inflammation: Saliva and blood tests can provide clues to inflammatory processes triggered by dental toxins.
Specialist tests: Microbiological tests can identify disease-causing bacteria, for instance in cases of periodontitis.
TMJ diagnostics: If dental toxins are causing tension or misalignment in the jaw, special functional analyses can reveal TMD (temporomandibular disorder).

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.10.titel.text: Detecting dental toxins through modern diagnostics

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.11.bloec.text: When treating dental toxins and their causes, the dentists at KU64 take an individual approach that considers both dental health and general health. The most common treatment options include:

Treatment of dead teeth: Dead teeth, which are a source of dental toxins, can either be treated with a root canal treatment or, if the damage is beyond repair, removed and replaced with an implant if needed.
Periodontitis treatment: Targeted treatment of gum inflammation reduces the release of toxins and thereby protects the immune system.
Holistic approaches: For systemic complaints, an interdisciplinary treatment is often recommended, with dentists working alongside other specialists.

If removing a tooth is unavoidable, implantology offers a lasting solution. Dental implants replace lost teeth and restore the function of the bite without placing strain on the organism or body. High-quality materials and precise fitting make implants an aesthetic and durable alternative. Please feel free to contact us for individual advice!

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.12.bloec.text: The best way to avoid the harmful effects of dental toxins is targeted prevention. Through regular dental care, professional teeth cleaning and early treatment of dental problems, you can significantly reduce the risk of dental toxins and their effects on the body. Consistent preventive care is key not only to healthy teeth but also to a healthy body.

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.13.bloec.text: Regularly removing plaque and bacteria is essential to prevent dental toxins from developing. Important measures include:
Professional teeth cleaning: Removing plaque and tartar removes bacteria that can cause tooth decay, gum inflammation and, ultimately, dental toxins.
Regular check-ups: Problems detected early, such as the beginnings of decay or inflammation, can be treated in time before they affect the whole body.
Individual advice: Tailored recommendations on dental care and diet help maintain oral health in the long term.

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.13.titel.text: Professional teeth cleaning and preventive care

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.14.bloec.text: Sustainable prevention of dental toxins also involves considering the whole body and lifestyle:
Healthy diet: Avoiding sugary foods and consuming nutrients such as calcium and vitamin D strengthen teeth and gums.

Stress reduction: Stress can weaken the immune system and encourage chronic inflammation. Relaxation techniques and a balanced lifestyle have a positive effect on both general health and dental health.
Interdisciplinary approaches: For complex complaints such as TMD or chronic conditions, dentists can develop holistic solutions in collaboration with other specialists.

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.15.bloec.text: Alongside professional care, daily oral hygiene is also essential:
Brushing twice daily: Fluoride toothpaste fights bacteria and strengthens tooth enamel.
Antibacterial mouthwash: Using mouthwash regularly keeps bacteria in check.
Floss and interdental brushes: Cleaning between the teeth prevents plaque from building up in hard-to-reach areas.

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.16.bloec.text: Dental toxins are often an underestimated factor that can have far-reaching effects on your overall health. From local problems such as tooth decay and gum inflammation to systemic conditions such as cardiovascular problems, rheumatic complaints or chronic fatigue – the link between dental health and general wellbeing should not be underestimated.

With modern diagnostics and individual treatment approaches, we at KU64 Berlin treat dental toxins effectively and minimise their impact on the body. Even more important, however, is prevention: regular dental cleaning, early treatment of dental problems and a holistic view of dental health play a decisive role in preventing dental toxins from forming in the first place.

A conscious approach to your own oral health is therefore the key to protecting your entire body from strain and preserving your quality of life in the long term. Please visit us for a check-up and individual consultation at our practice in Berlin!

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.3.bloeck.text: The symptoms of dental toxin exposure can be divided into acute and chronic complaints:

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.4.bloeck.text: Pain in the mouth, particularly with dead teeth or untreated tooth decay
Gum inflammation such as redness, swelling or bleeding
Localised abscesses and sensitivity to pressure

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.5.bloeck.text: General tiredness and exhaustion, which may indicate a strain on the immune system
Headaches and tension, often linked to TMD (temporomandibular dysfunction)
Long-term inflammatory processes that can weaken the body and encourage illness

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.6.bloeck.text:
Dental toxins don't only affect the mouth – they can also cause systemic complaints, including:
Chronic illness: dental toxins can promote inflammation, which in turn can trigger conditions such as cardiovascular disease, arthritis or respiratory illness.
Strain on the immune system: the ongoing release of toxins can weaken the body's defences, making infections more likely.

It's important to recognise these symptoms and take them seriously, so the underlying problems can be treated and resolved. A holistic view of dental health and general wellbeing is essential here. At KU64 Berlin, your dentist will take the time to discuss all your complaints thoroughly, identify the causes and offer you the best possible treatment.

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.7.bloeck.text: Dental toxins don't just affect the mouth – through complex mechanisms, they can impact the whole body. Toxic substances can reach other organs and tissues via the bloodstream and immune system, which over time can lead to chronic illness.

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.7.titel.text: From tooth to body: how dental toxins can lead to illness

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.8.bloeck.text: Dental toxins enter the body via the bloodstream and can cause inflammation in other parts of the body, or worsen existing conditions. Examples of these connections include:
Inflammatory substances: chronic gum inflammation or periodontitis releases toxins and inflammatory substances that put the body in a constant state of alert, increasing the risk of inflammation.
Strain on the immune system: dental toxins weaken the immune system, making the body less able to fight infections or inflammation effectively. This encourages the development of chronic illness.
Links to organs: studies show that dental toxins can increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes and rheumatic conditions.

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.8.titel.text: The link between dental toxins and systemic illness

beschwerde.zahngifte.abschnitte.9.bloeck.text: Cardiovascular disease: chronic inflammation caused by dental toxins encourages plaque build-up in blood vessels, increasing the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Autoimmune conditions: dental toxins can overstimulate the immune system, triggering autoimmune reactions.
TMD (temporomandibular dysfunction): dental toxins can encourage muscle tension and uneven strain on the jaw joint, leading to headaches and tension.
Chronic fatigue: ongoing strain on the body from dental toxins is often linked to persistent exhaustion and difficulty concentrating.

Dental health and general health are closely linked. To prevent the diseases mentioned above from developing, it is crucial to identify and treat problems in the mouth at an early stage. Regular preventive care, such as dental cleaning and check-up appointments, plays a central role here. If you already have symptoms, please contact your dentist without delay.

beschwerde.zahngifte.faq.0.antwort.text: Yes, dental toxins can also be problematic for dental restorations and may threaten their durability or function. If dental toxins cause the gums to become inflamed, the foundation for restorations such as crowns, bridges or implants is weakened. The surrounding tissue loses stability, which can cause the restoration to become loose and, in the worst case, be lost.

Yes, dental toxins can cause pain both in the mouth and in other parts of the body. Many patients suffer from local toothache. This is triggered by dental toxins released through tooth decay, periodontitis or a dead tooth.
Dental toxins can irritate nerves, causing pain to radiate into neighbouring areas such as the jaw, temples and neck.
Muscle or joint pain is also recognised in dentistry as a possible consequence of dental toxins.

beschwerde.zahngifte.faq.2.antwort.text:
The causes of dental toxins can be treated well, especially if they are detected early. Depending on the cause, modern dentistry offers effective methods to restore dental health:
In the case of tooth decay, the affected area can be treated and the tooth restored with a filling or an inlay.
In the case of a dead tooth, the source of infection is removed through root canal treatment. If the tooth needs to be extracted, it can be replaced with an implant.

beschwerde.zahnschmelzdefekte.abschnitte.text: Enamel defects are damage to or malformations of tooth enamel, the outer protective layer of the teeth. Tooth enamel is the hardest tissue in the human body and protects the sensitive inner structures of the teeth from damage caused by chewing, cold, heat and chemical substances. Although extremely resilient, this enamel cannot regenerate itself. Damage to the enamel, whether caused by external influences or genetic factors, leads to increased tooth sensitivity and a higher risk of tooth decay or other dental conditions.
What are enamel defects?
There are various types of enamel defects, each with different underlying causes:
Hypoplasia: This is an underdevelopment or malformation of the enamel, usually caused by genetic factors. Affected teeth have a thinner or incompletely formed enamel layer from birth.
Erosion: Tooth erosion develops through frequent contact with acids that attack the enamel and gradually wear it away. This can be caused by acidic foods, drinks, or stomach problems such as reflux.

Wear: Mechanical wear of the enamel, for example through teeth grinding (bruxism) or incorrect brushing with too much pressure or a toothbrush that's too hard, gradually wears down the protective layer and makes teeth more vulnerable to damage.
If you notice signs of enamel damage, you should not hesitate to book an appointment at KU64. Our experienced dentists will help you find the best treatment to protect your teeth in the long term.
Different types of enamel defects

Enamel defects should be treated early to prevent further damage to the teeth and protect dental health in the long term. There are various treatment options, chosen according to the severity of the defects and the underlying cause.
Treatment options for enamel defects

Fluoride is a proven way to strengthen tooth enamel and repair defects. In cases of enamel defects, regular fluoride treatments can help make the enamel more resistant to acid attacks and support the mineralisation process. Fluoride aids remineralisation by rebuilding important minerals within the enamel. At the dental practice, fluoride treatments are applied directly to the teeth in the form of gels or varnishes to give the enamel optimal protection.
Fluoride treatments and enamel strengthening

For enamel defects caused by bruxism (teeth grinding), using a dental splint is an effective way to protect the enamel. These special splints are worn at night and prevent the teeth from further wear caused by unconscious grinding. Dental splints act as a buffer, relieving pressure on the teeth, which can slow down or stop further enamel damage.
Dental splints and protective measures

If the enamel is already badly damaged and the defect affects deeper layers of the tooth, fillings or crowns may be needed to protect the affected teeth. Fillings are used to repair small to medium-sized defects, while crowns cover more extensive damage. Crowns provide stable protection by completely encasing the tooth, shielding it from further strain and wear. These measures are particularly important for preserving both the function and appearance of the teeth.
Fillings and crowns

Adjusting your diet is an important step in preventing enamel defects or stopping them from getting worse. Acidic foods and drinks in particular, such as fizzy drinks, citrus fruits and vinegar-based products, attack tooth enamel and should be reduced or avoided. In addition, eating sugary foods can encourage tooth decay, which further weakens already damaged enamel. A balanced diet rich in minerals such as calcium and phosphate supports the build-up and stability of tooth enamel.
Dietary adjustments

Preventing enamel defects starts with good oral hygiene and healthy habits. Brushing your teeth regularly and gently with a fluoride toothpaste strengthens the enamel and helps prevent tooth decay. The right brushing technique also matters, so as not to damage the enamel through too much pressure or a toothbrush that is too hard.

You should also cut down on highly acidic foods and drinks, such as fizzy drinks and citrus fruits, as these can attack tooth enamel. Drinking water after eating such foods helps neutralise the acids in your mouth. Regular dental check-ups and professional teeth cleaning also help detect and prevent enamel defects at an early stage.
Preventing enamel defects – act now!

If you notice signs of enamel defects, it is advisable to seek advice early on. Our experienced dentists at KU64 in Berlin offer thorough examinations to assess the condition of your enamel and put together an individual treatment plan for you.

From preventive measures such as fluoride treatment to advanced techniques for repairing damaged teeth – at KU64 you get solutions tailored to your dental health. We also offer other services such as dentures, professional preventive care and teeth cleaning. Treatments specially designed for children are part of our range as well. Our trained team creates a child-friendly environment where young patients feel well looked after.

The KU64 team in Berlin is available to you seven days a week. We offer professional diagnoses, detailed information on dental conditions, and tailored treatment options. Book an appointment today on 030 864 73 20 or contact us by email at info@ku64.de.

An enamel defect occurs when the tooth enamel – the outer protective layer of the tooth – is damaged or has not developed fully. This can be caused by external factors such as acids, or by genetic factors.
What is an enamel defect?
Symptoms include discolouration, rough patches or grooves on the teeth, and increased sensitivity to hot, cold or sweet food. An increased risk of tooth decay can also be a sign of enamel problems.
How do I recognise an enamel defect?
Causes include genetic factors, an acidic diet, teeth grinding (bruxism), poor oral hygiene, and certain medications that weaken tooth enamel.
What causes enamel defects?

It consists of the hardest substance in the human body and protects the sensitive inner layers of the tooth, such as the dentine and the nerve, from mechanical damage caused by chewing as well as from chemical influences such as acids in food and drink. Without sufficiently strong enamel, teeth are more prone to decay, wear and sensitivity. Once lost, enamel cannot regenerate itself, so it is important to protect it through good oral hygiene and a tooth-friendly diet.
What exactly is tooth enamel?
Unfortunately, once tooth enamel is lost, it cannot grow back on its own. However, there are treatments that help protect the remaining enamel and strengthen the tooth, such as fluoride treatments.
Can tooth enamel regenerate on its own?

Possible treatments include fluoride treatments to strengthen the enamel, fillings or crowns to protect damaged teeth, and dental splints for bruxism to prevent further damage. Dietary adjustments can also help prevent further enamel loss.
What treatment options are available for enamel defects?
Yes, because untreated enamel defects can lead to further problems such as tooth decay or tooth loss. Early diagnosis and professional treatment are essential to prevent serious damage.
Should I always see a dentist if I have enamel defects?

Genetic predisposition can play a decisive role in the development of enamel defects. Hereditary conditions such as amelogenesis imperfecta mean that enamel does not form correctly, or does not form at all. This leaves the teeth weaker and more easily damaged. Other genetic factors can also influence how resistant enamel is to outside influences, meaning some people are more prone to enamel defects than others.
1. Genetic factors

Inadequate oral hygiene leads to a build-up of plaque and bacteria on the teeth. These bacteria produce acids that attack and weaken the enamel. If plaque and tartar are not removed regularly, this leads over time to enamel defects that significantly reduce the protection of the teeth. Regular brushing and correct use of dental floss are essential to prevent this process.

Certain medications, such as antidepressants and antihistamines, or excessive exposure to fluoride, can encourage the development of enamel defects. Fluoride is beneficial for dental health in small amounts, but an overdose can lead to dental fluorosis, in which white spots or cracks appear in the enamel. Environmental factors such as high acid levels in drinking water or contact with harmful chemicals can also weaken the enamel.
3. Poor oral hygiene

Acidic food and drink, such as fizzy drinks, citrus fruits or sour sweets, attack the enamel directly, slowly eroding it. Frequent contact with acids makes it increasingly thin, which makes teeth more prone to decay and sensitivity. Drinking sugary beverages combined with inadequate oral hygiene is particularly problematic, as the acids can act on the teeth for longer.

Bruxism, meaning unconscious teeth grinding or clenching, is another cause of enamel defects. The constant pressure and friction of the teeth against each other wears down the enamel excessively. This often happens during sleep, so those affected frequently do not notice the problem until visible defects or sensitivity appear. Night guards can help protect the enamel and prevent further damage.
2. Diet and acidic food and drink

Enamel defects can show themselves in various ways. They not only affect the structure of the teeth but can also lead to functional problems. As enamel forms the outer protective layer of the teeth, damage to this tissue is particularly critical. The most common signs include visible changes to the tooth surface, increased sensitivity and greater susceptibility to decay. If you notice any of the following signs, please book an appointment at KU64 as soon as possible.

One of the first signs of enamel defects is a visible change to the tooth surface. This can appear as discolouration, grooves or rough patches. Affected areas are often darker or more yellowish, as the dentine underneath can show through once the enamel has worn away. Small notches and rough surfaces are also typical features of damaged enamel.

Enamel defects also increase the risk of tooth decay. Enamel normally offers effective protection against the bacteria and acids that cause decay. When this protective layer is damaged or worn away, bacteria can penetrate the tooth more easily and cause decay. This not only leads to further damage to the tooth but can also require extensive dental treatment to repair or preserve the affected teeth.

Another common symptom of enamel defects is increased sensitivity to pain. As enamel acts as a protective layer, its loss means that outside stimuli such as hot, cold or sweet food and drink reach the layers beneath directly, particularly the dentine. This can cause sudden, sharp pain, especially when eating and drinking.
Are you affected? Symptoms and signs

Early detection of enamel defects is crucial to prevent serious further damage. Using modern diagnostic methods, dentists can identify even the smallest changes to the enamel and take appropriate action. A thorough examination by a dentist is necessary to accurately assess the condition of the enamel and minimise the risk of further complications.
Diagnosing enamel defects

Enamel defects can be identified using various diagnostic techniques. First, a thorough visual examination is carried out, in which the dentist checks the condition of the tooth surface and looks for visible signs such as discolouration, grooves or rough patches. X-rays may be taken to obtain more detailed information. These allow a closer look at the structure of the teeth and help identify enamel defects or underlying damage that cannot be seen with the naked eye.
Dental examination

Regular visits to the dentist are essential for diagnosing enamel defects at an early stage. The sooner such defects are detected, the better the chances of taking steps to prevent the damage from progressing. Early diagnosis not only protects dental health but also reduces the need for invasive and costly treatment in future. It is therefore important to attend a dental check-up at least twice a year, so that any problems such as enamel defects can be identified early and treated in a targeted way.

beschwerde.zahnschmerzen.abschnitte.0.bl.text: Toothache can present itself in various ways and range widely in intensity: from a mild pulling or stinging sensation to intense throbbing pain.
